en: *Annotated Commentary on the Meaning and Text of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, Scroll One, composed by Shi Jingxing.
Regarding the title of the sūtra, "The Buddha Speaks the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, Volume One," the commentary states: Prior to expounding this sūtra, [the author] briefly provides...
There are three sections:
first, the intent of the introduction; second, the explanation of the names; third, the interpretation of the main text.
First, regarding the intent of the introduction, there are briefly three meanings:
First, it is to reveal the causes of the Pure Land.

That is to say, although the preceding sutra stated that the flowered seats were accomplished through the power of the vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, it had not yet been explained that the adornments of both the environment and the inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *sambhoga*) of Sukhāvatī were all accomplished through the power of the fundamental vows based on the accumulation of merit; therefore, it is now necessary to further explain in detail the forty-eight vows of his past lives to reveal the present causes of that land.
Second, it is because one wishes to demonstrate that the original vows are not in vain.

This means that although all Buddhas have made their original vows, there are instances where those original vows cannot be fully realized, such as the vow in the *Prajñāpāramitā* to bring all sentient beings to nirvāṇa.

The power of Dharmākara’s vows was not like this; therefore, he now extensively describes the adornments and purity of his primary and secondary merits to demonstrate that his past vows will certainly be fulfilled, thereby increasing the practitioners’ aspiration for rebirth there.
Third, it is because he wishes to demonstrate the suffering and affliction of the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*).

Although the *Contemplation Sūtra* states that all sentient beings of the future will be harmed and oppressed by the thieves of affliction (*kleśa*), if sentient beings do not hear of the specific characteristics of such pain and distress, they cannot give rise to the intention of longing for the pure land and loathing this world; thus, the karma for rebirth there would remain unaccomplished. Therefore, [the Buddha] now extensively proclaims the five evils and their agonizing torments as forms of harm, so that practitioners may come to loathe this realm of suffering and long for that region of bliss. By cultivating meritorious contemplative practices, they may swiftly depart from the Sahā world and be born in the Pure Land.
In their respective order, these refer to the two categories of those who have attained realization and those who are to be transformed.
For these three reasons, this sutra is taught immediately following the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra).

Second, regarding the explanation of the title: although the titles of the various editions of the scripture transmitted through successive dynasties have followed many different paths, I shall here first set forth the original title of the scripture from the Three Dynasties period.
During the Wei period, Bo Yanxian established the title *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing*;
during the Wu period, Zhi Qian established the designation *Zhufu amituo sanyesanyfo saloufutan guodu ren dao jing*, also known as the *Da amituo*;
and now, in the Western Jin, Dharmarakṣa names it the *Wuliangshou jing*.
Therefore, although the titles of the sutras differ in their brevity or detail, their essential meaning is largely the same.
To explain the title of Dharmarakṣa’s version of the sutra, there are four pairs of contrasts:
first, the contrast between the general and the specific; that is, "spoken by the Buddha" and the [general] name of the sutra are general, while the name "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) is specific.
Second, the correspondence between person and dharma: that is, "Buddha" refers to the person, while the remainder is termed "dharma.
Third, the correspondence between the expression and its meaning: that is, "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) is the meaning, while the "sūtra" is the expression;

this is because the discourse encompasses both. Fourth, the correspondence between beginning and end: that is, "above" is a term corresponding to "below," and "below" is likewise a term corresponding to "above," as they follow one another from beginning to end.
The meaning of "in detail" is as explained previously.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, “Thus have I heard,” the commentary says:
Third, the explanation of the main text.

Furthermore, there is a second approach that directly applies the fundamental vows and joyful fruits of Amitābha’s attainment of Buddhahood in his past life as a paradigm for the causes and effects of sentient beings’ birth [in the Pure Land].
Within this context, some say:
"This sutra extensively opens up ten aspects:"
First, from the beginning up to "at one time they assembled," is called the Section on the Introduction;
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One’s faculties were joyful and serene" onwards, is the Section on Manifesting Signs;
third, from "Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s holy command" onwards, is the Section on the Request for Instruction.
4. From "Then the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda" onwards is the section on the occasion of the discourse;
5. From "Ānanda, listen attentively; I shall now speak for you" onwards is the section on the formal exposition;
6. From "Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying" onwards is the section on successive births.
7. From "The Buddha said to Maitreya, 'Should there be those who hear this... onwards is the section on Encouraging Faith; 8.
From "At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this sutra-dharma... onwards is the section on Explaining the Benefits;
9. From "At that time, the trichiliocosm... onwards is the section on Solicitation.
10. "When the Buddha had finished speaking the sutra, there was no one who did not rejoice," and so forth; this constitutes the section on the conclusion and rejoicing (*parinirvāṇa-pramoda-bhāga*).
Although these ten sections have been presented in succession to explain the underlying meaning, they do not fully exhaust the principle; therefore, they are not included here.
What remains unfinished?

Since the Tathāgata manifests signs to reveal the holy teaching, the dharma-gates he expounds ought to be designated by their proper names; why, then, do you speak of them as "portions of manifested signs"?
If what is spoken were not the *nidāna* (introductory section) of the arousal [of the teaching], whom would Ānanda have witnessed?
If it is not a *samyaksampratyaya-nidāna* (section for attesting to faith), it cannot possibly be called the *nidāna* because it belongs to the *vibhaṅga* (analytical exposition) portion.
Furthermore, since the World-Honored One’s faculties have never before been so joyful as they are now, why is it that this section is titled "The Section on the Introductory Exposition" (*nidāna*)?
It cannot be designated by a name derived from being combined with something else; the title "Introductory Exposition" is established solely to certify the faith.
Furthermore, Ānanda poses the questions first and the Tathāgata provides the answers afterward; this clearly reveals the purport of what is being taught.
What could possibly be lacking? Having listened attentively, that which follows is called the "Correct Exposition."
Since the main exposition and the introduction cannot be distinguished, the intent of the subsequent sections would likewise become contradictory.
If it were as you say, then every chapter and segment should constitute a separate division, for such divisions are not limited to ten.
Some say: This sūtra text is divided into three parts;
from the beginning, "Thus have I heard," up to "I wish to hear with joy," constitutes the introduction (nidāna).
The section beginning with "The Buddha told Ānanda, 'In the distant past... constitutes the *zhengzongfen* (the main body of the teaching);
the section beginning with "The Buddha said to Maitreya, 'If there are those who hear it... constitutes the *liutongfen* (the dissemination of the teaching).
First, the introduction has two parts:
first, "Thus have I heard," which is the *samyakpratyaya-nidāna* (序分 of authentication);
second, from "At one time the Buddha" onwards, as it encompasses both meanings, it corresponds to the *nidāna of origination* (*pratyanubhava-nidāna*) by reference to the former.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, identifying the principal emanator;
second, identifying the retinue.
Third, it is not the case that the Tathāgata manifested a sign and Ānanda submitted a request.
If Ānanda’s request were the initiator [of the discourse], then the Buddha’s response to Ānanda would not constitute the primary teaching (samyag-mūla).
If the response pertains to the main body of the teaching (*samyak-deśanā*), the question must necessarily not be the introduction (*nidāna*).
Examining various sūtras and śāstras, we find that what is termed a "response" refers to the formal exposition, which invariably addresses the question.
Although a question may serve as an introductory catalyst, there is no precedent for a response that constitutes the main body of the teaching while the question remains merely introductory.
Furthermore, regarding time, place, and so forth, they should be understood according to the *Śraddhā-pratipatti* (The Section on Faith). Is it not the case that my inquiry is thus?
For both the "Initiation" (*utthāna*)—whether referring to what was heard or to the Buddha—are said to have preceded [the discourse].

Moreover, to specify the time, the Buddha, and the location as defining the Teacher of the transformation would also contradict the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which comprehensively reveals the five meanings beginning with "what was heard."
Now, observing this single scripture, it should be divided into three parts:
first, from "Thus have I heard" up to "his radiant countenance was majestic," which is titled the Section on the Causes and Occasion for Preaching the Sūtra;
second, from "Venerable Ānanda" down to "only briefly explained," which is titled the Section on the Extensive Exposition through Question and Answer.
Subsequently, from the passage beginning with "The Buddha spoke to Maitreya" up to "all were filled with joy," this section is named the "Division on Questioning, Explaining, and Rejoicing.
Regarding the intent behind these three chapters, the explanation is identical to that in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
The first part also has two sections:
first, the section on transmitting the Dharma and exhorting faith;
second, the introduction to the inspiration of the holy teaching.
At the beginning, there are furthermore five [elements]:
"Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). This is the primary transmission of the Dharma.
Bo Yan and Zhi Qian both lacked this phrase; however, Dharmarakṣa’s preserved translations maintain it, as their wording accords with Indian tradition.
Regarding the phrase "at one time" in the Sūtra, the commentary states:
This is second, the transmission of the time.
Regarding the word "Buddha" in the Sūtra, the commentary states:
This is the third, the transmitter.
As for the scripture’s statement, “In Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain,” the commentary says:
This is the fourth, the place of transmission.
If one were to explain these four passages, they would be identical to the preceding sutra; therefore, there is no need for further elaboration.
As for the sutra’s statement, “Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus,” the commentary says:
Fifth, the transmission of the capacity [to receive the teaching].
The various versions of the sutra differ; Bo Yan provides a complete enumeration of the three assemblies:

first, the assembly of śrāvakas, namely "the great assembly of disciples consisting of one thousand two hundred and fifty persons, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seven thousand upāsakas, and five hundred upāsikās";
second, the assembly of bodhisattvas, namely "seventy nayutas of bodhisattvas."

Third, the assembly of devas consists of eighty thousand sons of the desire realm (*kāmadeva*), seventy thousand sons of the form realm (*rūpadeva*), sixty nayutas of sons of the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, and one hundred million Brahmās.
Zhi Qian mentions only the assembly of śrāvakas, namely "the great bhikṣu-saṃgha of twelve thousand people.
In this present translation by Dharmarakṣa, only two assemblies—the bhikṣus and the bodhisattvas—are briefly mentioned; all others are absent.

The reason for these variations between the complete and the abbreviated versions is that the translators' preferences regarding the extent of detail differed; this is the source of their differences.
Regarding the explanation of the assembly of listeners (*śrāvaka*), there are two parts: first, the assembly of *śrāvakas*; [second, the assembly of bodhisattvas].
Subsequently, regarding the assembly of Bodhisattvas:
the sequence of this assembly is also to be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are five initial categories:
This first section indicates the practice.

As stated in the *Dharmapada-śāstra*: "Regarding the śrāvaka, because he cultivates the practices of the Hīnayāna and sustains himself by means of begging and so forth, his deportment is fixed and differs from that of a bodhisattva; therefore, he is designated by the name 'bhikṣu'."
Regarding the scriptural passage "twelve thousand people together," the commentary states:
"This is the second [instance of] announcing a number.

That treatise also says: "'Accomplishment of number' refers to the fact that the great assembly is incalculable; although there are differences between the general and the specific, their meaning is one and the same."

As for Bo Yan’s mention of "one thousand two hundred and fifty people," this is a brief enumeration of the regular assembly and does not exhaust all members; thus, it is not in contradiction [with the scriptures].
Regarding the scripture’s statement, "All great sages have already attained supernatural powers (abhijñā)," the commentary states:
This is the third [section], praising their virtues.
"All" (*sarva*) refers to the expression of universal pervasiveness reaching the ultimate limit.
"Great Sage" (*mahāmuni*) refers to the virtue of realizing the principle, for his fame reaches both the mundane and the sacred.
As the Treatise says: "Attaining mastery of mind and reaching the other shore—this is its greatness."
"Supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to the name for the sixfold supernormal knowledges; it carries the meaning of being unobstructed and unfathomable.

"Already" (*ita*) means "completed," and "attained" (*prāpta*) carries the sense of "realization through direct witness," because one has fully realized and witnessed them all through the six supernormal powers.

Some say: "Since Ānanda was still at the stage of a learner (śaikṣa), although he had not yet attained supernatural powers (abhijñā), he possessed superior virtues and was thus called 'one who has already reached [the goal]';
this is incorrect.
Ānanda was a person whose character was beyond the comprehension of ordinary people;

in fact, as the Sūtra states: "Although his outward manifestation was that of a Stream-enterer, even at the stage of a Stream-enterer he had suppressed the obstacles of desire and attained the fundamental dhyāna."

"Even if they have not yet exhausted all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya), since they have already manifested the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), it is reasonable to say that they have reached [the goal] based on their predominant qualities;
there is nothing at all to be wondered at. The Sūtra says: 'Their names were Venerable Ajita-Kauṇḍinya' up to 'Venerable Ānanda. The commentary states:
This is the fourth section, the listing of names."

Because the order in which assemblies are listed in various sūtras is not fixed, there are instances where the sequence follows the relative magnitude of their conduct and virtues; for example, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Kāśyapa is placed second, while Śāriputra is listed after Kātyāyanas and others.

Alternatively, some take the sequence of his renunciation as the chronological order: as in the *Sutra on Repaying Kindness*, he first ordained the five bhikṣus; next, he ordained the fifty disciples of Yaśas; next, he ordained the five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; next, he ordained the three hundred disciples of Gayā-Kāśyapa; next, he ordained the two hundred disciples of Nadī-Kāśyapa; next, he ordained the one hundred disciples of Śāriputra; and finally, he ordained the one hundred followers of Maudgalyāyana.

Alternatively, there are those who establish the sequence based on their virtues and eloquence; for instance, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, one inquires after the illness by means of their life-force, as it requires the employment of wisdom and eloquence to respond to such an inquiry.

In this present sutra, however, the sequence follows that of entering the holy stages (*ārya-mārga*) as in the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness). Bo Yan listed thirty-six names, while Zhi Qian and Dharmarakṣa both designated thirty-one, because Kauṇḍinya was placed at the beginning.

Zhi Qian referred to him as "the worthy one" (xianzhe), while Dharmarakṣa called him "the venerable one" (zunzhe); both are terms of praise for his virtue, equivalent in meaning to the "Great Sage" (dasheng).
As for "one who has realized the ultimate limit" (liaobenji), this is what Zhi Qian translated as *Kūlin* (拘隣).
In Sanskrit, his name is Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya. Kauṇḍinya is a Brahmin clan name; "nya" is a masculine suffix, and "Ajñāta" means "one who has understood.
He was the first to understand the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa), and it is also said that he had already attained understanding; for this reason, he is known as "The First Understanding" (Ajñāta).
The clan name Kauṇḍinya was also very common; he was designated by this title because of his realization.
To distinguish him from women, the term "na" (male) was added.
What is now called the "original limit" (pūrvakoṭi) refers to the true nature of the Four Noble Truths.
One who has "comprehended" (liao) is one who understands; thus, although the expressions differ, their meaning is one and the same.
As for "Zhengyuan" (正願), it is what Qian (謙) calls "Bazhi" (拔智); this is likely the name "Badai" (拔提).
Some say that because the horse trainer (Aśvajit) made a vow never again to visit the homes of others as a result of the rules for expulsion, he subsequently attained arhatship;
however, this is likely incorrect.

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is impossible for the horse trainer Pūrṇa, whose body manifested the marks of a nāga, to have been born among them; for there is no such case as one who has attained the fruit of arhatship yet receives the body of an animal.
Some say that Right Speech (samyag-vāc) is Piṅgalavatsa; this is incorrect.
That person was of a wicked nature and used coarse language; although he had attained arhatship, his residual habits remained, and it is therefore impossible to say that he possessed Right Speech.

The present treatise refers to him as Mahānāma, which means "Right Speech" (Sanskrit: *samyag-vāk*); this was likely his personal name, while Bo Yan referred to him as "the worthy one capable of praise."
Regarding the "Great Proclamation," the treatise states that the "Virtuous One Who Contained a Corpse" was likely Revata.

This man maintained the precept of non-false speech; because he witnessed a dispute between spirits, he substituted his own body for a corpse and consequently ascended to the throne. His virtue and fame thus spread throughout all quarters.

As for "Benevolent and Wise" (Renxian), Paramārtha translates it as "Must-Full" (Xuman); this means that while harboring virtue and goodness within, one manifests benevolence and kindness without, and thus he was named accordingly.
As for "Free from Defilement" (Lijou), Paramārtha translates it as "Vimala"; this refers to the purification and removal [of impurities].

The *Sūtra on the Account of Past Events* states that Cunda swept and purified the monastery, vowing that his mind might be free from dust and defilement just as the monastery was; therefore, it is called "purifying and removing" (*jìngchú*).
Since "purifying and removing" and "leaving behind defilement" (*lígòu*) differ in expression but are identical in meaning.
Regarding the term "Yashas" (Renowned):
some say that because the Brahmin Dīrghanakha was widely known for his extensive learning throughout the ten directions, he is called "Yashas.
This is likely incorrect, as it contradicts the *Sūtra on the Account of Past Events* (*Mahāvadānasūtra*), and there is no other basis upon which this interpretation could be relied.
Now, according to that sutra, the Venerable Yajñeya is named Yaśas because his pure brahmacarya is honored by all.

As for Subhūti, he was originally the elder Gṛhapati, named Śubhadatta; because he made offerings to the stupa of the Buddha Vipaśyin and thereafter was constantly reborn among gods and humans for ninety-one kalpas, he eventually attained arhatship.
"Endowed with" refers to what was stated in the *Mūlapariyāya* concerning Jyotiṣka: "Venerable sir, may I receive the full ordination and become fully endowed as a śramaṇa."
The "Ox-King" (Go-rāja) is Guhyapāda, which means "Ox-Aspect" (*go-lakṣaṇa*); he is called "King" merely as a mark of excellence.
In Sanskrit he is called Uluvilva, which means "wood-apple" (*kapittha*); this is because a single protuberance like a wood-apple fruit arose upon his chest.
The current term "Uruvilvā" is a corruption.
"Gayā" refers to Elephant Head Mountain (Gajapṛṣṭha), as it is the name of the specific location.
In Sanskrit it is called Nadi; the *Sūtra of Adornment* calls it Nandi, which is the name of a river.
These three Kāśyapas were all brothers of the Bhṛgu (Drinking-Light) clan.

In the *Póyán jīng* (Baiyan jing), there is additionally mentioned the "Worthy Clan Kāśyapa" (*Xiànzhěshì jù Kāshēyè*), which likely refers to the Sañjayī Kāśyapa mentioned in the *Shuōběnqǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Exposition of Past Events). It should be noted that the *Zūnjù jué jīng* (Sūtra on the Fully Awakened Honored One) omits the "Clan" (*shì*) and "Gathering" (*jù*) and subsequently refers to him as the "Cowherd" (*niúsì*). Thus, [the name] here is complete.
Since there is no definitive explanation and two paths have been opened, scholars should understand that the choice between them is left to one's own discretion.
In Sanskrit he is called Kāśyapa, which here means "Drinker of Light" (Drinking-Light); this is a Brahmin clan name.
In ancient times there were immortals whose bodies possessed a radiance that could eclipse the light of the sun and moon.
Kāśyapa was of this lineage; he himself also possessed light capable of eclipsing the sun and moon, and thus he inherited the name of his ancestral nature.
"Mahā" means "great. Since he was the son of a wealthy elder of great means and was also recognized by great men, his name is prefixed with "Great" to distinguish him from the other three.
In Sanskrit, his name is Śāriputra; "Śāri" refers to the śārikā bird, which is the hundred-tongued bird, also known as the spring warbler.
Potalaka was the son of a woman whose eloquence was like that of a śāri bird; because he was her son, he was named after her, and thus he is called Śāriputra.
To call him "Śāriputra" is an error.
In Sanskrit he is called Mahāmaudgalyāyana, which translates here as "Great Mung-bean Gatherer.
In ancient times there was a rishi who dwelt in a secluded mountain retreat; he constantly gathered mung beans (mudga) to sustain himself, and thus that became his clan name.
The Venerable One’s mother belonged to that clan, and he was named after it.
Because he attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and distinguished himself from the rest of that lineage, he is also called "Great" (*Mahā*).
As for the name "Maudgalyāyana," it is a corruption of the original sound.

Kapphiṇa means "Lunar Mansion of the Room" (Hōshuku); because the Buddha shared the same room with him as a lunar mansion, he manifested as an old bhikṣu to preach the Dharma for him, whereby he attained enlightenment.
In Sanskrit it is called Mahākātyāyana; here it means "one of the Great Shaving Lineage," which is a Brahmin clan name.

In ancient times there were many sages who dwelt in quiet places in the mountains. As years passed and their beards and hair grew somewhat long, people would shave them for them, because it is the custom of the Brahmins to practice the shaving of the hair.

A certain seer had two sons who both came to visit their father. The younger son had his hair shaved by the various seers, who vowed to protect him; later he attained the nobility of a seer. From that time on, this lineage has been called "the Shaved" (Jianti).

"Those who have shaved their heads" refers to men whose physical presence and majestic virtue are exceptionally honored; they are distinguished from other such types, hence they are called "men of the great tonsured lineage.
The ancient name Kātyāyana is translated here as "Rope-Fan," which is a corruption.
The present term "Great Abiding" (Dazhu) likewise inherits the name from antiquity.
Because the mother was so attached to this son that she refused to remarry—like a fan tied with a cord—it may be said that he "abided."
The one of Great Pure Resolve was Rāṣṭrapāla in the *Sūtra on the Past Deeds*.
Having no other delight, he resolved upon the joy of the pure and white dharmas; as he was foremost in dwelling in seclusion, he was named Mahāśubhamati (Great Pure Resolve).
Mahācunda is Cunda-bhaṭṭa, which is translated here as Lusheng (Road-born).
Since there were both a senior and a junior Lusheng, the prefix Mahā was used to distinguish him from the junior one.
In Sanskrit, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, which in Chinese is translated as Mǎnzīzǐ (Son of Maitrāyaṇī).
To call him Fúlóunmǐduōluóní zǐ (Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra) is an error.
Pūrṇa is his personal name, and Maitrāyaṇī is his mother’s clan name.
Since his mother’s clan is Maitrāyaṇī, the Venerable Pūrṇa is the son of a daughter of Maitrāyaṇī; thus he was named accordingly.
The current appellation "Son of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇī" is an error.
In Sanskrit he is called Aniruddha, which here means "Unextinguished. He was the Buddha’s maternal cousin and was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
The present expression "free from hindrances" carries the same meaning.
The name "Anuruddha" is a corruption [of the original].
As for "Liuguan" (Flowing Irrigation), some say it refers to Revata; since this is translated as "artificial combination," it is called "Liu-li" (Flowing Separation).
This is likely not the case.
Since it is not a name apart from the character "zi" (字),
and since Qian also says it is "Nanti," this must be the name Nanti found within the *Shuobenyi* (說本起).
In Sanskrit he is called Sundarananda; here it is translated as "Glorious Joy. "Joy" (Nanda) is his own name, while "Glorious" (Sundara) is the name of his wife.
To distinguish him from Nanda the Cowherd, his name is designated by means of his wife's name.
He was the Buddha’s own younger brother, born of the Great Sage King.
Because he had offered a warm bathhouse during the era of Vipaśyin Buddha, he possesses such upright beauty and great power that one never tires of beholding him.
The current mention of "flowing and irrigating" is likewise an adoption of that [previous] name.

As for "firmly submissive," this refers to Jyotiṣka in the *Sūtra on the Exposition of Past Events*; that sūtra states: "Firm in vigor and concentrated in mind, because it is unconditioned and immovable. Bo Yan also said: "The worthy one has realized profound concentration."
As for "Face-King" (Mianwang), Zhi Qian translated it as the "Venerable Pāṭala.
In Sanskrit it is called Bakula, which means "Fine Countenance" (Shanrong).
Although there are many such [names] meaning "fine countenance," because the face is primary among them, it is given the interpretive name "Face-King."
Regarding "those of a different vehicle" (yisheng): this refers to what Bo Yan called the "Venerable Śīla-skandha.
Because his observance of the precepts was exceptionally eminent, he is described as being of a "different vehicle.

Regarding "the nature of benevolence" (renxing): this corresponds to Śrīra in the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising). That sutra states: "He bestowed wealth and property to rescue those who were impoverished and to aid the lowly and inferior."
"Jiālè" (嘉樂) refers to Nanda in the *Benqǐ* (本起), whose name means "Delight.
Zhī Qiān also transcribed it as "Nánchí" (難持); the correct pronunciation is Nanda, which here means "Excellent Root" (嘉本).

He was originally a cowherd who, by questioning the Buddha on eleven matters concerning the tending of cattle, realized that the Buddha possessed all-encompassing wisdom and attained the state of an Arhat;
this was because he was exceedingly intelligent and his voice was most exquisite.
The term "Jiālè" (嘉樂) is likewise not a direct translation [of the original].
As for "Shànlái" (善來), Zhi Qián translated it as Xiánzhě Cǎijié (賢者蔡揭), while the *Benqǐ* (本起) also renders it as Huòjié (貨竭).
The tradition states that the Sanskrit term *svāgata* is translated as "Welcome.
"Coming" (*lai*) means "to return"; because there is great benefit in returning to the Buddha and the Dharma, it is called "Welcome."

The term "Welcome" (svāgata), though it generally refers to the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples, is established as a collective designation; thus, there are no individual titles.
The constant retinue of the Tathāgata all received the precepts through the "Welcome" formula, as described in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*.
In Sanskrit he is called Rāhula, which here means "Moon-Grasper"; the current name Lóuyún (Rāhula) and Yánbó’s rendering "Born in the Royal Palace" are both corruptions.
In Sanskrit he is called Ānanda, which here means "Joyous Celebration"; the current name Ānán and Yánbó’s rendering "Extensive Learning" are both abbreviated forms.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “All such as these are the foremost,” the commentary says:
This is the fifth point, a brief conclusion.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “Furthermore, together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna,” the commentary says:
Second, there are four categories of the bodhisattva assembly;
this first [section] indicates their practice.
As stated in the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, a bodhisattva cultivates the great practice, seeks awakening to benefit sentient beings, and takes "sattva" as its defining characteristic.
Furthermore, by the power of their supernormal faculties, they manifest at appropriate times as being able to practice the Mahāyāna.

For instance, the sixteen individuals such as Bhadrapāla and others, who were fully endowed with the inconceivable deeds of bodhisattvas, manifested in the forms of the four assemblies, including laymen (*upāsaka*), and were declared to be bodhisattvas.
According to the seventy *nayuta* of Bodhisattvas mentioned by Bhadrapāla, the fact that they are not all spoken of here is due to the brevity [of this text].
The passage from "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" to "all Bodhisattvas" is described as:
second, the enumeration of names.
There are two [types];
this first one refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa.
"Universal" (pu) means all-pervasive; it is the wisdom that realizes the truth.
"Worthy and virtuous" refers to conduct engaged with worldly affairs.
Because his inner virtues are universal and his outward transformation is worthy and good, he is named Samantabhadra.
As for "Wondrous Virtue," it should properly be called Mañjuśrī.
"Śrī" (Auspicious) signifies merit; its meaning is "Wondrous Virtue.
As for "Maitreya," he first conceived the aspiration for enlightenment under the Buddha Maitreya and was also born into the Maitreya clan; therefore, he is called Maitreya.
In Sanskrit it is called *Veda*, which here means "good"; thus it is also named the "Good Kalpa" (*Bhadrakalpa*), as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
As for the term "Worthy One" (*Bhadra*), this is simply its name from the present time onward.
The duration and brevity of the kalpas, as well as the number of Buddhas, are explained in detail in the *Commentary on the Maitreya Sūtra*.
Regarding the passage in the sūtra from "Furthermore, Bhadrapāla and others" up to "the Bodhisattvas of Liberation," the commentary states:
"These are the bodhisattvas of the subsequent remaining kalpas."
Regarding those who say there are sixteen noble beings (*satpuruṣa*) beginning with "the Worthy" (*ārya*), the term "beginning" is used to encompass the subsequent ones as a general designation;
the terms "skillful reflection" (*sukalpa*) and so forth are listed individually according to their respective equivalents.
This is likely not the case.

If "those who have well-considered [the Dharma]" and so forth were identical to the sixteen noble beings (*satpuruṣa*), one should have spoken of fifteen noble beings; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the enumeration and the specific designations.
Even if one were to grant this, it would contradict the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, which states: "The sixteen bodhisattvas such as Bhadrapāla.

Since the names such as Susamīkṣita differ from the names of the sixteen bodhisattvas in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, one can by no means claim that Susamīkṣita and the others are identical to the sixteen noble sons (*satpuruṣa*).

Some say that Bhadrapāla and the others are themselves two bodhisattvas; thus, they pervade the sixteen noble men (*satpuruṣa*). Because they possess the virtue of being "worthy and benevolent" internally, they are called "Worthy Men" (*xianshi*); because they harbor the intention to protect sentient beings externally, they are called "Protective Intent" (*huyi*).
This is also not the case.
Bhadrapāla—here translated as Xiangu (賢護, "Worthy Protector")—is divided into two [entries], which would necessarily be contradictory.
Furthermore, since Samantabhadra and the others each have their own distinct names, Xiangu should not be the name of two different bodhisattvas.

Some say: although sixteen numbers are indicated, fifteen names are listed with one missing, as the *Dharmadeśanā-sūtra* states: "There were two bodhisattvas, the first named Bhadrapāla and the second named Sarvalokapriyadarśana."
This is also not the case.

Since those [Bodhisattvas] are only two, whereas these are sixteen, they cannot be listed as one; furthermore, it is not the case that all Bodhisattvas appearing in various sūtras after Bhadrapāla must be included within this number of sixteen.
Now, regarding the Bodhisattvas of other kalpas, there are naturally two categories; thus, the sixteen virtuous ones such as Bhadrapāla and others constitute one category.
Some say that each of the sixteen great kingdoms had one of them, and therefore there are sixteen.
No. It is because there must logically be many Bodhisattvas within a single land;
yet there is only one [Buddha] per land, as there is no reason for there to be more than one.

Now, because these sixteen vows share similar characteristics in their manifestation, the holy teachings everywhere designate them by the number sixteen. They are fully equipped with inconceivable matters, manifesting transformations in accordance with sentient beings; this is explained in detail in the *Commentary on the Maitreya Sūtra*.
The fourteen bodhisattvas, such as Susamīkṣaṇa and others, constitute these two categories.
Although there are fourteen, they can be briefly grouped into seven pairs:

first, the pair of *dharmacintaka* (one who contemplates the Dharma) and *adhimukta* (one who has resolute faith). This refers to Susamīkṣaṇa, who contemplates the teachings and follows the instructions with faith; this is called "faith-wisdom" (*śraddhā-prajñā*).

2. The Confrontation with Realizing Emptiness and Engaging with Existence: This refers to internally realizing the principle of emptiness, which is called "Emptiness-Non-existence" (Kongwu), because one employs supernatural powers to travel and transform within all that has names (existence).

3. The Confrontation of Great Compassion and Great Wisdom: This refers to the torch of compassionate light, which is called "Light-Flower" (Guangying), because the faculty of wisdom is unsurpassed, which is called "Wisdom-Supreme" (Huishang).

4. Regarding the pairing of self-benefit and benefit for others: practicing the path to enlightenment is called the "Wisdom Banner" (*jñānaketu*), because guarding the sense faculties is termed "tranquil faculties" (*śāntendriya*).

5. Regarding the pairing of the name of the Dharma and the name of the metaphor: that which possesses aspiration and wisdom is the "Dharma," while the "Fragrant Elephant" (*gandhahastin*) is the metaphor.

Sixth, the correspondence between the equipment of merit and the equipment of wisdom: that which is fully equipped with the equipment of merit is called "Jewel Excellence" (*ratnottama*), while being endowed with the equipment of wisdom is called "Abiding in the Middle" (*madhyastha*).

Seventh, the correspondence between practice and the removal of bonds: that which cultivates noble conduct is called "Restrained Conduct" (*vinīta-vṛtta*), and the extinguishing and removal of the two bonds is called "Liberation" (*vimukti*).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "All follow Samantabhadra" to "the dharmas of merit," the commentary states:
This is the third section, praising his virtues.
It consists of two parts:
First, the virtue of being fully equipped with both the provisional and the ultimate;
second, the practice of benefiting both oneself and others.
Regarding the first, there are three further points:
First, a brief praise;
second, an extensive praise;
and finally, a concluding praise.
The first section further has two parts;
this is the first: praising his actual virtues.
"One who follows the virtue of Samantabhadra" refers to one who cultivates the practices of the higher stages.
"One who possesses the practices and vows of a bodhisattva" means that they are fully equipped with the vows of the lower stages.
"One who abides in the dharma of merit" means that they have clearly distinguished the dharma of their own station.
"To follow" (zun) means to track or to accord with.
Samantabhadra is one who, based upon suchness (tathatā), is fully endowed with all virtuous practices and thus bears the title of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).
Therefore, those such as Bhadrapāla, by adhering to the virtues of the Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, are known to occupy the rank of the Dharma-cloud Stage (dharmameghā-bhūmi).

"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to the practices of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), the maturing of sentient beings, and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to vast wisdom.

In the sutras, one knows all dharmas; having obtained the boat of prajñā and encountered the wind of wisdom, and having attained skillful means, one ferries all people across the great ocean of suffering, attains the perfection of the Way, ascends the mountain of nirvāṇa, enters the house of the unconditioned, and realizes the ten vows of the dharma-nature body.

Without the practice of aspiration, one sinks into the sea of suffering; without the aspiration for practice, there is likewise nothing to ripen. Therefore, the complete integration of both practice and aspiration may be called the path to bodhi.
"Merit" (kung) refers to functional capacity.

Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess the merit of benefiting the state, they constitute the virtues of those who practice goodness; thus, they are called "meritorious qualities" (*guṇa*).
Since these qualities must be perfected, it is said that they are "all-encompassing."
Because they have attained perfect completion, it is said that they "abide securely.
The Sūtra states, "They traverse the ten directions, practicing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)," which the commentary explains as follows:
following this, there is a praise of the virtue of skillful means.
"Stepping" refers to walking.
His physical manifestations are unimpeded, and there is nothing that his response does not reach; thus it is said he "wanders through the ten directions.
His transformative actions are skillful, and there is no form in which he does not appear; thus it is said he "exercises provisional means."
Regarding the scriptural passage, "Entering the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and reaching the ultimate other shore," the commentary states:
Second, the extensive praise.
This has two parts:
This first [verse] praises his true virtues.
Some say: "Entering the treasury of the Buddha-dharma" proclaims the ascent through causes, while "reaching the ultimate other shore" manifests the finality of the fruit.

The claim that the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the Tathāgatagarbha are called the "Dharma-treasury of the Buddha," that "entering" refers to realization and comprehension, and that "reaching the shore of nirvāṇa" refers to the ultimate state—
this is likely not correct.

The Tathāgatagarbha is synonymous with the meaning of Buddha-nature; therefore, to claim that realizing and attaining merits and dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constitutes "ascending due to causes" contradicts the sūtra which states, "When one sees the Buddha-nature, one attains unsurpassed enlightenment."
If the realization of Buddha-nature were not the fruit of Bodhi, then reaching the shore of Nirvana would likewise not be the fruit of Parinirvāṇa.

Since one who now enters has attained ultimate understanding and realized comprehension—knowing reality as it is for the sake of self-benefit and accomplishing the benefit of others—it is said that they have entered the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha.
This refers to "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom and attaining great insight" as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"The other shore" (*pāra*) signifies ultimate truth; because one realizes this true nature, it is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*).
This refers to "reaching the other shore" within that very sutra.
Because he constantly illuminates the two truths to benefit both himself and others, he may be said to possess true virtue.
As the sutra says, "Manifesting the attainment of equal enlightenment in immeasurable worlds," the commentary states:
Following this, there is an extensive praise of the virtue of expedient means (*upāya*).
This section has two parts;
this first part is a general praise.
Some say: "Because each and every bodhisattva attains buddhahood and manifests through transformation-birth within a single realm, it is called 'immeasurable worlds.
This interpretation is not correct."

If the scope of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) already extends to a hundred Buddha-worlds, how much more so for the worlds where a Bodhisattva of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) transforms sentient beings—how could they possibly be counted?
Therefore, the claim that each dwells within a single world-system is certainly not the correct principle.
Now, each and every bodhisattva manifests transformations within immeasurable worlds; therefore, they manifest the attainment of equal enlightenment within immeasurable worlds.
As for the passage in the Sūtra stating, "Dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, he extensively proclaims the True Dharma," the commentary says:
this follows and is a separate eulogy.
There are nine:
first, relinquishing this life to ascend to heaven;
second, descending in spirit to enter the womb;
Third, the extraordinary manner of his birth from the womb;
fourth, his mastery of all arts and sciences;
fifth, his demonstration of skills and his taking of a wife;
Sixth, departing from the mundane and following the heterodox;
seventh, subduing Māra and achieving enlightenment;
eighth, universally moistening all with the transformation of the Dharma.
9. Returning to Truth to Benefit Beings.
This is the first [section].
"Dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven" refers to ascending to that heaven.
Those who widely proclaim the True Dharma transform and perfect the assembly of devas.
The Brahmā and Tuṣita devas— *Tuṣita* here being translated as "Heaven of Joyful Contentment"—
are those among whom all Bodhisattvas are born, for all Buddhas constantly practice the Middle Way.

As the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states: "He once followed one hundred billion nayuta koṭi Buddhas into the homeless life; he once practiced great giving in the presence of fifty hundred billion nayuta koṭi Buddhas; he has already drawn near to three hundred and fifty koṭi pratyekabuddhas; and he has already taught and transformed immeasurable asaṃkhyeya śrāvaka assemblies, causing them all to abide in right skillful means, so that, desiring to realize unsurpassed enlightenment, he may proceed to the stage of being born only once more before buddhahood."
When his life there ended, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven as a son of the gods named Śuddhadhvaja.

Hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sons of the gods gathered in the Dharma Hall; surrounding the Bodhisattva, they listened to and received the unsurpassed Great Dharma he preached, severing all afflictions and giving rise to a vast mind.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “Leaving that celestial palace, he descended into his mother’s womb,” the commentary states:
This is the second [event], the descent of the spirit into the womb.
Desiring to cause sentient beings to give rise to a mind of reverence and to easily receive what is taught, he leaves the celestial palace to descend into the womb.
That sutra states: "Twelve years before the Bodhisattva was about to descend to be born, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven came down to Jambudvīpa and appeared as a Brahmin who expounded the Vedas."

Twelve years hence, a superior person shall appear, manifesting in the form of a white elephant as he enters his mother’s womb; endowed with the marks of a great man, if he renounces the world, he shall attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, a certain devaputra descended to Jambudvīpa and informed a pratyekabuddha:
"You should abandon this land; a bodhisattva is about to descend his spirit and enter a womb.

At that time, on Mount Vaipulya in Rājagṛha, there was a pratyekabuddha named Madhyama. Having heard these words, he rose up and leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees, where he manifested fire to incinerate his body and entered nirvana, leaving behind only his śarīra relics which fell from the sky.
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, five hundred pratyekabuddhas were likewise all thus.

When the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the celestial palace and observing the time, the country, and the clan, he ascended a great hall named High Banner (*Ucchrayadhvaja*), which was sixty-four *yojanas* in length and breadth, equal on all sides. For the sake of the assembly of devas, he expounded one hundred and eight Dharma-gates, beginning with the Dharma-gate of Faith and ending with the Dharma-gate of Empowerment (*Abhiṣeka*). From that celestial palace, he descended to be born and entered the womb.
On one occasion, a son of heaven named Jyotiṣprabha spoke thus:
"According to what is taught in the Vedas, when a Bodhisattva descends to be born, he shall take the form of an elephant and enter his mother's womb."

When the winter season had passed and it was the spring equinox during the month of Vaiśākha, at the conjunction of the lunar mansion Rohiṇī—a time neither cold nor hot—the white moon was full and pure, and the Puṣya constellation was in perfect alignment with the moon. While his mother was observing the pure fast and sleeping peacefully, he descended into her right side in the form of a white elephant, complete with six tusks, golden in color, with a crimson radiance upon its head; its physical features and sensory faculties were all perfectly formed, and with clear mindfulness and awareness, it entered her womb.
One should not raise the objection: "How can this be an explanation of the nine aspects when it is praising the virtues of the bodhisattvas?
For the eight aspects of Śākyamuni are themselves the supreme progression of all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, when the eight manifestations appear, each of the bodhisattvas manifests these signs individually; yet sentient beings, being similar in perception, regard them as one.

Therefore, what contradiction is there in citing that sūtra to explain the adornments of the World-Honored One and thereby elucidate this passage concerning the nine manifestations of the bodhisattva?

However, as the scriptural text is extensive and detailed, I fear it would be too cumbersome to discuss it at length; therefore, I shall now infer its meaning through concise language and align it with the sūtra to fully elucidate its principles.
Although the adornments of the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the womb are numerous, I shall briefly set forth three types:

first, the palace. That is to say, the various devas of the desire realm each brought exquisite palaces to King Śuddhodana; the king also constructed a magnificent palace for the Bodhisattva, the likes of which do not exist among humans.

By the power of the Bodhisattva, the bodies of Queen Māyā appeared within all the palaces; in each, the Bodhisattva was seen sitting cross-legged against her right side, while the various devas each claimed, "The Mother of the Bodhisattva dwells only in my palace."

The Bodhisattva’s precious palace was three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal in all dimensions. It was adorned with three tiers of enclosures, all fashioned from celestial ox-head sandalwood incense; a single portion of this incense was worth as much as a trichiliocosm.
The celestial palaces of all the heavens in the desire realm appear within the Bodhisattva’s palace.
Whenever he is about to enter the womb, this palace first manifests at his mother’s right side; subsequently, he descends from the heavens into the womb and sits cross-legged within this palace.

Second is the matter of food and drink: on the very night the Bodhisattva entered the womb, a lotus flower surged up from the depths of the water, piercing through the earth wheel and reaching as high as the Brahma world. It was sixty-eight *lakṣa* yojanas in both length and breadth, and none were able to see it except for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Great Brahma King.
All the exquisite flavors existing throughout the trichiliocosm, like ambrosia (*amṛta*), appeared within these flowers.
Mahābrahmā, using a vessel of vaidūrya, filled it with this pure and wondrous ambrosial flavor and offered it to the Bodhisattva, who accepted and partook of it.

Except for the Bodhisattva in his final existence who has reached the ultimate goal, no one is able to consume it; this is brought about by the karmic reward of having provided medicine to save the sick and offered exquisite flowers to serve the sages throughout the long night of saṃsāra.

Third, regarding the transformation of sentient beings: the radiance from the physical form of the Bodhisattva while in the womb pervades the entire world. The Four Great Heavenly Kings and their yakṣa generals with their retinues, Śakra-devānām-indra and the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, and Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, together with immeasurable hosts of Brahmā followers, all behold the Bodhisattva at dawn, midday, and the third watch of the day respectively, in order to hear the Dharma. The Bodhisattva comforts them, preaches the Dharma for them, and they pay their respects before withdrawing to depart.
At sunset, immeasurable bodhisattvas from the ten directions came to hear the Dharma and engaged in mutual dialogue; these were seen only by those of like practice, and Māyā was unable to see them.

Furthermore, according to that sutra, immeasurable Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) from the ten directions, as well as the devaputras of the desire and form realms from the worlds of the ten directions, all arrive at Tuṣita to make offerings to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva then descends from the most excellent celestial palace of Tuṣita; at that time, he emits light from his body that illuminates the three thousandfold world-system, which shakes in six ways with eighteen signs.
That which is absent now is merely an abbreviation.
As for the scripture stating, "born from the right side," the commentary says:
third, his emergence from the womb was extraordinary.
There are three [points]:
this first one concerns the unusual nature of the place of birth. Some say:
When ten months had passed, Māyā, riding in a cloud-crystal chariot, went to the Lumbinī Grove; there, grasping the branch of an *aśoka* tree, she gave birth from her right armpit.
This is not so, for upon examining the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, these words are nowhere to be found.

Now, when the Bodhisattva had completed his ten months in the womb and was about to emerge, the Queen-Mother became aware of it; during the first watch of the night, she requested the King that they go to the Lumbinī Garden. The King commanded his ministers and officials to prepare twenty thousand elephants—white as clouds in color and resembling celestial beings—along with an array of chariots and troops bearing weapons. They adorned the Lumbinī Garden with various exquisite jewels, making it like the Nandana Grove.

When the Noble Queen ascended the precious carriage, the world shook in six ways; Śakra purified the road, the Four Great Kings drove the chariot, and Brahmā went before her leading the way to clear away all inauspicious signs as they arrived at the garden for a stroll.

Upon reaching those jewel trees—where the mothers of immeasurable Buddhas of the past had all sat beneath these very trees—the hundreds of thousands of Śuddhāvāsa devas also arrived at the foot of this tree, surrounding the Noble Queen, greeting her with joy, prostrating, and offering praise.

The future Buddha emitted light from his body and looked up at the tree; he then reached out with his right hand and grasped an eastern branch of the tree. Stretching and yawning, he stood upright and majestic, emerging calmly from his mother’s right side.

Then Śakra and Brahmā, bowing their bodies forward, immediately covered the Bodhisattva with two hands using a *kauśeya* robe to receive and support him, and led the Bodhisattva’s palace back to the Brahma-heaven.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “manifestly taking seven steps” to “becoming the Unsurpassed Honored One,” the commentary states:
This sequence demonstrates that he does not possess the characteristics of ordinary beings.

Once born, the Bodhisattva required no support; he immediately took seven steps in each of the ten directions, and at every place where his feet touched the ground, lotus flowers sprang forth, and he was free from all fear. He took these seven steps because he wished to demonstrate the vigorous power of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) who transcends the six realms of existence.
Regarding "light illuminating the ten directions," this refers to the radiance of the body benefiting sentient beings.

In that sutra, the Bodhisattva emits light of immeasurable and diverse colors that fills the trichiliocosm; those sentient beings who encounter it find peace and joy in their hearts, distancing themselves from greed, anger, and delusion, and leaving behind all karmic obstacles.
Regarding the six kinds of earthquakes, they are intended to cause the Māras to be cowed and submit.
"Earthquake" (zhèn) means "to move.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there are three types of these six movements:
First, the six movements: these refer to entering the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving home, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvana.
The movement occurring now is that at the time of emerging from the womb.

Second, the six directions shook, meaning that the east surged while the west subsided; the west surged while the east subsided; the south surged while the north subsided; the north surged while the south subsided; the center surged while the periphery subsided; and the periphery surged while the center subsided.
Third, the six signs of movement, namely: shaking, surging, quaking, striking, roaring, and bursting.

To sway and flutter restlessly is shaking; to have ridges and hollows, highs and lows, is surging; to have a deep, rumbling sound is quaking; to be struck or tapped is striking; to produce a crashing resonance is roaring; to emit a startling and extraordinary sound is bursting.

Each of these has three aspects, termed the eighteen characteristics (*aṣṭādaśākāra*): namely, movement (*calana*), equal [movement] (*samudīraṇa*), and extreme movement (*paramasamudīraṇa*). The same applies to the remaining five [elements].
Among these, the six movements are the movements of the six characteristics; therefore, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states that the six movements possess eighteen characteristics.
To be called the "Unsurpassed Honored One" is to proclaim one's own title so that beings may take refuge and turn toward it.
To speak of it in full, the practice in the East is to say:
"I have attained all wholesome dharmas; I shall preach them for the sake of sentient beings."
In the south, he said:
"I am one who should receive offerings from devas and humans.
In the west, he said:
"I am the most honored and most supreme in the world.
In the north, he said:
"I shall be unsurpassed among all sentient beings."
In the direction below, he said:
"I shall subdue all the armies of Māra.
In the direction above, he said:
"I shall be one who is gazed upon by all sentient beings.
When the Bodhisattva spoke these words, his voice was heard throughout the entire trichiliocosm.
Although there are these differences, because they are all without exception the deeds of the World-Honored One, he is collectively called the Unsurpassed Honored One.

As that sutra says: "Because the Bodhisattva cultivated the power of diligence for incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of kalpas, at the moment of his birth, he was immediately able to take seven steps in each of the ten directions."
"The majestic power of all Buddhas pervades this ground, transforming it into vajra, so that when Bodhisattvas walk upon it, they do not sink or split.
The Sūtra says, "Śakra and Brahmā serve him, and devas and humans look up to him in refuge. The commentary states:
This clarifies that devas and humans attend upon and take refuge in him.
After the Bodhisattva was born, for seven days and seven nights in the Lumbinī Garden, humans and devas played various kinds of subtle and exquisite music as an offering to his honored countenance.
Thirty-two thousand brahmins of renowned and superior wisdom were all fully satisfied according to their needs.
King Brahmā and Śakra, having manifested themselves in the form of handsome māṇavas, sat upon the foremost seat within the assembly and performed auspicious and subtle praises.
Maheśvara and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven made great offerings and proclaimed that this bodhisattva would certainly attain buddhahood.
Upon returning to his original abode, seven days after his birth, Queen Mānasa passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
After seven days had passed, he returned to Kapilavastu with a grandeur and splendor that was twice as magnificent as when the Noble Queen had gone to the Lumbinī Garden.
Five hundred members of the Śākya clan each constructed a palace and invited the King, saying:
"Excellent, O Sarvārthasiddha!"
"May the God among Gods deign to visit my palace.
Because of these auspicious causes and conditions for his benefit, the Bodhisattva was named Sarvārthasiddha.

Out of compassion for the Śākyas, the King then led the Bodhisattva into the palaces of the Śākyas; after four months had passed and he had visited them all, he finally brought the Bodhisattva back to his own palace.

Within his palace was a great hall named Ratnavyuha. Once the Bodhisattva had been placed there, the King summoned the elders and virtuous leaders of his kinsmen and requested Mahāprajāpatī to serve as the Bodhisattva’s foster mother. The King personally took him in his arms and entrusted him to his maternal aunt; she then appointed thirty-two nurses to raise the Bodhisattva, who grew like the bright moon from the first day until the fifteenth day, becoming pure and full.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "manifesting calculation" to "mastering the various scriptures," the commentary states:
This fourth [category] refers to being fully equipped with skills and possessing broad understanding.

Calculating refers to mathematics; writing refers to poetry; calligraphy and the arts refer to ritual and music; archery refers to the art of shooting; and charioteering refers to driving a carriage—these are called the Six Arts.
Having long mastered the Six Arts, he nevertheless displayed his learning; thus it is said that he "manifested" them.

*Zōng* (pronounced *zǐ sòng*) means to practice; Lu Fayan’s *Qieyun* states that it means "the threading of a shuttle," and the pronunciation is the same, though this is not the meaning in this context.
The "arts of the Way" (daoshu) are the methods for attaining the divine transcendence (shenxian).
The various secular classics are termed the "multitude of records" (qunji).
Since there is no secret technique of the immortal path that he has not thoroughly studied, it is said that he "comprehensively mastered" them.
"Pervasive" (*guàn*) means "to penetrate," and "refined" (*liàn*) means "to be thorough.
Since worldly customs and heterodox teachings are likewise both penetrated and mastered, it is called "pervasive and refined.
This refers to the passage in that sutra where the Bodhisattva, at the age of seven, was fully prepared with the auspicious rites.
The devas, the eight classes of beings, and all the Śākyas followed King Śuddhodana as he led the Bodhisattva to the schoolhouse.

At that time, there was a master named Viśvāmitra; upon seeing the Bodhisattva arrive, he was overcome with great awe and trepidation, and fell to the ground in a faint. A son of the gods from the Tuṣita heaven named Sunirmita supported him and helped him rise.

The King returned to his palace, and the Bodhisattva, holding in his hand a tablet of celestial sandalwood inscribed with heavenly script, adorned with celestial incense and mani-jewels as ornaments, asked the teacher:
"There are sixty-five scripts; which script would you use to instruct me?"
At that time, Viśvamitra heard what he had never heard before; his joy dispelled his pride as he marveled at how the Bodhisattva was peerless in the world.

Ten thousand youths resided and studied together with the Bodhisattva in the schoolhouse; when the letters of the alphabet were recited, they issued forth the sounds of immeasurable Dharma-gates, causing thirty-two thousand boys and thirty-two thousand girls to all resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For this reason, he manifested his entry into the schoolhouse.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "roaming in the rear garden" to "between form and flavor," the commentary states:
This is the fifth [chapter], concerning his mastery of the arts and his taking of a wife.
Practicing martial arts and testing one's skills refers to the events prior to taking a wife;
dwelling amidst the flavors of sensual desire refers to the events following the taking of a wife.
Someone cites the *Benqi* (The Origin) as saying:
Throwing elephants and wrestling were called military exercises; shooting at golden drums was said to be a test of skill.
Since these were still not exhaustive, the Bodhisattva’s age having now reached maturity, the King asked whether he was fit to have a consort for the crown prince.
The daughter of the Staff-Bearer was named Yaśodharā, foremost in her beauty and grace.
The King commanded the National Preceptor to go and present her to the Staff-Bearer;
the Staff-Bearer replied, "According to my family tradition passed down through generations, it is our custom to give our daughters in marriage only to those whose skills surpass all others."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with sorrow and distress.
The Bodhisattva said to the king:
"Summon those who possess extraordinary arts and let them display their skills before me."
The king established a testing ground outside the city and issued a proclamation throughout the world to assemble those skilled in various arts.
On the seventh day, five hundred Śākya youths, led by the Bodhisattva, were about to go together to the testing ground; the king dispatched a white elephant to welcome the Bodhisattva.
Devadatta arrived first and, conceiving a heart of jealousy, stepped forward, seized the elephant’s trunk, and struck it with his hand until it died.
Nanda followed shortly after; as he was about to exit the city gate, he saw that white elephant lying dead across the road, so he dragged it by the hand to the side of the path.

The Bodhisattva soon arrived and sat upon his precious chariot; with the toe of his left foot, he gently lifted the white elephant and cast it into the air. It leaped over seven layers of city walls and traveled one *krośa* beyond them. Where the elephant fell, a great pit was formed, which people thereafter called the "Elephant Pit."
Five hundred members of the Śākya clan all arrived at this arena and requested Viśvamitra to serve as the judge of skill, saying:
"You should observe which among the Śākyas is most proficient in calligraphy."
Viśvamitra smiled and said,
"The Prince has thoroughly investigated all the scripts existing in the heavens and among men.
The King also spoke to Aṇḍuṇa:
"Observe which of these youths is superior in calculation.
Then the Bodhisattva himself announced the numbers, commanding the youths to place their counting-slips (śalākā) in succession; none were able to equal him.
The young boys took turns counting one by one, yet the Bodhisattva’s calculation was beyond their reach;
even when five hundred boys chanted simultaneously, they were not at all confused.
Aṇḍaśuna felt a sense of wonder and marveled at the extraordinary agility and sharpness of his mind, noting that none among the Śākyas could equal him.
All the Śākyas, as well as devas and humans, praised him as the foremost.
Five hundred Śākya youths engaged in a contest of physical strength and wrestling, dividing themselves into thirty-two teams.
Nanda stepped forward and displayed his fierce valor; however, as soon as the Bodhisattva raised his hand and touched his body, he was struck down instantly by the power of that touch.

Devadatta emerged from the assembly, intending to defeat the Bodhisattva; the Bodhisattva waited with composure and slowly extended his right hand, which gracefully caught him and, crushing his arrogance, tossed him three times through the air. Out of compassion, he ensured that Devadatta suffered no injury.
"The Śākya clansmen, all born with wrathful intent, rushed forward together; yet when the Bodhisattva pointed at them, none failed to fall prostrate.
Great Minister, you may now try your hand at shooting."
Ānanda said, "Two *krośas* of iron drums may be placed [there]. Devadatta said:
"One may place the iron drum at four *krośas* [from here]," said Suddhodana. Sundarananda said,
"One may place the iron drum at six *krośas*."
The minister Daṇḍapāṇi said,
"An iron drum may be placed eight *krośas* away.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Place the iron drum ten *krośas* away.

The Bodhisattva placed seven iron shields and seven iron *tāla* trees ten *krośas* outside; Ānanda, Devadatta, Nanda, and Daṇḍapāṇi could only reach their respective limits, but none were able to go beyond.
When the Bodhisattva drew his bow, both the bow and its string snapped simultaneously; he then sought out a superior bow.
He took the bow of a former king and gave it to the son of Śākya, but the son of Śākya was unable to string it at all.

He bestowed it upon the Bodhisattva; the Bodhisattva sat down in composure, took the bow in his left hand, and with his right forefinger drew the string upward. Suddenly, as if without exerting any effort, he released the bow, and the sound of its twang resounded throughout the city of Kapilavastu, causing all people to tremble with fear.
Thereafter, he drew his bowstring and shot at various iron drums, piercing them all completely.
He passed through iron shields and iron trees without exception; the arrows sank into the earth, forming wells which thereafter were called "Arrow Wells" by the multitude.
The humans and devas proclaimed:
"In all the years since the Prince was born, he has never practiced or studied, yet he is fully prepared in these arts.
Thereupon, Daṇḍakin took the girl as his queen.
Therefore, what is now called "discussing martial arts" refers to wrestling and archery at the drums;
"testing skills" refers to testing calligraphy and strategic calculation;
and "the rear garden" refers to the park outside the city walls.
Regarding "manifesting a dwelling": because Nanda’s desire for sensual pleasures was such that it required him to demonstrate a dwelling, that same sutra states:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva, in conformity with worldly conventions, manifested a dwelling within the palace; he resided there enjoying himself with eighty-four thousand court ladies, with Yaśodharā as his chief consort."

While dwelling in the royal palace, he was able to inspire eighty-four thousand court ladies to resolve upon unsurpassed awakening; immeasurable devas all attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they spoke subtle verses exhorting the Bodhisattva to quickly renounce the household life.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, “Having seen old age, sickness, and death, he entered the mountains to study the Way,” the commentary states:
Sixth, leaving the secular world to follow heterodox paths.
This has three parts:
This first section concerns his departure from the mundane world.
Regarding "abandoning the kingdom, wealth, and status," these are what he renounced.

After the various devas had exhorted the Bodhisattva, he led his officials and attendants out through the eastern gate of the city; there he encountered an old man manifested by a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, and filled with sorrow and anxiety, he returned to the palace.
When he went out through the southern gate of the city, he again saw a sick person and was unwilling to return to the palace.
When he went out through the western gate, he again saw a corpse and turned his carriage back to enter.
Therefore, it is said that the sights of old age, sickness, and death were the loathsome signs manifested by the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
All who are born, regardless of noble or humble status, possess old age and sickness and must inevitably return to death.
Yet birth is something to be rejoiced in, and thus it is shown so that they may see it.

For those who realize that the world is impermanent, as the Sūtra says: "The afflictions of the three realms are like a fierce fire; deluded beings cannot escape them and are constantly being burned."
It is like floating clouds that vanish in an instant; having gathered, they disperse again like a marketplace.
Therefore, it is said to be impermanent (*anitya*).

Regarding the abandonment of kingdom, wealth, and status, as the verse says: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely impermanent; the five desires, wealth, and status are all unstable."
"May all sentient beings oppressed by suffering quickly leave the household life so that they may be rescued.
Regarding the renunciation of wealth, as the sutra says: "Attachment to the five desires is like a bird caught in a net; desire is like a hostile thief and is truly terrifying."
"To dwell amidst the five desires is like treading upon a blade; to be attached to the five desires is like embracing a poisonous tree.
The sages abandon them as they would spit out mucus or saliva.
As for "entering the mountains to study the Way," this refers to that which is studied.
The Prince went out through the northern gate and saw a renunciant;
he immediately alighted from his carriage and asked, "What benefit does one who has left the household life obtain? The bhikṣu replied:
"Dwelling in space, practicing the Noble Path, subduing the sense faculties, and mindfully protecting sentient beings;
unstained by the world, one attains eternal liberation."
The Bodhisattva joyfully exclaimed:
"Among gods and humans, this alone is supreme; I shall certainly practice and study it.
As the sutra says: "As the Buddhas of the past dwelt in mountain forests, they attained all-knowledge and extensively rained down the rain of Dharma."
"Now it is fitting that he leave the household life.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "clad in white garments and riding a white horse" to "shaving off his beard and hair," the commentary states:
"This describes the sequence of entering the Way."
The jeweled crown and necklaces were sent back, and the precious, exquisite robes were what was discarded.
Some say that "clothing and vehicles" is a specific designation for the [relics] contained within them.
It is not so; one should not ride upon a jeweled crown or necklaces.
Here, "wearing" (fu) means to don, whereas "riding" (cheng) means to mount.
As for the white horse, it is Kanche.
"Jeweled crowns and necklaces" refers to various articles of adornment.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"To leave the household life in private would violate the teachings of the Dharma and fail to accord with worldly propriety."
He went before the king and said, "I now wish to leave the household life; I only pray that you will grant me your compassionate permission.
The king then ordered five hundred members of the Śākya clan for each of the four sides of the city to maintain watch without a moment's rest.
The Bodhisattva said to Chandaka, "I wish to have Kanthaka. Having heard the celestial command,
Chandaka immediately took the finest gold bit, the precious saddle, and all the various ornaments to caparison the King of Horses, which he then brought forward to offer.
At that time, the Deva Śāntamati caused all the people of the city to fall into a deep sleep, while the Devaputra Vyūhamati manifested a jeweled path in the void.

Having mounted [the horse], when the Bodhisattva first lifted his foot, he ascended into the air and proceeded; the Four Heavenly Kings supported the hooves of the horse, and Brahmā and Śakra pointed out the way for the jeweled path, as they departed from the city of Kapilavastu and arrived at the Nyagrodha Garden.
When the night had turned to dawn, he had traveled six *yojanas* along the road; the gods and the eight classes of beings, having completed their tasks, vanished from sight.
The Bodhisattva then proceeded until he reached the forest where the seers practiced austerities; there he dismounted from his horse and addressed Kaṇṭhaka:
"Now that I have reached this secluded place, you shall return with Candaka."

He immediately untied his own hair-knot, took the maṇi jewel, and gave it to Chandaka to return to the Great King; he removed the necklaces from his body and offered them to the Great Holy Lord, and gave his remaining ornaments to Yaśodharā, saying:
"In this world, those who are born must inevitably part from their loved ones."
"Now, in order to sever this suffering, I have left the household life to study the Way.
When the horse heard the Bodhisattva’s words, it raised its voice and wept bitterly;
it bent its two forelegs before the Bodhisattva, licked his feet, and neighed piteously as tears flowed down.
The Bodhisattva then took the mani-jewel sword from Chandaka and shaved his own topknot, casting it into the air.
Śakra-devendra caught it and returned to pay homage and make offerings to it.
When the Bodhisattva observed himself wearing the precious robes and thought they were improper,
a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven manifested as a hunter, wearing a *kāṣāya* robe, and stood silently before the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva said:
"That which you wear is the robe of the Buddhas of the past.
If you give it to me, I shall give you a garment of *kauśeya* silk."
The hunter immediately responded;
he suddenly returned to his original form and ascended as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva shaved off his beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya robe, and declared himself a true renunciant.
Having sent Chanda back with the horse Kanthaka, he walked slowly toward the forest of asceticism where the seer Uruvilvā resided.
The Great King had instructed five men to enter the mountains to seek him out as attendants, but they could not find him; he had consequently fled into the mountain forests.

Having accepted the invitation from the female ascetic Vīrā, the Bodhisattva proceeded to the female ascetic Padmā and likewise accepted her invitation; then, having accepted the invitation from the brahmacārin seer Revata, he subsequently accepted the invitation for the following day’s meal from the two seers Āloka and Dānta, and eventually arrived at the city of Vaiśālī.
Beside the city was a seer named Ārāḍa, who led three hundred disciples and constantly taught them the meditative absorption of "nothingness.

Having heard what the seer taught, [the Bodhisattva] practiced diligently without weariness; while remaining at the stage of the "small hour," he attained realization, yet there remained nothing further to cultivate, as this was not capable of exhausting suffering entirely.
He immediately departed from that city and went to Rājagṛha, entering Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain where he dwelt alone in a certain place, protected by the devas.
At dawn, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, he entered Rājagṛha through the Hot Springs Gate and went on his alms-round in due order.

The King, hearing this report, sighed in lamentation; he ascended a high tower to behold the Bodhisattva’s body and commanded his attendants to present him with food and drink, desiring to know his dwelling place.
He went to where the Bodhisattva was and prayed: "May you, out of great compassion, realize Buddhahood within the borders of this kingdom, so that you shall not be far from me."
Having completed the rites, he returned to the palace.

As for the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that he went "twelve yojanas from the city to the abode of the seer Bhārgava," this refers to the place where he shaved his hair; thus, it does not contradict the fact that he traveled more than six yojanas.
What is here called "precious and exquisite clothing" refers to the ornaments and implements used for adorning the body;
what is called "donning the dharma-robes" refers to seeking out the disfigured garments of hunters.
If one wears these robes, one will surely be free from dust and defilement; therefore, they are called "Dharma-robes.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "sitting upright beneath a tree" to "acting as is appropriate," the commentary states:
"After this, 'acting' refers to following what is deviant."
