Some say: "Pervading the *dharmatā* of all phenomena is the sovereign activity of wisdom and perfect enlightenment, because it penetrates the *dharmatā* of the two truths.

Penetrating the characteristics of sentient beings is the sovereign activity regarding the world of sentient beings, because it thoroughly understands the various physical forms and natures of sentient beings."

Regarding the statement that "clearly understanding all lands" refers to mastery over the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), with the initial term "penetrating" (*tong*), followed by "reaching" (*da*), and finally "clarifying" (*ming*)—this is merely a matter of verbal emphasis.
This, however, is not correct, for otherwise, the external vessel-world of sentient beings would not be considered conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
If one is a worldly person, there is nothing further to be known once the two truths have been mastered.
Now, "mastering the nature of phenomena" refers to the immeasurable practices of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
"penetrating the characteristics of sentient beings" refers to the immeasurable practices of the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).
"Clearly understanding all lands" refers to the immeasurable practices of the world-realms (*loka-dhātu*).
The realms to be tamed (*vineya-dhātu*) are immeasurable and cannot be fully encompassed because there is no fixed lineage (*gotra*).
The immeasurable skillful means for taming are omitted from discussion; this is also not mentioned because they were already addressed previously under the heading of "skillfulness."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "making offerings to all Buddhas" to "the nature of illusory transformations," the commentary states:
Third, the qualities accomplished through self-mastery.
This has four parts:
I. The expedient means of cultivation;
II. The virtues accomplished through cultivation;
III. A further analysis of the arousal of cultivation.
IV. Reiterating the Accomplishment of Virtue.
This section further has four parts;
the first concerns the cultivation for one’s own benefit.
To make offerings to all Buddhas by manifesting forms like flashes of lightning is the practice of merit (*puṇya-caryā*).
To skillfully study fearlessness and understand illusory manifestations is the practice of wisdom (*jñāna-caryā*).
Some say that those who wish to make offerings to all Buddhas manifest their bodies so that they reach everywhere in a single thought-moment as swiftly as a flash of lightning.

It is called "skillful learning" because it discards the heterodox and adopts the orthodox; it is called "fearlessness" because it penetrates the orthodox and transcends the heterodox; and it is called a "net" because it comprehensively encompasses all dharmas—this is precisely wisdom as skillful means.

Furthermore, one perceives that all phenomena are neither definitively existent nor non-existent, for their nature is like an illusion; thus it is said, "to understand illusory transformations" is the accomplishment of wisdom.
Moreover, because one is not timid toward others, one studies fearlessness.
Because one is able to know phenomena, one understands them as illusory transformations.
Some say: although all phenomena are neither non-existent nor existent, one does not perceive a single phenomenon that is to be feared.
Because it gathers sentient beings without abandoning them, it is called the "learning of the net of fearlessness.
Although it is neither existent nor non-existent, because it is free from both existence and non-existence, it is called "illusory transformation. Some say:
Just as Avalokiteśvara gathers in sentient beings through the net of the gift of fearlessness, it is therefore called the "fearless net.
None of these three [explanations] are correct.
For if one has not yet mastered the skillful means to discern the heterodox from the orthodox, one would not be "fearless."
All phenomena are neither existent, for no object of fear is perceived, nor are they non-existent, for no object of fear exists.

Accordingly, in this very sequence, he now manifests emanations to make offerings to the Buddhas; though he suddenly reaches everywhere, he does not abide anywhere, and is therefore like a flash of lightning.
To study the net of fearlessness is the wisdom that masters the verbal expressions.
To understand the dharma of illusion and transformation is the wisdom that awakens to the essential meaning.
"Net" refers to the teaching.
Because the Buddha is fully endowed with the four fearlessnesses, he is called "Fearless.
Because both principle and phenomena are without exception like illusions, they are called "illusory transformations.

The Bodhisattva accords with the intent of the Buddha's teaching; because he has realized that the self-nature of the verbal expression of all dharmas is ungraspable, he is said to be "well-trained and thoroughly understanding."
Regarding the sutra passage, "Tearing asunder the net of Māra and liberating all fetters," the commentary states:
This is the second [stage], the cultivation for the benefit of others.
As for the "net of Māra," it refers to the teachings of the celestial Māras.
The "envelopments" (paryavasthāna) consist of the eight envelopments and the three bonds (bandhana).
Some say they consist of ten envelopments and four bonds.
Although this principle exists within the Hīnayāna schools, it does not belong to the Mahāyāna.
It is precisely because it destroys the net of Māra that even those with evil karma can be released from their entanglements and cause their afflictions to be severed.
Regarding the passage from "surpassing the śrāvakas" to "the samādhi of wishlessness," the commentary states: this is the third [section], which again distinguishes self-benefit.
"Transcending the stages of the Two Vehicles" refers to manifesting superiority in contrast to other vehicles.
"Attaining emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness" directly proclaims the excellence of the practice itself.
Since even the initial arousal of the Great Mind surpasses that of the Two Vehicles, how much more so after long-term cultivation; therefore, it is called "transcendence."
To enter Great Nirvana, one must necessarily take the three samādhis as the gateway; therefore, these three are specifically taught. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because my dharmas do not exist, they are empty; because they are empty, they are signless; because they are signless, they cannot be the object of aspiration."
However, there are passages stating that "emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness are practiced in common with the Two Vehicles," and thus there is no contradiction. Some say:
the former refers to the practice of the teaching (śāstra-caryā), while this refers to the practice of realization (adhigama-caryā); therefore, they differ.

It is not so. Although the study of the net of fearlessness may be taught as a practice, because one must realize that all things are illusory transformations, it should be said that this constitutes realization.
Now, the former is the path to Bodhi and the latter is the gate to Nirvana; therefore, it must be explained once more.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "skillfully establishing expedient means" to "manifesting parinirvāṇa," the commentary states:
This fourth section further distinguishes the benefit of others.
Although skillful means (*upāya*) are manifold, in this context "skillful means" is a synonym for "expedient mastery.
Some say that "virtuous skillful means" is synonymous with "mental skillful means."
Manifesting the three vehicles to bring about extinction is the skillful means of speech;
skillfully establishing the three vehicles and delivering beings according to their circumstances is called the skillful means of excellence.
This is because it reveals and manifests extinction by teaching the names of the causes of the three vehicles and the fruit of extinction.
This is certainly not the case.

Manifesting parinirvāṇa within the lower and middle vehicles is, by its very nature, a manifestation of transformation; it is therefore impossible to speak of the fruits of the two vehicles [as being attained therein].
Otherwise, how could one say that parinirvāṇa is manifested without speaking of [the attainment of] the fruits?
Some say: "Skillfully establishing the means is the expedient of speech; demonstrating the Middle and Lower Vehicles while manifesting their respective cessations is the expedient of body.
This, too, is not correct.
The meaning of manifesting the three vehicles is already fully established.
Furthermore, it is said that he manifests parinirvāṇa because [the other means] would otherwise be useless.
If this were not so, what would the three vehicles not encompass? For they also speak of the middle and lower [capacities].

Therefore, "skillfully establishing expedient means" (*upāya*) here refers to the mental expedient (*manas-upāya*), because it accords with all Buddhas in seeking transformation through the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

"Manifesting the three vehicles" refers to the verbal expedient (*vāk-upāya*), because one distinguishes the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) while preaching the three vehicles; for the three vehicles are themselves the Buddha's expedient means.
The "middle and lower" parinirvāṇas refer to the skillful means of the very body;
"middle" designates the Pratyekabuddhas and "lower" designates the Śrāvakas. This is identical to the meaning in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that there is neither two nor three [vehicles].

Because a bodhisattva wishes to lead those of indeterminate lineage among the two vehicles toward the Buddha-vehicle, he manifests parinirvāṇa within their realm of nirvana; this is identical to what is stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: "It is called 'intention' because it is a transformation."

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done initiates the transformation of beings through the three vehicles and performs the four types of categorical responses"; this refers precisely to that matter.
Regarding the passage in the sūtra from "Furthermore, there is nothing to be done" to "attaining the dharma of equality," the commentary explains:
second, the virtues accomplished through cultivation.
There are two:
first, the virtue of self-benefit;
second, the virtue of benefiting others.
Furthermore, there are four [aspects] at the beginning;
this first one refers to the equality of what is attained (*prāpta-samatā*). Some say:

Because the nature of the three vehicles is empty, there is nothing to be done; because one does not perceive a separate realization of the fruits of the three vehicles, there is nothing that exists; and because one penetrates the reality of the absence of intrinsic nature and thereby understands that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, they neither arise nor cease.
This is not so. Since it is certain that those of the two vehicles have entered the nirvana without remainder, one cannot definitively say that there is no distinct realization.
Furthermore, because it reveals the three vehicles, it is not without purpose; and because it manifests parinirvāṇa, it is not nothingness.

Some say: because there is no cause that can be produced, there is nothing produced; because there is no fruit that can exist, there is nothing that exists; and because there is no purity to arise and no defilement to cease, it is called "equality."
This is also not the case.
Because the cause possesses functional efficacy, it is not without action; because the effect exists by depending on conditions, it is not non-existent.
Now, that which is both without action and without existence is the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*).
That which neither arises nor ceases is the equality of principle.
Because it lacks any real activity, there is nothing to be done; because it cannot arise of itself, it possesses nothing.
Although pure dharmas increase, the Truth does not increase accordingly; therefore, it is said that there is no arising.
Although the defiled dharmas have ceased, they do not cease along with them; therefore, it is said that they do not cease.
All dharmas have a single characteristic, which is the so-called "markless"; therefore, it is said that they are equal.
Because one realizes and attains this, it is also called "attainment."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "fully accomplished" to "the wisdom of the faculties," the commentary states:
Second, the multitude of qualities to be accomplished. Some say:
To say that what is initially practiced is called *samādhi* and what is perfected is called *dhāraṇī* is incorrect. For if it were so,
there would be no *samādhi* at the stage of Buddhahood, which would contradict the various teachings.
Now, although the dhāraṇī encompasses both concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), it is essentially the nature of wisdom.
The hundreds of thousands of samādhis are that upon which the dhāraṇī relies, as explained at length in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
Some say: "The faculties (indriya) collectively refer to all wholesome dharmas, while individually they refer to faith, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration.
This is incorrect.
Generally speaking, "wholesome dharmas" (kuśala-dharma) encompass all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
Although the term "faculties" (indriya) occurs among conditioned wholesome factors, it certainly does not apply to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Furthermore, if faith, diligence, and so forth were designated as "faculties," one should not have mentioned wisdom separately.
Since "samādhi" has already been explained as a specific designation for meditative concentration (dhyāna), what is the reason for also mentioning the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya)?
Therefore, that which is now referred to as the faculties refers to the purification of the six sense-faculties (ṣaḍindriya).
These bodhisattvas occupy the stages of the ten bhūmis; because they have already attained mastery, their six sense faculties function interchangeably.
Although dhāraṇī is wisdom, wisdom is not necessarily dhāraṇī; and because it guides all practices, it must be explained separately.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Extensive Universal Quiescent Samādhi" to "the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas," the commentary states:
This is the third [section], concerning the extensiveness of what is realized.
As for the "Dharma-treasury," it refers to the one hundred thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
Because it excludes the two vehicles’ collections, it is called "Bodhisattva";
this refers to the profundity of that which is realized. Some say:
Universal stabilization is able to realize the vast, because one does not give rise to deluded thoughts regarding any phenomena.
The treasury is that which realizes the profound, because one is able to penetrate deeply into the true Dharma-treasury.
If that were so, it would contradict your own accepted definition of "profound and vast" as the meaning of what is realized.
The Sūtra says, "He attains the Buddhāvataṃsaka Samādhi," and the commentary states:
"This is the fourth [point], the marvelous excellence of what is accomplished."
The merits of the Buddha-ground are able to adorn the Buddha-body; therefore, it is called "Adorned by Buddha-flowers.
By entering this samādhi, one directly perceives the Buddhas and their lands in all directions; for this reason, it is also said that [one] "attains" it.
This is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka*: "That single samādhi encompasses the entire dharma-realm, and all Buddha-dharmas enter therein.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, "proclaiming and expounding all sūtras," the commentary says:
"This is the second [virtue], the merit of benefiting others."
Because he assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of beings], it is called "proclaiming and spreading.
This distinguishes him from the Tathāgata, for the Tathāgata is the one who personally expounds [the teachings].
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "abiding in the gate of profound concentration" to "there is nothing that is not universally pervaded," the commentary states:
Third, a further analysis of the arousal of cultivation.
This has two parts;
this first concerns the arousal of cultivation for one's own benefit.
Some say: "Deep concentration" refers to the concentration of principle that serves as the basis for the arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Others say:
Regarding the claim that "a single thought-moment is all-pervasive," which refers to entering meditative concentration to observe sentient beings—both [positions] are untenable.

Since "pervasion" (tong) is a functional quality (*guṇa*), the meditative concentration upon which it relies must necessarily not be a concentration of principle (*li*); furthermore, beholding immeasurable Buddhas should not be accomplished in a single thought-moment.

In their respective order, these now correspond to the meditative concentrations that serve as their bases; since there is no object that is not contemplated, they are called "profound concentrations.
As for "beholding all Buddhas," this refers to the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
"Pervading in a single thought-moment" refers to the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).
By relying on this profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to manifest the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one is able to see all Buddhas; thus, it encompasses the vastness of practice.

Furthermore, by giving rise to supernormal powers, one reaches the Buddha-fields that are beheld in a single thought-moment; thus, because it encompasses the generation of merit and wisdom, it gives rise to the swiftness of practice.
Regarding the passage from "relieving all severe hardships" to "transforming and enlightening all," the commentary states:
Following this, the cultivation of benefiting others begins. Some say:
The followers of the Two Vehicles are proficient in saving sentient beings, whereas Bodhisattvas are not.
Ordinary persons are proficient in cultivation, whereas Bodhisattvas are not.
The followers of the Two Vehicles and ordinary persons are proficient in the unsurpassed path, whereas Bodhisattvas are not.
None of these [explanations] are correct.
If it were as you say, one should have stated it as "due to indolence and diligence.
Furthermore, "seclusion" (*khaṇa*) refers to a secluded place; it certainly does not mean laziness.
Some say there are eight severe hardships: three pertaining to the evil destinies, namely the three miserable realms;

and four pertaining to the human realm: first, being blind, deaf, or mute; second, being born when a Buddha has not appeared or after he has passed away; third, lacking wisdom, intelligence, or eloquence; and fourth, being born in Uttarakuru.
Among the heavens, there is one called the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Therefore, among the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*) are the most severe, and the Bodhisattvas deliver those therein.
Because the suffering of humans and devas is slight, they are described as being in "leisure" (*kṣaṇa*).
It is argued that because Bodhisattvas diligently transform [sentient beings], they are said to be "unfamiliar" [with those realms]; however, this is not the case.

For if there were only one [Bodhisattva] in the heavens, it would contradict other sutras which state that the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) constitutes the eighth difficulty.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it is difficult for humans and devas [to encounter] those who are at leisure," there are some humans and devas who are not included among those in difficult circumstances; if they were so, they would not be among those to be converted by a Bodhisattva.
Some say: "The 'extreme difficulties' refer precisely to the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa)."
In this context, because suffering in Avīci is uninterrupted, it is called "non-leisure" (akṣaṇa); the other seven are called "leisure" (kṣaṇa).
To say that a bodhisattva is called a "rescuer" (tāyin) because of their ability to save others is also not correct.
One should speak of the remaining seven. What are these seven?
If it is said that the latter seven difficulties are called "leisure" (*kṣema*), then the seven hells would not be "non-leisure," because they would be subsumed under leisure.

If one were to say that the seven hells are called "leisurely" (*kṣema*), then the eight cold hells would likewise not be included within those two categories, for the Bodhisattva’s salvation would then not be universal.
Therefore, these eight [hot] hells are here termed "extreme difficulties" (*durgati*), which includes the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Furthermore, those who possess the two kinds of obstacles—karma and afflictions—are termed "unfettered" (akṣaṇa).
If one is free from the eight difficulties and lacks these two obstacles, they are all termed "fettered" (kṣaṇa).
Because Bodhisattvas, through their great compassion, are able to uproot and eliminate these [obstacles], they are also said to provide "rescue."
The "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) is that which is realized.
Since the suchness of the two-fold emptiness is unsurpassed, it is called the "limit of reality.
Because the Bodhisattva’s great compassion distinguishes its terminology and reveals its meaning so as to lead others to realization and entry, it is said to "distinguish and manifest."

The wise one with eloquent wisdom possesses the understanding that prompts speech, for they have attained the Tathāgata’s four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and thus understand all meanings.
One who enters into the various sounds of speech possesses the words that initiate discourse, for they have attained the samādhi of liberating language and thus give rise to all forms of exposition.
"Entering" means understanding.
With eloquence filling the interior and skillful speech manifesting externally, there is nothing that is not transformed; thus it is said, "to transform and enlighten all.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "surpassing the world" to "the way of transcending the world," the commentary states:
Fourth, restating what has been accomplished.
This section has two parts;
first is the accomplishment of one's own virtues.
"Transcending the world" refers to the fulfillment of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), because one has transcended the two types of death.
As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Transcending the world is a general manifestation of the meaning of liberation from the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
Those who abide in the path that transcends the world are characterized by the perfection of wisdom and virtue, because they possess both types of knowledge.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Because [the mind] turns spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma."
"Dṛ" (諦) means "peaceful stability," and "tāra" (度) means "transcendence"; thus, it is an alternative name for the supramundane path.
As for the passage in the Sūtra from "regarding all phenomena" to "as a heavy burden," the commentary states:
following this is the perfection of the virtue of transformation.
Because one has perfected wisdom and severed [afflictions], exercising mastery over all things—whether they undergo transformation or metamorphosis—at will, this is called "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*).
"Ordinary folk" (*shù*) refers to the common masses, and "categories" (*lèi*) refers to various classes; these are collective terms for sentient beings.
Therefore, some versions of the sūtra refer to them as "the class of sentient beings.
Having lacked the roots of the Path in the past and lacking faith and joy in the present, they do not know how to move the sages; hence, they are said to be "those who do not request [teaching]."
Since he still extends his guidance to others, how much more so when there are those who request it; thus, he is called the "uninvited friend.
This refers to the meaning in the sutra of "not waiting for the proper time.

As for "the multitudes of sentient beings," these refer to the four types of beings mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: namely, those who have not heard the Dharma, those who follow non-Dharma, and those who seek the three vehicles.
Some say: "Among the four groups, the first group consists of those who do not conform to the Dharma; because they lack the capacity to evoke noble goodness, they are said to be 'uninvited.
This is incorrect."
Regarding the latter three types of lineage, it is not necessarily the case that all possess the capacity to evoke the Buddha’s goodness;
however, even those who have never heard the Dharma in the beginning should possess such capacity, as they encounter the goodness of the world of the Sages.

Both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* contain these four types; while the latter three types are common to both those with fixed and unfixed natures, the first type consists of sentient beings without nature (*agotra*). Therefore, the roots of goodness of humans and devas should be brought to fulfillment.
The Bodhisattva takes these four classes of sentient beings upon himself as his own primary burden and brings them to fulfillment; hence, it is called "bearing the burden.
Acting as an uninvited friend applies to all four classes alike.
Regarding the passage from "upholding the Tathāgata" to "constantly ensuring it is not interrupted," the commentary states:
Fourth, a further analysis of the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the superior portion.
There are two parts:
first, the analysis of the practices to be cultivated;
second, the presentation of the virtues accomplished thereby.
The first [section] further has two parts;
this is the first: the cultivation for one's own benefit. Some say:
The profound treasury of Dharma is the Tathāgatagarbha; once the darkness of obstructions is removed, it manifests within one’s own mind, and thus it is said to be "upheld.

The various perfections of the Dharmadhātu are the Buddha-lineage; to protect them so that they remain free from obstructions and to give rise to goodness without interruption is called "constant non-interruption."
This is likely not the case.
Since the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is the true essence itself, it can by no means be said that one "receives and upholds" the Dharma-treasury.
Since it is called the "Dharma-treasury" and yet spoken of as being "received and upheld," we know that the teaching of the Dharma is not the Buddha-nature itself.

Now that you have received and upheld the Buddha’s teachings so that they may long remain in the world, sentient beings of virtuous nature will rely upon them to cultivate goodness; therefore, ensure that this lineage never ceases.
This is identical to what is said in the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Heavens*: "You must skillfully receive and uphold [the teachings], and do not sever the seed of the Buddha."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "arousing great compassion" to "bestowing upon all the common people," the commentary states:
Following this is the cultivation for the benefit of others.
It consists of three parts:
This is the first: the Dharma.
"Great compassion and pity for sentient beings" refers to the practice of uprooting suffering.
"Expounding compassionate eloquence and bestowing the eye of the Dharma" refers to the practice of granting happiness.
"Dialectician" refers to the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
Because one preaches the Dharma with a mind stabilized by loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), it is called "expounding the eloquence of loving-kindness.

Because one acts according to what is taught and will necessarily enter the stages of the noble ones (*āryabhūmi*) and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*), it is called "bestowing the Dharma-eye."
The Dharma-eye is the Wisdom-eye; it is a name derived from its essential nature.
Because one preaches the Dharma through compassionate concentration to uproot the sufferings of the three realms of existence, it is said that "the three destinies are closed off."
"Du" (杜) means "to block.
By unfolding the eloquence of compassion, one causes people to cultivate the karmic deeds of devas and humans; therefore, it is called "opening the gate of goodness.
To bestow [benefits] upon the common people, one serves one's father with reverence and likewise loves one's mother; thus, compassion is like reverence for a father, for joy is worthy of honor.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is like a loving mother, because suffering is what she cherishes.
Regarding all sentient beings as oneself is the subsequent synthesis.

"As oneself" means regarding them as one's own only child; this is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Regarding all sentient beings as if they were one's only child," for both compassion and pity are directed toward them just as toward one's own child.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "all roots of goodness" to "inconceivable," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], concerning the virtues that are accomplished.
The "roots of goodness" are the causes of merit and wisdom.
"To cross over" means to arrive.
Since the practices of merit and wisdom both reach the further shore of Bodhi and Nirvana, they constitute the fulfillment of the cause.
To obtain the merits of a Buddha is the adornment of merit and virtue.
That the noble wisdom and clarity are inconceivable is the fulfillment of the fruit of the adornment of wisdom.
Regarding the passage from "those such as these" to "assembled at one time," the commentary states:
This is the fourth section, the summary.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, the World-Honored One" to "his radiant countenance was majestic," the commentary states:
This is the second section, the introductory narrative concerning the causes and conditions for the preaching of the sutra.
"The various faculties are joyful and content" refers to the mark of joy and delight.
That the five material faculties all manifest joy and contentment serves to symbolize that there is uninterrupted happiness in the Pure Land.
"Yù" (豫) is also written as "yù" (悆).
One whose appearance and countenance are pure is free from sorrow and affliction.
Their features lack any sign of distress, manifesting that the Buddha-field is devoid of all suffering.

"Sublime" (weiwēi) is a designation for loftiness and greatness; "radiant countenance" (guāngyán) is a general term encompassing the colors of the sense organs. Thus, these terms doubly express that in that land there is joy and no suffering.
"Appearance" (*zī*) means "wondrous.

This is what both Bo and Qian said: "The face has nine colors, and the radiance undergoes thousands upon thousands of transformations; the brilliance of the light and color is exceedingly great and clear."
Some say: The Buddha never possesses an unsettled mind; being endowed with all the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), when could his physical appearance ever not be serene?
It is simply because he wishes to respond to those who come to question him that he thereby manifests what he has to say.

This is not so. Although the Buddha is free from both sorrow and joy, he nevertheless manifests delight and smiles; how could he be fully endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) without manifesting joy?

Therefore, the reason the World-Honored One now manifests joy is that the conduct and virtues accomplished by that Buddha are worthy of celebration, and the time when sentient beings are to receive benefit is drawing near.
Regarding the passage from "Venerable Ānanda" to "kneeling with palms joined," the commentary states:
Second, the Section on the Extensive Exposition through Question and Answer.
It consists of six parts:
First, questioning the Buddha to clarify the manifestation;
second, inquiring into the reason why;
third, manifesting the inquiry as a personal request.
4. Praising the question and granting permission;
5. Ānanda’s desire to hear;
6. The Tathāgata’s detailed exposition.
The first section further contains two parts;
this is the first: the ritual for submitting a formal inquiry.
"The Sage’s Intent" refers to the intent manifested through the physical form of the Tathāgata.
Because he was empowered by secret grace, it is said that he "received the intent.
"Kneeling long" (chángguì) refers to the act of placing both knees upon the ground.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "and addressed the Buddha, saying" to "as wondrous as now," the commentary states:
Following this, there is the section on the meaning of manifesting the characteristics through formal inquiry,
which has three parts;
first, the presentation of what was seen.
Next, one recites what is to be contemplated;
finally, one examines the reason for doing so—this is the first [point].
When the light of the mirror shines outwardly, it is called "shadow-manifestation" (yingbiao), which is identical to the outward extension of the Buddha-body’s radiance.
The light shining outward manifests images clearly within the mirror; this is called "images enveloped.
Likewise, the emitted light returns to illuminate the Buddha’s countenance; therefore, it is called "outer and inner."
This refers to what he himself has seen.
"Never having gazed upon" means he finds it strange that the present differs from the past;
"gazing" (zhān) is also synonymous with seeing.
Regarding the passage from "Only so, Great Sage" to "extraordinary dharma," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], which clarifies what he himself has contemplated.
Master Yuan said: "Although there are five recollections, the first expresses them collectively, while the latter four are presented individually; therefore, there are only four meanings.
These latter four objects of recollection do not exist in the mundane world, and thus they are called "extraordinary."
This is likely not the case.
The dharmas in which the Buddha dwells cannot be fully encompassed by these five recollections, much less by four; therefore, one cannot generally speak of four while omitting the fifth.

If it is argued that because this is extraordinary, we know it is a general statement, then the virtues of the Tathāgata would likewise have no specific reference and should not be considered distinct categories.
Thus, Ānanda has now briefly set forth five types of mindfulness, each with its own designated object; this is the first such mindfulness.
Some say: "The word 'only' (唯) has the meaning of 'exclusive' (專), because one proclaims one's own exclusive mindfulness.
This is not correct.
Because it would contravene the protocols for responding prescribed in the various secular classics,
"now indeed so" (*jī wéirán*) is used as a respectful response to a superior.
The general term "today" (*jīrì*) is employed to distinguish it from expressions of past and future.

Based on the manifestations produced by the wheel of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-cakra*), these signs are not only extraordinary but have no equal; therefore, they are called "marvelous" (*āścarya*).
This is precisely the reason for establishing the name of the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
The Sūtra says: "Today the Hero of the World abides where all Buddhas abide.
The commentary states: This is the second thought-moment. Some say:
That which is the place of abiding is Great Nirvana, for it is where all Buddhas dwell together.
It is not correct to say that the Buddha is called the "Hero of the World" (Lokavīra) simply because he is the most valiant and fierce among those in the world.
The Buddha eternally abides in nirvana, for he does not abide [in it] only today.

Now, the Tathāgata abides in the samādhi of the equality of all Buddhas and is able to subdue the fierce and powerful devas who are the Māras; thus, abiding in the "abode of the Buddha" is the cause for his being named the Hero of the World.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “Today the Eye of the World abides in the conduct of a Guide,” the commentary states:
This is the third recollection (*anusmṛti*). Some say:

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the practices by which the Buddha, the Guide, gathers and transforms sentient beings; because the Buddha abides in these practices and is able to open the eyes of the world so that they may see the correct path, he is called the "Eye of the World."
This is also incorrect.
Although the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) transforms sentient beings, it does not possess the meaning of "eye.
Now, the five eyes themselves are designated as the "conduct of the Teacher," for there is nothing superior to the Buddha abiding in the five eyes to guide sentient beings.
This is because it explains the meaning of the Teacher’s conduct and the Eye of the World.
The Sūtra says: “Today the Hero of the World abides in the most supreme path”; this is the fourth mindfulness.
The "Supreme Path" refers to the four categories of wisdom-mind of Great Bodhi.
Because the Buddha abides in these four wisdoms, standing preeminent and peerless, he is given the title "Hero of the World" based upon this Supreme Path.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, “Today the World-Honored One practices the virtues of a Tathāgata,” the commentary states:
This is the fifth mindfulness.
“World-Honored One” (Tianzun) refers here to the *paramārtha-deva* (the ultimate heavenly being), because it explains the meaning that the Buddha-nature is not empty.

That is to say, only those unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma) possessed by the Buddha alone are called the virtues of the Tathāgata; since these are not shared by other noble ones, the name "Celestial Honored One" (Tianzun) is explained by means of the virtues of the Tathāgata.

Although the names and virtues of the Dharma Masters are explained separately elsewhere, here we interpret their names according to their virtues because this scriptural passage follows that method of explaining meanings based on titles.
As for "names," these refer to such titles as "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) and "Hero of the World" (Lokavīra).
"Virtue" refers to that which dwells in the extraordinary and so forth.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "The Buddhas of the past, future, and present" to "Do they bring to mind the Buddhas?", the commentary states:
Third, an inquiry into the purpose for which [the practice] is performed.
There are two [parts];
this is the first: that which is intended by mindfulness. Some say:
Regarding "the Buddhas of the past, future, and present," this refers to the Buddhas of the three periods of time being mindful of one another.
To say that the Buddhas are mindful of one another means that the Buddhas of the ten directions are mindful of one another; however, this is not the case.
Since there are no ten directions apart from the three periods of time, and the Buddha is likewise not otherwise, one now contemplates the characteristics of the Buddhas of the three periods;
by analogy with this, does one not thereby contemplate all Buddhas as the present Tathāgata?
The word "ye" (耶) is a term of uncertainty.
Regarding this contemplation of the Buddhas, since the various Buddhas have not yet granted permission, I venture to resolve it on my own authority.
As for the scripture’s question, “For what reason is the majestic spiritual power so radiant? the commentary states:
This follows as an inquiry into what was done.
"Radiant radiance" refers to the state of manifest splendor.
The passage from "At that time, the World-Honored One" to "did you inquire about his majestic countenance? describes as follows:
Second, the reason for the Buddha’s detailed inquiry.
The scripture states, from “Ānanda addressed the Buddha” up to “he questioned him on this meaning,” which the commentary explains:
this is the third section, describing the reason for Ānanda’s proclamation of his question.
In truth, although he received the empowerment of the Tathāgata, he addressed the devas as if asking himself;
therefore, it is said that he "asked himself. The Sūtra states: "The Buddha said, 'Excellent,' up to 'your question is most excellent. The commentary explains:
Fourth, praising the question and granting permission.
There are two parts:
first, praising what was asked;
second, commending his virtues and granting permission.
The first section further contains three parts;
this is the first, which is a general praise.
Because Ānanda’s questions accorded with the capacities [of the audience] and the Dharma, and were appropriate for the occasion, it is said that they were "most excellent."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "generating profound wisdom" to "inquiring about the meaning of this wisdom," the commentary states:
This section specifically praises the inquiry itself.
"Generating profound wisdom" praises the wisdom of the inquiry.
"True and wondrous eloquence" refers to the words of the inquiry;
"compassionately mindful of sentient beings" refers to the intent behind the inquiry. Some say:
To say that one generates profound wisdom by recollecting the Buddha’s five virtues,
and that because one praises the Buddha as abiding in these five virtues he possesses "true and wondrous eloquence," is likely not the case.
The five virtues of mindfulness of the Buddha and the praise of the Buddha’s five stages are non-different in meaning.
For if there were no praise when there is mindfulness, or no mindfulness when there is praise, neither would accord with the correct principle.
Now, by invoking the five titles of the Buddha, one gives rise to profound wisdom;
by employing the virtues of the five stages of abiding to extol the meaning of these five titles, one possesses truly wondrous eloquence.
Although five virtues were questioned, since all five virtues have wisdom as their primary essence, it is said that the meaning of "wisdom" was being inquired about.
The Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata, with his unobstructed great compassion, takes pity on the three realms. The commentary explains:
Following this, there is a separate praise for the benefit of the inquiry.
There are four [points];
this first one reveals the Buddha’s compassionate pity.
A version of the scripture reads "inexhaustible great compassion," and some explain this by saying it arises based on the inexhaustible dharmas within.
Now, this is precisely the Great Compassion of the Buddha; as there is nothing further to cover it, it is called "Uncovered" (Anāvaraṇa).
This "Uncovered" state is the ultimate correctness and requires no further cultivation.
"Jin" (矜) also means "to pity."
Regarding the passage from "The reason for appearing in the world" to "the benefit of reality," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], which clarifies how the Buddha benefits sentient beings.
"To brilliantly expound the Way and seek to rescue the multitudes" means to discern the teachings so as to benefit all things.
"Brilliantly" (*guang*) means extensively; "expound" (*chan*) means to manifest fully.
"Using wisdom for the benefit of reality" refers to benefiting things through principle.
"Wisdom" means giving.
An alternative version reads, "Universally causing all sentient beings to obtain the true benefit of the Dharma," which is likewise not inconsistent with the meaning.
The reason the Tathāgata appears in the world is that he wishes to benefit sentient beings through the teachings and principles.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "immeasurable billions of kalpas" to "only appearing from time to time," the commentary states:
This is the third section, which distinguishes the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Bai Qian said, "It is as when there is the udumbara tree in the world: it has only fruit but no flowers; only when a Buddha appears in the world do flowers emerge."
What is here called the "spiritually auspicious flower" (nirmāṇa-puṣpa) is precisely the name used in China [Zhendan].
"From time to time" means that it appears rarely, because it emerges only at auspicious times.
Regarding the passage from "As for what you have now asked" to "the devas and the people," the commentary states:
This is the fourth [section], which formally sets forth the benefit of the inquiry.

Bai Qian then said: "If one asks about the Buddha, it is superior to making offerings to a single Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, or to bestowing gifts upon the various devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas; it is a hundred thousand million times greater."
The Sūtra says, “Ānanda, you should know,” up to “no one can obstruct or cut it off. The commentary states: second, citing virtues and granting permission.
This has two parts:
first, citing the Buddha’s virtues to provide corroboration; [second, citing the Bodhisattva’s virtues to provide corroboration].
Subsequently, an imperial edict was granted to answer the questions posed.

This section has two initial parts: first, a direct description of the excellence of the fruit; second, [the explanation of its causes]. Regarding the first: a direct description of the excellence of the fruit.
The subsequent section will clarify its superiority.
This initial part also has two sections;
here, first, is the narration of Ānanda’s thoughts.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is indeed a marvelous phenomenon.

That his wisdom is immeasurable is because he has given rise to supreme and wondrous wisdom through the samādhi of equality; thus, by virtue of that immeasurable wisdom, he is described as abiding in the abode of a Buddha.
"One who guides many" refers precisely to the conduct of a guide.
Some say that unimpeded wisdom-vision is the virtue of the Tathāgata.
No. To further describe the virtue of the World-Honored One is itself to realize the most supreme path; there is no other reason for this.
Thus, one who possesses unimpeded wisdom and vision describes the most supreme path.
"That which cannot be obstructed or cut off" refers to the virtue of the Tathāgata.
"Ē" (遏) is pronounced with the tone of "ādá" (阿達); it means to block or to cut off.
Since the Buddha's virtue is already supreme and wondrous, it cannot be suppressed by other sages; therefore, it is said to be "without obstruction or cessation."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "by the power of a single meal" to "his radiant countenance was no different," the Commentary states:
"From this point onward, it describes what Ānanda saw."
"The power of a single meal" refers to the cause of giving food.
"Able to sustain one's life-span, even exceeding it," praises the longevity [of the recipient].
"The faculties are joyful and at ease, even to the point that the radiant countenance shows no change," precisely describes what was observed.
"The sense faculties being joyful and content" refers to what was previously seen.
"Not being impaired" clarifies the meaning of that joy and contentment.
"Physical appearance remaining unchanged" refers to the previously mentioned purity of physical appearance; since purity carries the meaning of being unchanging.
"Radiant countenance without difference" means that the aforementioned radiant countenance is majestic and sublime; "majestic and sublime" carries the sense of being without difference.
Although there are five fruits resulting from the giving of food, only life and form are mentioned here: because form is what is manifested, and life is what it depends upon.
Some say: "One does not establish permanence by means of non-destruction, immutability, or lack of difference.
This is incorrect.
If this were always the case, Ānanda would not have said that he had never before seen anything as wondrous as what he saw now.
The Sūtra says, from "For what reason? up to "and attained mastery," which the commentary explains:
This is the second [point], wherein excellence is revealed by means of its causes.
Samādhi is stillness; prajñā is contemplation.
"Thoroughly penetrating" (jiuchang) carries the meaning of ultimate and pervasive penetration.
"Infinite" (wujie) is a name for that which is vast, remote, and boundless.

Thus, when the Tathāgata attains the five virtues of wisdom and the three marks of the body, it is because wisdom has reached its ultimate consummation that he attains the five virtues of mindfulness, and because meditative concentration has reached its ultimate consummation that he attains the three manifested marks.

Although causes are numerous, the two practices of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) constitute the path to the Pure Land; they serve as the basis for all myriad practices and guide the multitude of deeds.
Thus, when these two practices are taught, all others are implicitly included.

Since these two causes are fulfilled, there is no virtue that is not perfected; thus, one attains mastery over all resultant phenomena, which is what Anahua refers to when he says, "one realizes mastery over all dharmas."
Some say: when concentration and wisdom reach ultimate perfection, this is the practice of mastery over the mind;
when one attains mastery over all phenomena, this is the practice of mastery over phenomena.
It is because they skillfully enter all gateways of the dharma-realm, manifesting in all places.
It is not so; for one who has attained mastery over all dharmas must necessarily be sovereign, and that which is not a fruit cannot be sovereignty.
The previous interpretation is correct.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, “Ānanda, listen attentively; I shall now speak for you,” the commentary explains:
this is the second [section], wherein the Buddha issues a command and grants permission to answer the questions posed.
"Listen attentively" means he commands his subsequent mind.
"To explain for him" means he grants the preceding request.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, "He replied, 'Yes, indeed; I wish and desire to hear,'" the commentary says:
This is the fifth point, which Ānanda wishes to hear.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "The Buddha told Ānanda" up to "throughout incalculable kalpas," the commentary states:
this is the sixth section, wherein the Tathāgata provides a detailed exposition.
There are two parts:
first, an extensive explanation of the causes and effects of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land, which refers to that which is practiced and accomplished;
second, an extensive elucidation of the causes and effects of sentient beings’ rebirth there, which refers to that which is encompassed and benefited.
The first part further has two sections:
first, the explanation of the causes for rebirth in the Pure Land;
second, the explanation of the results of the present Buddha-land.
The first section also has two parts:
first, a general indication of the superior conditions;
second, a detailed presentation of the superior practices.
The first section further has two parts:
first, indicating the distant conditions;
second, unfolding the proximate conditions.
The first section also has three parts;
this is the first, which indicates the time. Some say:
"It reaches an incalculable number of kalpas.
This is not so, for according to the numerical system of the Western Regions (India), once one reaches the sixty-fold cycle,
it is no longer countable.
Although it may be counted, it is still called a *kalpa*;
furthermore, this would contradict the one hundred and twenty revolutions described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Now, "kalpa" is precisely the general designation for time.
In Sanskrit it is called *asaṃkhyeya*; here it is translated as "immeasurable" (*wúyāngshù*).
Wang Yi stated: "'Yāng' means 'exhaustion'.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "'Āng' refers to the leather strap on the neck."
This is not the correct form of the character.
Furthermore, since an *āṅkuśa* (hook) is used to restrain oxen and horses, it should follow the radical *yāng*.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata" to "next named Chu-shì," the commentary states:
This section lists the Buddhas.
While Bo Yan’s *Jinglue* enumerates thirty-six Buddhas, most preserve names from this region; the thirty-second Buddha, however, bears an Indian name.
Therefore, in the sūtras translated by Zhi Qian, only thirty-two Buddhas are mentioned, all retaining their original Sanskrit names;
now, in this [translation] by Dharmarakṣa, fifty-three Buddhas are fully enumerated.
Generally speaking, translators intend to expand upon or condense their material;
this is not to be considered strange. *Dīpaṃkara* is what *Qiān* (謙) calls *Tíhuójīluó* (提惒竭羅). Some say:
That which has a stand is called a *ding* (censer-lamp), and that which lacks a stand is called a *deng* (lamp).
*Dingguang* and *Randideng* are one and the same.
Because [Dīpaṃkara] was the master who bestowed the prediction of the Way upon Śākyamuni, he is placed at the beginning.
Some raise this objection:
"If that is so, since Śākyamuni had already received his prediction [of enlightenment] earlier, why did he attain Buddhahood after Amitābha?
If it were not later, it would contradict the fact that ten minor kalpas have passed since Amitābha attained Buddhahood."
He then set forth his own view, saying:
"Although the names are the same, the Buddhas are indeed different;
both [positions] are incomplete."

If they were identical, then since the lighting of the lamp occurred at the end of the second kalpa, it would necessarily contradict the scriptural passage stating that Amitābha attained Buddhahood ten kalpas ago.
If they were merely different, this would also contradict the fact that various Buddhas appearing in the world share the same names.
The present Dīpaṃkara (Jiàngguāng) and the Lamp-Lighter (Rán-dēng) are both the same and different.
They are different because, although Dīpaṃkara indeed lit a lamp, he was not the Buddha who bestowed the prediction upon Śākyamuni.
They are the same because, prior to his existence as Śākyamuni, there was also a Lamp-Lighter who could be identified as Dīpaṃkara.

One should not raise the objection: "If Dīpaṃkara was not Śākyamuni receiving the prediction of enlightenment, what is the causal reason that Dīpaṃkara was the first [Tathāgata] and not some other Buddha?"
It is said thus because, since that Buddha, fifty-four Buddhas have successively appeared in the world.
Furthermore, it is because from the time of Dīpaṃkara onwards, there has gradually been the practice of embracing the pure land.
For this reason, Dīpaṃkara is also named Dīpankara; there is no fault in this meaning.
As for the Sūtra’s statement, “All such Buddhas have already passed away,” the commentary says:
This concludes what follows.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time, next there was" to "the Buddha, the World-Honored One," the commentary states:
This is the second, the proximate superior condition.
In Sanskrit he is called Lokeśvararāja; in Chinese, he is called Shizizaiwang (World Sovereign King), because he has attained mastery over all dharmas.
This refers to the specific names.

Since the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable, his names must likewise be boundless; therefore, for the time being, he briefly indicates his benefits for himself and others to establish the ten titles, which constitute the general titles.
Although there are ten titles, they may be briefly categorized into two types:
first, those based on his own virtues, which comprise the first five;
second, those based on his benefit to sentient beings, which comprise the latter five.
The names of these virtues also consist of two pairs:
first, the pair of "perfection of the Way" and "extreme cessation," as the name Tathāgata signifies the perfection of the Way and the name Arhat signifies extreme cessation.

Second, the correspondence between the fulfillment of causes and the perfection of the fruit: "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*) and "One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct" (*Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*) are termed the fulfillment of causes, because their practice and conduct are perfected in due order;
"Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*) is termed the perfection of the fruit, because he has ascended and does not return.
The names for "benefiting beings" also consist of three pairs:

first, the pair of general name and specific designation; that is, the preceding four are specific while the final one is general, because he is named the World-Honored One (Bhagavān) for dwelling among beings without adding anything to them.

2. The correspondence between transformative wisdom and the transformative mind: "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*) is termed transformative wisdom, and "Unsurpassed Tamer" (*anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi*) is termed the transformative mind.

3. The correspondence between the capacity for transformation and the virtue of transformation: "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*) is termed the capacity for transformation, and "Buddha" (*buddha*) is termed the virtue of transformation.
A detailed explanation of these ten titles is found extensively in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time there was a king" to "the mind set on the true and correct Way," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], which sets forth the superior practices (*viśiṣṭa-caryā*).
Master Yuan said: "There are two types of practice:
from the beginning up to the end of the verses, the mundane practice is distinguished, which refers to that practiced prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
From the point where Bhikṣu Dharmākara speaks these verses downward, the supramundane practice is distinguished, which refers to that cultivated after reaching the stages."
This is unlikely to be the case.

For Bodhisattvas on the stages constantly cultivate the benefit of all sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-lands in every thought-moment; it would not be appropriate for them to devote five kalpas exclusively to the practice of receiving a pure land.
There are now two parts:
first, a brief exposition of the sublime practices;
second, an extensive exposition of the sublime practices.
The first section also has three parts;
this is the first: generating the resolve upon hearing the Dharma.
"Generating the intention for the unsurpassed path" refers to further increasing that initial resolve.
This does not contradict the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa* or the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the passage in the sutra from "abandoning his kingdom and renouncing kingship" to "surpassing the world," the commentary states:
"This is the second [stage]: leaving the secular world to cultivate the Way."
"Śramaṇa" is *śramaṇaka*; its meaning is as explained previously.
Bo Yan says that *Dharmakālu* is Dharmakara;
by omitting the character "kālu," he refers to one who practices the path of a bodhisattva, namely the Bodhisattva Dharmākara of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Those of high talent, courage, and wisdom possess human character and conduct that stand out from the world; thus, they are said to be "extraordinary.
The passage in the Sūtra from "approaching the World-Honored Sovereign King" to "kneeling long and joining the palms" is described as follows:
this is the third section, praising the Buddha and giving rise to vows.
There are three [forms]:
first, physical prostration;
second, verbal praise; and third, mental recollection.
Later, he made a self-vow;
this is the first instance.
"Ji" (稽) means to reach, and "shou" (首) means the head.
"Touching one's head to the ground and receiving [the Buddha's] feet with reverence is why it is called 'prostration' (*kāśaya*).
Regarding the 'three circumambulations,' this indicates that the Tathāgata has cultivated the three virtues.
As for the phrase in the sutra, 'He praised him in verse,' the commentary states:"
Second, the verbal praise.
This consists of two parts;
this is the first, the detailed textual portion.
The verse is sublime and also encompasses many meanings; therefore, it is used to offer praise.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, “His radiant countenance is majestic,” the commentary says:
this follows [the previous section] and constitutes the formal praise.
There are four [parts]:
first, a specific praise of bodily action;
second, a specific praise of verbal action; [and so forth].
Third, a specific praise of mental karma;
fourth, a general praise of the three types of karma.
The first [section] further has two parts:
This first section is the introductory praise.
"The light is majestic" indicates the excellence of the light;
"the countenance is majestic" indicates the excellence of the body.
Regarding the passage from "His majestic spiritual power is infinite" to "it is like a mass of ink," the commentary states:
This follows the explanation and constitutes the praise.
It is twofold:
This first section praises the majesty of the light.
"Majestic power" (vīrya) refers to that upon which the light depends.
"None can equal it" expresses the excellence of the superior in contrast to the inferior.
If one were to gather the ink [of all descriptions], it would be in comparison to the actual object that its excellence is praised.
Some say: "The 'radiant ones' (yào) are the five planets."
No. This is because Bo Yan said, "Its radiance is unattainable," referring to it as a specific designation for light.
When compared with the Buddha’s radiance, the light of the sun, moon, and so forth is like a mass of ink placed beside a white conch shell.
The Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata’s countenance transcends the world and is peerless. The commentary states:
This refers to the subsequent description of the Buddha’s majestic and lofty appearance.
"Peer" (lún) means a match or equal.
The Sūtra says, "The great resonance of Perfect Enlightenment flows throughout the ten directions. The commentary states:
This is the second [section], praising the vocal karma.
"Great resonance" refers to the sound of the secret speech (*vāg-guhya*).
The voice of the Tathāgata can never surpass this; therefore, it is called the "Great Sound.
As for "resonance," it refers to a clearly manifest sound that arises with specific limitations according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “precepts, learning, and diligence” up to “extraordinary and rare,” the commentary states:
Third, the praise of mental karma (*manas-karman*).
This has two parts:
First, there is the praise of the excellence of the activity, which is the "Chapter on Bodhi";
second, there is the praise of the excellence of the fruit, which is the cessation that is the fruit of the fruit.
Within the first, there are further two parts:
This first section praises the excellence of his engagement with worldly affairs.
Precepts are the very substance of karma, because they are the seeds of volition (*cetanā*).
Hearing, diligence, and so forth are the retinue of karma; since nothing else can equal them, he is said to be "without peer."
"Companion" (*li*) also means "match.
Since the Buddha’s virtues surpass all others, they are called "rare.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "profoundly and attentively reflecting well" to "reaching its very depths," the commentary states:
Following this, there is a praise for the excellence of realizing the principle.
"Truth" (諦) means thorough investigation.
"Ocean of Dharma" (法海) refers to the one true dharma-realm (一真法界).

Subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) deeply contemplates and observes with precision that which accords with the true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); therefore, it is called "skillful mindfulness.
Non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) thoroughly penetrates the profound truth and exhausts its ultimate reality; therefore, it is called "reaching the furthest limits."

This is not so. It would not only disrupt the sequential order, but it would also contradict the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, which states that one need not avoid the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).

However, while that sūtra says, "one who has committed the five heinous crimes can be born in the Pure Land," this vow states, "except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes and slandered the true Dharma. Thus, there is a contradiction.
Since ancient times, interpretations have diverged into a hundred schools.
Some say that those who slander the True Dharma are also excluded [from rebirth], except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes.
An objection is raised to this statement:

That sutra also says, "possessing all unwholesome [deeds]. If one does not slander the Dharma, it cannot be said that they possess all unwholesome deeds; how, then, can it be said that only those who commit the five heinous crimes can be born in the Pure Land?
This objection is not valid.

If you claim that because that sutra contains all unwholesome states, it also subsumes those who slander the Dharma, then the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) should likewise be included among the unwholesome states and need not be mentioned separately.

Now, one should immediately refute the interpretation that combines the meanings of "conformity" (*anuvartana*) and "aggregation" (*samuccaya*); for this combined interpretation contradicts the sense of the head of the dispute (*vivāda-mūla*), since the offenses are distinct and their names are likewise distinct.
Some say: "This excludes non-regret, while that [text] speaks of regret.
This is also not correct.

Since each individual thought within the ten recitations extinguishes the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, there ought to be no distinction between having regret and not having regret;
furthermore, if there were any other distinct method for repentance, it would not be mentioned at all in the passage concerning the lowest grade of the lowest birth.
Some say: "Exclusion" refers to those who have not yet committed [the act], while "arising" refers to those who have already committed it.
This, too, is incorrect.
If those who have not yet committed [an offense] are still exempted from it, how much more so those who have already committed it?
If you argue that there is no such fault because one causes those who have already committed it to progress, then should one cause those who have not yet committed it to regress?
Some say: "Those who commit the five immediate transgressions (ānantarya) are excluded, while those who commit acts similar to the five immediate transgressions are born [in the Avīci hell].
This is also not correct.

Since there is no authoritative teaching that states that those similar to the five heinous crimes (ānantarya) are themselves called the five heinous crimes, one cannot apply the term "heinous crimes" from that sūtra to these cases by way of analogy.
Some say: "Does this mean that those committed with a heavy mind are excluded [from rebirth], while those committed with a light mind are produced?"
This is also not the case.
Slandering the True Dharma necessarily has degrees of gravity; one cannot simply say it is eliminated because [the seed] does not arise. Some say:
To say that those who commit the five heinous crimes on the third level are excluded, while those who commit them on the second level are born [there],
is also not correct. This is because there are three types of sentient beings, and this is not the teaching of the Noble Ones.

Even if there were such a sacred teaching, it would contradict your own admission that those of the third stage do not practice the Universal Dharma (samantabhadra-caryā), and thus neither the presence nor the absence of heinous offenses (*ānantarya*) can lead to rebirth [in the Pure Land].
If it were as you claim, one should have stated "excepting only the third stage"; therefore, your statement that "excepting heinous offenses" is merely empty words.
Some say: "The term 'except' serves as a prior prohibition, while the term 'arising' serves as a subsequent allowance.
This too is incorrect.
This is because it was previously refuted that if [the result] were truly produced, it would follow that it could not subsequently be truly produced. Some say:

those who commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) before having generated the bodhicitta are excluded, whereas those who commit an immediate transgression after having already generated the bodhicitta do give rise to it.
This is also not the case.
If one who has already resolved upon bodhicitta were to fall back, they would be unable to give rise to it, just as one who has not yet resolved upon it cannot.
Conversely, if one does not fall back from that resolve, they will certainly not commit the heinous crimes.

Some say: [The case of] those who speak of the five heinous crimes (ānantarya) directly to the Buddha is determinate, whereas those who speak of the five heinous crimes and so forth directly to the Buddha are all indeterminate.
This is also not correct.

Unwholesome karma that leads to birth in subsequent lives and so forth should all be understood by analogy with this; for otherwise, [the classification of] the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and the like would result in a great logical error.

Some say: "If one lacked the capacity for the Path (*mārga-bhājana*) in previous lives, once the five heinous crimes have been committed, there will ultimately be no possibility of attaining birth in the Path."

Those who have previously awakened the bodhicitta, even if they encounter conditions that lead them to commit the five heinous crimes and the like, will certainly give rise to deep remorse and shall likewise attain rebirth; for among those in the happy realms, there are some who commit the five heinous crimes and slander the True Dharma.
It is argued that since each of the two texts discusses only one [aspect], they do not contradict one another.
This is also incorrect,
for [if so] the statements regarding past lives would be rendered useless.
If one has already manifested the bodhicitta, even if one encounters adverse conditions, [the thought] should still arise.

Furthermore, since those in the good realms are precisely those at the stage of the ten faiths, it is logically impossible for them to commit the heinous crime of slandering the Dharma, as this has already been explained previously.
Some say: "Those who practice Buddha-recollection for a single thought-moment are excluded, while those who practice it for ten thought-moments are reborn.
This is certainly not the case.
This would contradict the statement [in the sutra], "up to ten recitations. Some say:

those who are excluded are those who neither complete nor incomplete ten recitations, and thus none of them attain birth; whereas those who do attain birth are exclusively those who complete ten recitations.
This is also not the case.
Although this [text] does not include all ten sounds, it nonetheless sets forth the complete ten recitations; therefore, like that sutra, they must not be omitted.
However, within the three births mentioned above in this very sutra, one certainly does not commit the heinous acts (ānantarya), and thus these must be excluded.

Since it is taught that even one who has committed the five heinous crimes can attain birth [in the Pure Land] if they possess ten recitations, there is no contradiction to be resolved; therefore, one should not raise the objection that those of the middle grade who undergo three births likewise do not commit such crimes.

There is no need for removal [of the offense] because one who has resolved to attain bodhicitta and cultivates various merits does not commit a transgression against the Dharma; this meaning is already manifest.
However, since the crime of slandering the True Dharma is profoundly grave, one will undergo the retribution of suffering for countless kalpas.

If one were to provisionally assume that ten recitations must necessarily arise [simultaneously], there would be no other explanation in the holy teachings; this is because those who enter into various unwholesome states encounter many difficulties. Some say:

"The ten recitations in this sutra are based on ten dharmas and do not refer to the name of the Buddha," referring specifically to the ten recitations in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā*. This, too, is not correct.
In that sutra, "ten recitations" (daśanāma) does not refer to ordinary beings, for it certainly cannot be accomplished by those of the highest grade within three lifetimes.

Here, it is identical to the "ten recitations" in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*; since there is no logical contradiction in the fact that those of the highest grade also practice ten recitations, the words "one," "two," and so forth are used up to "ten" in order to reveal this.
Let this digression cease for now; we should explain the main text.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If, when I attain Buddhahood" to "I shall not take perfect enlightenment," the commentary states:
This refers to the second [vow] among the middle-grade vows.

Since it is stated that one must "arouse the bodhicitta," it is understood that if one has not so aroused it, even though the Sages do not come to meet them, there is no fault of violating their original vows.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If, when I attain Buddhahood... to "...I shall not take perfect enlightenment," the commentary states:
This section follows and subsumes those of the lower grade.
Some say: Although the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* mentions the word "vow," it also states that mindfulness of the Buddha has the meaning of "another time. Others say:

He does not regard the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha as referring to a different time, for the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* states that "mindfulness of the Buddha is itself birth [in the Pure Land]," as it is not a matter of a separate time.

Since both the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* and the *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* were composed by Vasubandhu, their principles must necessarily be consistent; there can be no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

However, although sentient beings hear the teachings on the Pure Land, some slander them and do not believe, sinking themselves into evil realms; others, though they believe and do not slander, are entangled by sensual desire and do not dare to give rise to the aspiration, let alone practice it.

There may be sentient beings who, upon hearing this teaching, immediately give rise to a vow to be reborn there; yet, having encountered evil friends, they commit various evils extensively. When their lives are about to end, they do not meet virtuous friends and are unable to mindfully recite the Buddha's name. Although they do not attain rebirth immediately, this constitutes a remote cause for rebirth.

The Buddha praised such individuals for being reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; however, foolish people might assume that they will be reborn there immediately without further cultivating the causes. Therefore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* states that this refers to a "different time" (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*).
Neither of these two positions is correct.
For both aspiration and mindfulness serve as remote causes for birth in the Pure Land.
Otherwise, it would contradict the intentional (sandhyābhāṣa) teaching already explained previously.
If sentient beings give rise to the aspiration to mindfully recollect the Buddha, they will immediately be transformed into the Land of Transformation.
Thus, the phrase in this text, "binding one's mindfulness to my land," refers precisely to the practice for rebirth there.

this subsequent [section] is the aspiration to gain benefit by hearing the name.

this first one is the *dhāraṇī* of the patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
The Sūtra says, from "If, when I attain Buddhahood... up to "...I shall not take perfect enlightenment," which is explained as follows:
This is the second vow, which is to remain far removed from reproach and suspicion.

As for the statement in the *Ghoṣarāja-sūtra* that Amitābha Buddha has parents, some explain that this reveals the nature of the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*), where Buddhas have parents because it is not a pure land (*anupalipta-kṣetra*). This does not contradict the present text’s own mention of the Māra named Ajita and Devadatta named Śānta.
Some say: Not so;
for even though there is a Māra-king, he guards [it].
It is not so; for in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is stated that even the Māras and their followers who oppose the Pure Land of Kāśyapa protect the Buddha-dharma.

One should therefore say that this sutra reveals the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation) land, as it also mentions women who declare that the place where they are born is forever free from the foul forms of the womb and desire.
The absence of women therein refers to the land of enjoyment (*sambhogakāya-kṣetra*).
Retaining this statement accords well with the *Bodhisattvamaṇḍala-sūtra*.

As that sūtra’s eleventh chapter, "Explaining the Pure Land of Tathāgata Jñānakāra," states: "Only male and female sentient beings who have attained the Way in the land of Amitābha [are absent here]."
Although there may be men and women, they lack the desire for men and women;
this is certainly not the case.
Since it has already been stated that sentient beings of the male and female sexes are not like those in Amitābha’s land, it must not be saying that women exist there.

Some say that in that sutra, the parents, city, and so forth are all dharmas of merit, as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the bodhisattvas; skillful means is their father."

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī meets the youth Sudhana to the east of the city of Vairambhya; since the sūtra states that "Vairambhya" is itself a name for merit, there is no contradiction that requires further explanation.
This is also not the case.

Since the self-enjoyment body must necessarily arise from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), it would have to possess parents; to assert otherwise would entail a most serious error.
What exists here now inherently possesses two meanings:
first, although that Buddha indeed had a mother, she was a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), for such a state is unique to a Buddha alone.

As for the statement that there were no women, this excludes the Buddha’s own mother; beyond her, there were no other transformed women, let alone any who were real. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Thereafter, according to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there may be bodhisattvas who are born in that land to cultivate the bodhisattva practices and attain equal and perfect enlightenment within that very realm.
There are some bodhisattvas who, having been born in this world and practiced the path, proceed to other lands to attain equal and perfect enlightenment;
the dragon girl in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also of this same category.
Because their original vows differ, the manifestations of their appearances vary.

Thus, Amitābha Buddha likely also received a body born from a womb in another land while practicing the bodhisattva path, and subsequently attained the Way of Buddhahood in the Pure Land of Hon-sin (Glorious Sound) Buddha.
The *Ghoṣarāja-sūtra* states that those who have parents speak of the land where they were originally born;
when it speaks of a "Pure Land," it refers to the world-system of a Buddha. Therefore, there is no contradiction between these accounts.
Briefly opening up two paths, the student should reflect upon them.
Let this digression cease for now; we should return to the main text.
