This is the third vow, concerning the aspiration for the benefit of sentient beings.
There are five [aspects];
this first one concerns the excellence of the faculties and appearance.
The Sūtra says, from "If, when I attain Buddhahood... up to "...I shall not take perfect enlightenment," which is explained as follows:
This is the second vow, that of the simultaneous practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The Sūtra says, "If, when I attain Buddhahood," up to "I shall not take perfect enlightenment," which the commentary states:
this is the third vow, the vow for the noble transformation of sentient beings.
The Sūtra says, from "If, when I attain Buddhahood... up to "...I shall not take perfect enlightenment," which is the fourth vow: the vow to cultivate both merit and wisdom.
The Sūtra says, from "If, when I attain Buddhahood... up to "...I shall not take perfect enlightenment";
the commentary states: this is the fifth vow: never to be separated from all Buddhas.
"Universal" (pu) carries the meaning of pervasiveness, while "equal" (deng) carries the meaning of uniformity.
Because that which is perceived is vast and universal, as all Buddhas perceive it alike, the meditative concentration in which one abides is named "Universal Equality."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If, when I attain Buddhahood" to "I shall not take perfect enlightenment," the commentary states:

It has two parts:
This is first, the vow of non-retrogression through the power of others.
The Sūtra says, from "If, when I attain Buddhahood... up to "...I shall not take perfect enlightenment," which the commentary states:
this is next, the vow of non-retrogression through one's own power.

Some say that the first, second, and third types of Dharma-patience correspond, in their respective order, to the patience of subduing (伏忍), the patience of faith (信忍), and the patience of conformity (順忍) within the five patiences of the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This is likely not the case.

If *kṣānti* (patience) corresponds to the first, second, and third stages, and *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformity patience) corresponds to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, how could one obtain these two types of patience merely by hearing the name of that Buddha?
If it is claimed that one attains [the stages] gradually by hearing their names, then one should also state that they obtain the five patiences (*kṣānti*).

Now, the three stages of the Patience of Subjugation (*vinaya-kṣānti*) are designated as the "three dharmas," for the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states that the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) possesses the three grades of patience: inferior, medium, and superior.
Regarding the passage from "The Sūtra says, 'The Buddha addressed Ānanda'" to "He spoke in verse," the commentary states:
Fourth, the manifestation of auspicious omens through his own vow has two parts;
this is the first, consisting of the detailed textual account.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “I establish a vow that transcends the world,” up to “vowing not to attain equal enlightenment,” the commentary states:
Following this, he makes a vow.
This consists of two parts:
First, the making of the vow;
second, the request for an auspicious sign.

First, the reversal of the vow;
second, the fulfillment of the vow.
Within the first, there are further two parts:
This first section is a vow regarding one's own virtues made before the Buddha.
"To establish" (jian) means to initiate.
This refers to the aforementioned aspiration for the Buddha’s body and land, which is called the "Supramundane Vow."
Because his vow necessarily gives rise to practice, he will certainly reach the unsurpassed path.

The original text is not fixed; it may read, "I shall become a great donor to universally relieve all who suffer in poverty," or it may read, "I shall never fail to become a great donor to relieve the suffering of the poor. The former version should be considered correct.
Some explain this by saying it refers to the benefit of transforming others through the gift of Dharma;
however, this is incorrect,
for one must bestow material wealth in order to relieve poverty and suffering.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "When I have attained the Buddha-way" to "I vow not to become a Perfectly Enlightened One," the Commentary states:
This is the second [section], which sets forth the vow in response to the gift of Dharma.
Although his name and reputation are proclaimed, the intent lies in his verbal teachings.
The Sūtra says, from "Deeply mindful and free from desire" up to "Teacher of devas and humans," which the commentary explains as:
second, fulfilling his vows.
There are two parts;
this first section is the brief vow.
"Freedom from desire, right mindfulness, pure wisdom, and the holy life" are the causes of the vow; "seeking the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Teacher of Gods and Humans" is the fruit of the vow.
Regarding the passage from "The spiritual power manifests great light" to "penetrating the gates of the happy realms," the commentary states:
Following this, there is the extensive vow.
It consists of two parts:
First, a detailed praise of the Buddha's virtues;
second, a concluding summary and the making of a vow.
Within the first section, there are four parts:
This first section is a praise of the virtue of transformation.
"Radiating light that shines everywhere" refers to the transformation of bodily action (*kāyakarman*);
the remaining six phrases all refer to the transformation of verbal action (*vākkarman*).
"Removing the three defilements and rescuing beings from their many hardships" refers to the transformation through the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
The "three defilements" are namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Opening the eye of wisdom and extinguishing the darkness of blindness" refers to the transformation through the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
"Closing off the evil realms and opening the way to the good destinies" refers to the transformation of humans and devas.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "The merit and blessings are fully accomplished" to "all things remain hidden and do not appear," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], praising his own virtues.
"Zu" (祚) is pronounced with the rhymes *he* and *fan*; it means "to assist" and "blessing.
"Zhi" (戢) is pronounced with the rhymes *duo* and *liu fan*; it means "to gather" and "to collect. Lu Fayán’s *Qieyun* states that it also means "to stop."
"Merit and destiny are fully perfected" means that the essence of virtue and its resultant blessings are all completely fulfilled.
"Radiance illuminates the ten directions" refers to the vastness of the light.
"Celestial lights do not appear" indicates the extraordinary excellence of the radiance.
Some original texts read: "The light of the sun and moon is entirely obscured and does not appear. This meaning is not contradictory.
Because the Buddha’s radiance overwhelms them, the sun and moon withdraw their light and are unable to shine outward; thus it is said that they "retract their layered brilliance."
Regarding the passage from "Opening the Dharma-treasury for the multitudes" to "Proclaiming the Lion’s Roar of the Dharma," the commentary states:
This is the third [section], further extolling the virtue of his transformative activity.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Making offerings to all Buddhas" to "Pervasive penetration such that nothing is not illuminated," the commentary states:
This is the fourth [section], reiterating the praise of one's own virtues.
Regarding the sutra passage, “May the power of my merit be equal to that of this Most Victorious Honored One,” the commentary states:
This is the second [section], the formulation of the vow.
Regarding the sutra passage from “If this vow bears fruit” to “it shall rain down precious and wondrous flowers,” the commentary states:
This is the second [section], the request for an auspicious omen.
The Sūtra says, from "The Buddha addressed Ānanda" up to "scattered them upon him"; the commentary states:
Fifth, he then requested that an auspicious omen be manifested.
There are two [parts];
this first [part] concerns the manifestation of auspicious signs in accordance with his vow.
The Sūtra says, from "spontaneous music" to "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment," which the commentary explains as follows:
Later, he uttered a voice to offer a eulogy and record [the teaching].
The Sūtra says, from "At this time, in the Dharma-treasury" to "deeply delighting in quiescent extinction. The commentary states:
This is the sixth section, which provides a general concluding eulogy.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time, Ānanda" to "having established this vow," the commentary states:
Second, the presentation of the cultivation of sublime practices.
This has two parts:
This first section concludes the sublime vows. Some say:
"The utterance of this great vow constitutes the forty-eight vows; the one who establishes these vows is the one who makes the vow of the oath."
No. The sutra refers to the former as "vows" (praṇidhāna) and the latter as "oaths" (pratijñā).
What is now termed the "great oath" (mahā-pratijñā) is a synthesis that reverses and accords with those [distinctions].
Regarding these vows: they comprise forty-eight vows, which are formulated by proceeding from the end toward the beginning; thus, there is no error.
As for the sutra’s statement, “Single-mindedly and exclusively dedicated to adorning the land,” the commentary explains:
this subsequently and formally presents the sublime practices.
There are two parts:
first, the cultivation of the practices of the land;
second, the cultivation of the practices of the body.
The first section also has two parts;
this is the first: the cultivation of causes.
The Sūtra says, from "the Buddha-land he cultivates" to "without decay or change," which the commentary explains as follows:
This refers to the manifestation of the fruit hereafter.
"Vast and expansive" means that immeasurable virtues have been perfected; as the treatise states: "Ultimately like space, vast and without boundary."
*Kuò* (廓) is pronounced *è* (惡) in reverse; according to the *Erya*, it means "great.
That which is transcendent, supreme, and uniquely wondrous refers to the excellence of the land (*tǔ shèng*), for it is not within the sphere of ordinary bodhisattvas.
That which is established as eternally abiding is so because it is established through the fulfillment of causes and fruits, and because it is subject to no alteration.
That which neither decays nor changes is so because it cannot be destroyed by the three calamities.
The Sūtra says, from "Regarding the inconceivable" up to "immeasurable virtuous conduct. The commentary states:
Second, the cultivation of bodily practice.
This has two parts:
First, the cultivation of causes;
second, the praise of the fruit.
Within the first, there are again three parts:
First, a general statement;
second, a detailed explanation;
and finally, a concluding summary.
This is the first [category].

According to the calculations of the Yellow Emperor, there are three grades; let us cite one of them: ten thousand *koti* (billion) is a *zhao*; ten thousand *zhao* is a *jing*; ten thousand *jing* is a *hai*; ten thousand *hai* is a *zi*; ten thousand *zi* is a *pi*; and ten thousand *pi* is a *zai*. Therefore...
Some say that "zhào zǎi" (兆載) refers to a remote period of years;
this is incorrect.
Regarding the passage from "not giving rise to thoughts of desire" up to "odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas," the commentary states:
Second, the specific explanation.
This has four parts:
First, detachment from defilement; second, cultivation of virtue; third, detachment from karma; fourth, cultivation of virtue.
Regarding the first, there are further two aspects: first, personally detaching from afflictions; [second, causing others to detach].
Subsequently, they were taught and transformed so that they might be freed from [defilement].
Furthermore, there are four initial points;
this first one concerns the causes and conditions for becoming free from defilement.
"Not giving rise to thoughts of desire, hatred, or harm" is a partial statement that emphasizes the gravity of the fault without being exhaustive.
"Thoughts" (覺) means seeking or investigation. Some say:
Preconceiving distorted thoughts regarding an object before it is encountered is called "perception" (vitarka); the arising of the mind in response to an object is called "conception" (saṃjñā).
Therefore, not giving rise to the three types of perception is to be free from the beginning; not giving rise to the three types of conception is to be free from the end.
This is not so. It is precisely because the three types of awareness do not arise when facing an object that there is no other reason [for their non-arising].

Rather, they are the very causes of the three types of awareness; for it is only when the boundaries of the object are grasped through the three perceptions (*saṃjñā*) that desire and the others subsequently arise.

Thus, because one does not crave fame or profit, the thought of desire does not arise; because one does not afflict sentient beings, the thought of anger does not arise; and because one does not harm the lives of creatures, the thought of malice does not arise.
When the three types of awakening do not arise, one must sever the three perceptions; therefore, these are also included.
Since internal causes have been abandoned, external conditions cease; thus it is said that one does not cling to form and the other aggregates.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "the perfection of the power of patience" to "having few desires and being content," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], the cultivation of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
As for the "power of patience," it consists of the patience of enduring suffering, the patience of enduring injury and malice, and the patience of discerning phenomena (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*).
By means of this power of patience, one is able to endure harm and affliction; therefore, one is free from the three types of awakening and the three types of perception.
Having few desires brings benefit in the future, and contentment brings benefit in the present; thus, one does not become attached to form and the other sense objects.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “free from attachment, aversion, and delusion,” the commentary states:
This is the third [point], the correct abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
“Attachment” (*rāga*) refers to greed.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, “Samādhi is eternally quiescent and wisdom is unimpeded,” the commentary states:
This is the fourth [stage], the correct cultivation of the antidote.
“Samādhi is eternally quiescent” refers to the profundity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Unimpeded wisdom" refers to the excellence of knowledge (*jñāna-viśeṣa*).
The Sūtra states, from "free from hypocrisy" up to "anticipating the question," which the commentary explains as follows:
this is the second [point], benefiting others while remaining free from defilement.
One who is free from a mind of falsehood and flattery is thus free from faults of the mind.
One with a serene countenance is thus free from faults of the body.
One who speaks with affection and asks questions first is thus free from faults of speech.
Some say that first receiving the question with the mind constitutes mental action (*manas-karman*).
This is not correct.
Although it was stated previously that [the Buddha] intended to speak, this now explains the reason for his inquiry.
The Sūtra says, from "valiant and diligent" up to "benefiting all sentient beings," which the commentary states is:
second, the cultivation of speech.
There are three [types];
this is the first: uninterrupted cultivation (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).
"Vigorous diligence" refers to the initial diligence.
Because one vows never to be intimidated by the enemy, it is called "valiant.
As for "the aspiration being free from weariness," this refers to the second application of diligence (*prayoga-vīrya*), so called because one applies further cultivation to advance.
Seeking the dharma of purity and clarity constitutes the third form of tireless diligence, because one practices it without ceasing;
this is the cultivation for one's own benefit.
Benefiting the multitude of sentient beings constitutes the cultivation for the benefit of others.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Reverencing the Triple Gem" to "Accomplishment of Merit," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], the cultivation of reverence.
Reverencing the Triple Gem is the skillful means for merit.
"Serving the Elder Teacher" refers to the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*).

"Greatly Adorned" refers to having already accomplished the two adornments of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-dvaya-alaṃkāra*), and thus being fully equipped with the various noble practices such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth.
Because one benefits sentient beings by means of what one has cultivated oneself, one causes merit to be perfected.
The Sūtra says, from "Dwelling in emptiness and signlessness" up to "contemplating phenomena as like illusions. The commentary states:
This is the third [stage], the realization of the perfection of practice.

Some say: When one dwells in greed, hatred, and delusion, the karma of mental action is unregulated; now, by dwelling in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one is able to regulate the karma of mental action.
Because greed is like the skin, it is subdued upon entering emptiness.
Since anger is of the nature of flesh, it is subdued by the absence of aspiration;
since delusion is of the nature of mind, it is subdued by the absence of signs.
Within the characteristics of all phenomena, none of these principles exist; who then would weary themselves with refutation?
Therefore, because my Dharma is truly non-existent, it is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā); because even its provisional characteristics are non-existent, it is called "signlessness" (animitta).
Because within these two there is nothing that can be aspired to, it is called "wishlessness" (apraṇihita).

Some say: "Because there is no fruit to be produced within these three, they are called 'non-action' (wu zuo); because there is no cause from which they can arise, they are called 'non-arising' (wu qi).
This is likely incorrect.
If "action" (karma) is indeed an activity, how could it not be called a cause?
Since "arising" is also a process of coming into being, it can be termed an effect.
Now, because the cause lacks practical utility, it is said to be "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*); this is what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* means when it says, "although one practices non-action."
Because the fruit lacks a true essence, it is said to be "without arising"; this is what that sutra means by "though practicing non-arising.
Since it lacks substantial reality and function, one contemplates it as being like a magical transformation.

In sum, because there is no action and no arising, it is not existent; because one contemplates phenomena as being like illusions, it is not non-existent. This state of being neither non-existent nor existent is the principle of the Middle Way, which is what is meant by "realization."
The Sūtra says, from "staying far away from harsh speech" up to "harming both oneself and others. The commentary states:
Third, the abandonment of evil karma.
This has two parts:
This first point concerns the abandonment of faults.
"Abandoning coarse speech" means abandoning the faults of verbal action (*vākkarman*).
"Harming oneself, harming others, or harming both oneself and others" means abandoning the faults of physical action (*kāyakarman*).
"That" refers to another person.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "cultivating virtuous speech" up to "benefiting both self and others," the commentary states:
"Following this, there is the gathering of wholesome qualities."
Because he cultivates wholesome speech, he distances himself from coarse language; because he cultivates the three benefits, he distances himself from the three harms.
The Sūtra says, "Abandoning his kingdom and renouncing his kingship," up to "teaching others to practice. The commentary states:
This is the fourth [practice], the cultivation of goodness.
Because one has personally abandoned and cultivated something, one also causes others to abandon and cultivate something.
As for the scripture stating, "Accumulating merit over incalculable eons," the commentary says:
this is the third point, which serves as a concluding summary.
Regarding the passage from "according to the place of birth" to "the path of true reality," the commentary states:
Second, praising the fruit.
This has three parts:
This first section praises the retribution of merit;
it has three parts, of which this is the first: a general heading.
Regarding the passage from "or as a householder" to "all Buddhas," the commentary states:
This is a sequential and specific eulogy. Some say:

It is argued that the householder is born according to his class, such as a kṣatriya, which is a "superior birth" (abhyudaya-janman), while those in the six heavens of the desire realm are born with increased excellence, which is an "exalted birth" (abhyudaya-janman). This is not so;
for the householder should also be considered a superior birth, since the various devas are likewise not non-superior births.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “Such merits are beyond description,” the commentary says:
This is the subsequent conclusion and praise.
Regarding the sūtra’s passage from “the breath of the mouth is fragrant and pure” to “the marks and signs are exceptionally sublime,” the commentary says:
Second, the praise of the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya* and *puruṣakāra-vipāka*).
This section has two parts;
here, first, is the praise for the excellence of the primary retribution.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "His hands constantly emit... to "...surpassing all devas and humans," the commentary states:
This section following [the previous] praises the excellence of the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (the environment or external support).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra "He attains mastery over all dharmas," the commentary states:
This third section praises the fruit of the merit of wisdom.
The Sūtra states, from "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" up to "attaining Buddhahood and being present," which the commentary explains as:
second, setting forth the fruits that have been accomplished.
This is because the fruit of the body and the land is accomplished in accordance with one's vows.
There are two parts: first, a brief presentation of what is accomplished; [second, a detailed explanation]. Regarding the first: a brief presentation of what is accomplished.
Subsequently, that which has been accomplished will be extensively elucidated.
This initial section further contains four parts;
herein, the first is the discernment that the Buddha has already attained accomplishment.
This is because the qualities of the Lord are perfected.
As the Treatise says: "The Dharma King Amitābha, the Perfectly Awakened One, skillfully sustains [the land].
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "To the west of here" up to "called Sukhāvatī," the Commentary states:
This second point marks that the land has already been transformed.
Bo Qian both stated: "The country where he dwells is named Sumati; it is located in the west, a distance of ten million billion Mount Sumerus away from this Buddha-land."
Regarding the current statement, "ten trillion lands away from here," the causes for the [conflicting] spears and shields are as extensively explained previously.
The Sūtra says, from "Ānanda asked again" up to "having passed through ten kalpas in total"; the commentary states:
this is the third [section], concerning the duration since attaining Buddhahood.
The *Sūtra* translated by Zhi Qian states, "Since becoming a Buddha, ten small kalpas have passed," the meaning of which is the same as this [text].
As for Bo Yan’s statement, "Since becoming a Buddha, eighteen kalpas have passed," it is likely that the character "small" (*xiao*) was missing its medial dot.
Regarding the passage from "That Buddha-land" to "like the jewels of the sixth heaven," the commentary states:
This is the fourth [point], concerning the ultimate majesty and beauty of the land.
There are two [aspects];
this first one reveals the adornment of the land.

That the former [Buddha] attained Buddhahood corresponds to the vow for the Buddha-body; that this land is adorned and purified corresponds to the vow for the Buddha-field, meaning that various kinds of phenomenal virtues have been accomplished.
The treatise states: "Equipped with the nature of all rare jewels, fully endowed with exquisite adornment.
*Huī* (恢) is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *huī* finals;

it means "great. *Hè* (赫) is pronounced with the *hū* and *gé* finals. The *Qieyun* states: "Red. The *Mao Shi* uses the term "hèhè" (赫赫), and Master Yin’s commentary explains: "Hèhè describes a state of great abundance."
*Khun* (the initial *hu* is pronounced with the *fan* [classifier] *ben*)—the *Qieyun* states it means "firelight.
It is also written as *yù* (pronounced *chū jù*), meaning "flourishing" or "radiant.

Regarding "interspersed among the various [ornaments]," this refers to the boundaries of the adornments; that is, because the qualities of form and appearance are perfected, the treatise states: "The pure radiance is complete, like the disks of the sun and moon in a mirror."
"Radiant and brilliant" refers to the perfection of the virtue of sublime form; as the treatise states: "The stainless flames of light blaze forth, pure and bright, illuminating the world.
"Pure" refers to the perfection of the virtue of purity; as the treatise states: "Contemplating the characteristics of that world, they surpass the paths of the three realms."
"Adornment" refers to the perfection of adorned virtues; that is to say, because water, earth, and space are all adorned.

This is like the jewels of the Sixth Heaven: by comparing those celestial jewels with those of the human world, it merely serves to demonstrate that the jewels of the Pure Land surpass those of the mundane world.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Furthermore, its land" to "constantly harmonious and well-adjusted," the commentary states:
Following this, the adornment of the land is free from defilement.
This has two parts:
This first section generally sets forth that which is absent.
Since there is no lack of the accomplishment of merit, the treatise states: "Forever free from the afflictions of body and mind, one experiences bliss constantly and without interruption."

*Kxi* (also written as *kxi*, with the phonetic transcription *kǔ xī*) is defined in the *Erya* as: "Water flowing into a stream is called a *kxi*; water flowing into a *kxi* is called a *gu*; and water flowing into a *gu* is called a *gou*."

"Qú" (pronounced with the *lǚ* and *jū* finals) means a "ditch. The *Guǎngyǎ* states, "It is therefore a *kǎn* (pit)," while the *Zílín* defines it as "a small canal, four feet deep and four feet wide."
The Sūtra says, from "At that time, Ānanda" up to "relying on what does he dwell? The commentary states:
Following this, the lack of a basis for discernment is explained.
There are five [points]:
This is the first question.
The Sūtra says, from “The Buddha said to Ānanda” up to “on what do they all depend? The commentary states:
This is the second part, the Buddha’s counter-interrogation.
Regarding the passage from "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" to "inconceivable," the commentary states:
This is the third response given by Ānanda.
Regarding the passage from "The Buddha said to Ānanda" to "it is for this reason that it is so," the commentary states:
This fourth point is the Buddha’s confirmation and fulfillment.
It is because the sought-after virtues have been fully accomplished; as the treatise states: "He is able to satisfy all that sentient beings wish for and delight in."
Regarding the passage from "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" to "therefore I ask about this meaning," the commentary states:
This is the fifth [section], which sets forth the intent of the inquiry.

Since the sun and moon still exist, the *Jue jing* (Sūtra on Awakening) says: "The sun, moon, and stars all abide within empty space; they neither revolve nor circulate, nor do they possess any brilliant radiance."
For although Mount Sumeru does not exist there, the palaces for those reborn in that land do indeed exist.
By this, one knows that the heavens, earth, and space in that realm are different from ours; thus, all alternative explanations are merely laborious and empty words.
Regarding the passage from "The Sūtra says, 'The Buddha told Ānanda'" to "a single buddha-field," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], which extensively sets forth that which is accomplished.
It should correspond to the previous vows by separately setting forth what is accomplished; however, fearing prolixity, it briefly demonstrates the excellence of the fruit.
There are four [aspects]:
first, praising the fruit of the Buddha’s body, which is the retribution for the vow regarding the Buddha’s body;
second, extolling his retinue, which is the retribution for the vows regarding bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Third, praising the excellence of the Buddha-field, which is the fruit of seeking a pure land;
fourth, manifesting what has been accomplished, which is the fruit of the vow to gather in sentient beings.
The first [of these two] further has two parts:
First, the individual praise;
second, the concluding praise.
Within the first, there are again two parts:
First, praising the excellence and subtlety of the light;
second, revealing the longevity of his life.
Regarding the first, there are four parts:
This first section is Śākyamuni’s self-praise;
it has two parts, of which this is the first: praising his own excellence in contrast to those who are inferior.
This is precisely the retribution of the light of the vow that is unsurpassed.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Therefore, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life" to "the Buddha who Surpasses the Light of the Sun and Moon," the commentary states:
Following this, there is a concluding eulogy that reveals his excellence.

Some say: It is "immeasurable" because it is long; "boundless" because it is wide; "unobstructed" because it is sovereign; "without opposition" because nothing else can rival it; "flaming king" because its radiance surpasses all others; "pure" because it is free from defilement; "joyful" because the mind rejoices upon seeing it; "wisdom" because it illuminates objects excellently; "uninterrupted" because its illumination of things has no end; "inconceivable" because it transcends worldly perceptions; "inexpressible" because it cuts off verbal conceptualization; and "surpassing the sun and moon" because it exceeds all worldly forms.
Although one may have such an understanding, one cannot distinguish the light, nor is it treated with sufficient gravity.
Now, because this Buddha-light is beyond calculation, it is immeasurable; because there is no object that it does not illuminate, it is boundless;
because there is no person or phenomenon capable of obstructing it, it is unimpeded; and because it is not within the reach of any bodhisattvas, it is... [incomparable].
Indeed, because its sovereign radiance is unsurpassed, it is called the "Flame King.
It manifests from the Buddha’s root of goodness of non-attachment and is pure because it removes the turbid minds of greed in sentient beings;

it arises from the Buddha’s root of goodness of non-hatred and brings joy because it can eliminate the resentful and sorrowful minds of sentient beings; and its light arises from the Buddha’s root of goodness of non-delusion...
Because it arises from the fundamental mind and further eliminates the category of ignorance within the minds of sentient beings, it is wisdom;

because the Buddha’s constant radiance perpetually illuminates and benefits others, it is uninterrupted; because this light cannot be fathomed by those of the two vehicles and so forth, it is inconceivable;
because it cannot be adequately described even by other vehicles, it is beyond measure; and because it shines constantly day and night, it differs from the Sahā world.
The radiance of these two luminaries thus surpasses that of the sun and moon.

In summary, because they constitute the adornment of the body, the treatise states: "The light of the marks and signs extends one fathom, and its form and appearance transcend those of all living beings."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "There are sentient beings" to "all receive liberation," the commentary states:
This is the second [point], showing that those who see [the light] obtain benefit.

The extinction of the three impurities is the benefit of removing obstacles; the joy of body and mind is the benefit of generating goodness; the finding of rest from suffering is the benefit of uprooting pain; and the universal attainment of liberation is the benefit of obtaining happiness. That all are touched by the light so that their bodies and minds become supple is brought about by the power of their aspiration.
Regarding the passage from "Amitāyus Buddha" to "is likewise so," the commentary states:
This is the third point, the universal praise by all the sages.
It refers to the fact that immeasurable Buddhas all extol, proclaim the name of, and vow for this retribution.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If there are sentient beings" to "is also as it is now," the commentary states:
Fourth, the benefit gained by hearing the light.
This is accomplished through the act of prostrating with one's entire body to pay homage and offer reverent vows to the Joyful Deva (Nandikeśvara).
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra beginning with "The Buddha said, 'I have taught'" and ending with "is not yet exhausted," the commentary states:
This is the second section, the concluding eulogy.

It is because [the teaching] is performed without falsehood as a sustenance and adornment; as the Treatise says: "By the power of the Buddha’s original vows, no encounter passes in vain, for it can cause one to swiftly fulfill the great ocean-treasury of merit."
Regarding the passage from "The Buddha said to Ānanda" to "Do you know this?", the commentary states:
Second, the identification of the lifespan thus accomplished.
This has two parts:
This first section directly indicates the longevity [of the Buddha's life].
As for the passage in the Sūtra from "Suppose in the ten directions" to "knowing its ultimate limit," the commentary states:
This subsequent section uses concrete matters to manifest the length [of his life].
Some say: In Sanskrit it is called dhyāna, which here is translated as "meditative concentration" (靜慮).
What was formerly called "dhyāna" (禪那) or simply "dhyāna" (禪) are both corruptions and abbreviations.

Although it is known that "dhyāna" (禪) of the past is identical to "dhyāna" (靜慮) of the present, it is truly lamentable that we have not yet heard of what other referent the character "dhyāna" (禪) might possess.
That which is now termed "dhyāna-thought" (禪思) is a specific synonym for "exclusive reflection" (專思).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas" to "that which can be known," the commentary states:
Second, the presentation of their retinues.
This has four parts:
This first section illustrates the lifespan by way of analogy;
that is, the lifespans of devas and humans cannot be calculated or known, for it is accomplished through the power of vows.
The Sūtra says, "Furthermore, the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas... up to "...inexpressible," which the commentary explains as follows:
This second point reveals that the assembly is innumerable;
it is the fulfillment of the vow for boundless śrāvakas.
This is because the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* (Treatise on Rebirth) is titled "The Adornment of the Assembly."
The verse says: "Devas and humans, immovable, arise from the ocean of pure wisdom.
The Sūtra states, from "divine wisdom penetrates through" to "all worlds," which the commentary explains as follows:
This is the third [section], briefly praising the excellence of his virtues.
This is accomplished through the attainment of the knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the teaching of all-knowledge, wisdom, eloquence,
and so forth. The Sūtra says, from "The Buddha said to Ānanda" up to "it is the same for the Bodhisattva," which describes this fourth [section] as extensively manifesting the manifold [qualities].
There are two [parts];
this first [section] is a general heading.
The phrase "the first assembly" is a partial enumeration used to indicate that the assemblies are innumerable.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "As Mahāmaudgalyāyana" up to "the number, whether many or few," the commentary states:
This follows as a separate explanation.
It consists of two parts:
This first section praises the multitude [of qualities] in contrast to wisdom.
The Sūtra says, from "For example, like the great ocean" up to "what is meant by 'multitude'"; the commentary states:
This subsequent section manifests the multitude by means of illustrative matters.
There are three parts;
this first part establishes a simile and poses a counter-question.
The Sūtra states, from “Ānanda addressed the Buddha” up to “that which can be known,” which is explained as follows:
This section answers the question of its extent.
The scripture states, from "The Buddha said to Ānanda" up to "like the waters of the great ocean"; the commentary explains:
following this, the Buddha provides a summary and confirmation.

Regarding the explanation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-śāstra*’s statement that “those of the two vehicles are not born [there],” it has been explained at length as previously mentioned and need not be further analyzed here.
As for the passage in the Sūtra from “Furthermore, its land” to “musaragalva trees,” the commentary states:
Third, the manifestation of the retribution of the land.
There are four:
first, the adornment of trees;
second, the adornment of music.
Third, the adornment of the palace;
fourth, the adornment of the ponds.
Regarding the first, there are further three [subdivisions]:
First, the adornment of the jewel trees;
second, the adornment of the Bodhi tree;
and finally, the praise of its excellence.
The first section further has two parts:
first, the jewel trees;
second, the music.
The first section further has three parts;
this is the first: the trees made of pure jewels.
The Sūtra says, "Or two jewels," up to "with agate for fruit. The commentary states:
This section concerns the miscellaneous jewel-trees.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "the rows face one another" to "cannot be fully beheld," the commentary states:
this concludes with a general eulogy.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Pure breezes arise at times" to "naturally harmonizing with one another," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], concerning music.
As for "pure breezes," an alternative version reads: "neither the wind of heaven nor the wind of humans."
Regarding the five notes: as the *Shijing* says, Gong, Shang, Jiao, Zhi, and Yu correspond to the sounds of the five elements.
The current mention of "Gong and Shang" is a brief citation of the first two; "Gong" is coarse and "Shang" is fine.
"Harmony" means resonance.
Because it does not conflict with or override the sounds, it is called "spontaneous harmony.
Master Weishi said:

Regarding the five qualities of vocal sound: first, it is clearly understood; second, it is easy to comprehend; third, it is not scattered; fourth, it is never tiresome; and fifth, it is pleasing to the ear.
Although these qualities exist, if they are absent, the Sage says that [the teaching] cannot be established.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Furthermore, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life" to "manifesting according to circumstances," the commentary states:
Second, the identification of the trees of the bodhimanda.
This has three parts:
This is first, the essential characteristics of the Bodhi tree.

One *li* consists of three hundred paces; thus, four million *li* equals one hundred and twenty thousand *yojanas*, which corresponds to the previous statement that the Bodhisattva, through slight effort, beheld the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) by virtue of his vow.

Some say: In accordance with the height of that Buddha’s body—six million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand *yojanas*—by the Buddha’s supernatural power, even though the small paths and trees are close together, they do not obstruct one another.
If that were so, the remaining palaces should not each be designated according to their respective shapes and sizes.

However, since the Buddha’s measure mentioned in that sutra refers to his *paranirmita-vashavartin* body, this bodhi tree is therefore part of a manifested land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*); thus, there is no contradiction.
Twenty thousand *li* equals six thousand *yojanas*; [if it were otherwise], it would not correspond to its original measure.
Furthermore, another version of the text reads "two million *li*," which is likely the correct reading.
Regarding the passage from "a gentle breeze stirs slowly" to "not encountering suffering or affliction," the commentary states:
this describes the manifestation of benefits through the production of sound.

This is because the virtue of wondrous sound has been perfected; as the *Śāstra* says: "The Brahma-voice awakens [beings] to that which is profound, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous, heard throughout the ten directions."
Regarding the passage from "the eyes behold their forms" to "free from all afflictions and distress," the commentary states:
Following this, there is the acquisition of benefit through seeing and hearing.
This has two aspects:
This refers to obtaining benefit from the objective realm.
Because it was obtained through the power of past vows that the sense organs were not deficient, it is said that "the six faculties are pure.

As for the "patience" (kṣānti), it is because the mind of wisdom rests upon the Dharma;

Bo Qian stated that "when Amitābha Buddha, the various bodhisattvas, and the arhats wish to eat, natural pedestals made of the seven treasures appear, and they sit upon cushions of karpāsa and wool; whatever they desire, whether sweet or sour, they obtain. The statement that one "sees forms and hears fragrances" implies that in that land, taste and touch are not food, because they are not swallowed.
Some say: since form is not separate from food, the phrase "sees forms" refers to the substance [of food] itself, which consists of the three objects [of sight, smell, and touch].
No. Since it is not being experienced, how can there be flavor and contact?
For that which is tasted is what is called "food."
"Next" means "proximate," because there is no suffering remaining as a cause.
It is thus bliss, such as the retribution for the vow to exhaust the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The passage from the Sūtra beginning with "Those śrāvakas... up to "...the body of the ultimate" is explained as follows:
Second, the superiority of the retribution for those who have long resided [there].
This has two parts:
first, the superiority of the primary retribution;
Next is the excellence of the secondary retribution (*niṣyanda-vipāka*).
This section also has two parts;
here, first, the excellence of the retribution is directly revealed.
That which is of the same category is precisely the retribution for the fourth vow.
That which is "empty, non-existent, and infinite" is so because it is unobstructed and rare.
In their respective order, these are the retributions for the vows of the power of Guṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Some say: Since it is stated that they are neither gods nor humans, those born in that land, though they are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), do not belong to the realms of gods or humans.
If they were of the human realm, they would necessarily be among the four continents; therefore, there is the term "transcending the single continent" (*yue-dan-yue*).

If it were not one of the four continents, would there be a separate human realm outside the four continents? If there were such a thing as the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), there would necessarily be long-lived devas; therefore, within a Pure Land, there must be difficult places.
Because this Pure Land is neither among the realms of humans nor devas, it does not belong to the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because there is no desire, because they dwell on the ground, and because they possess form," which, in their respective order, means it is neither the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) nor the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This is likely not the case.
For the original vow speaks only of the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and does not mention the happy destinies (*sugati*).
If it were intended to include those who are not in the miserable realms, one would necessarily have stated that there are five destinies (*pañcagati*).

Furthermore, if one were neither a Buddha nor within the three realms, it would contradict the sūtra which states, "There are sentient beings outside the three realms," as this would not be the teaching of the Seven Buddhas.
As for the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that [this land] is not within the three realms (*tridhātu*), this merely excludes the defiled realms; thus, there is no logical fault.

Although humans and devas exist there, there is no distinction between them as such; rather, humans and devas are distinguished according to the karma of the defiled lands. Therefore, it is said that the names "human" and "deva" are applied because they conform to those in other directions.

Because these various devas all abide in space, Bo Yan said: "The first four heavens and the second Trāyastriṃśa heaven all naturally dwell and reside in the midst of space, without any support or cause."

In the *Jingxing zhuan jing* (Excerpts from the Scripture Compiled by Shi Jingxing), from the passage "The Buddha told Ānanda" up to "and the indeterminate group," the commentary states: Second,
the differentiation of the causes and conditions for sentient beings' rebirth.
Thereupon, one gathers the vows for the benefit of sentient beings and extends them toward rebirth.
There are four types of rebirth:
first, the rebirth of ordinary persons and those of the Lesser Vehicle;
Second, the birth of the Great Sage;
third, the exhortation for ordinary and small-capacity beings to be born by means of both gain and loss;
fourth, the praise of that land’s excellence to inspire the Great Sage to seek it.
The first section also has three parts;
this initial part clarifies the right concentration so that beings may look up to it and seek it. Some say:

Those possessing the nature for *nirvāṇa* are called the group of right certainty (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*); those lacking the nature for *nirvāṇa* are called the group of wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*); and those apart from these two are called the group of no certainty (*aniyata-rāśi*).
This is not correct.
Apart from those with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and those without it, there is no other assembly of sentient beings, for there should be only these two categories.

Some say: those prior to the good destinies (*sugati*) are called "wrongly fixed" (*mithyātva-niyata*); those in the stage of the good destinies who repeatedly regress and advance are called "unfixed" (*aniyata*); and those from the stage of the cultivated lineage (*śrutamaya-gotra*) onward, whose state does not regress, are called "rightly fixed" (*samyaktva-niyata*).

In the case of the two vehicles, those ordinary worldlings who are constantly submerged are termed "fixed in the wrong" (mithyātva-niyata); those in the six preliminary stages of application (prayoga) are termed "unfixed" (aniyata); and those from the stage of patience (kṣānti) upward are termed "fixed in the right" (samyaktva-niyata).

Therefore, it is claimed that those born in that land—regardless of whether they belong to the three vehicles—all abide in right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), as there is no other group remaining.
This is also not the case.
The meaning of those three groups contradicts various scriptural teachings and principles; one should reflect upon this according to reason.

Since the stage prior to the happy destinies is termed "wrong determination" (mithyā-niyata), if one were to enter that land and immediately abide in "right determination" (samyak-niyata), one would have to bypass the ten stages of faith and enter the stage of cultivated seeds (śikṣā-bīja) at once; however, such a principle is certainly impossible.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because those born in that land do not immediately enter the stage of the "cultivated seeds" (*śikṣamāṇa-bīja*), [we reply] that there are still those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-rāśi*) in that land. Some say:

according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, since the "arising of cultivation" (*śikṣā-pravṛtti*) occurs at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), the Bodhisattvas who take rebirth therein are exclusively those from the first stage upward.

No. If it were only bodhisattvas, it would contradict the sūtra’s statement that "all" [beings] are included, and there would also have to be those of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi). Some say:
Those who abide in the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) are identical to those described in the *Shorter Sūtra* as all being *avaivartika*;

since *avaivartika* means non-retrogression, according to the *Fundamental Karma Sūtra* (*Benye jing*) and other texts, this refers to the stages from the seventh mind of the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-vyākaraṇa*) onwards.
Although there are lower stages, [the opponent claims] they are all [included] because they are spoken of in terms of their superior [aspect].
This is also not correct.
Since those from the seventh mind upward are called "non-retrogressive," it follows that the various lower stages would not be non-retrogressive stages, as there would otherwise be an inconsistency.
Now, the three vehicles taught in other teachings are all of this defiled land, for it is because of the existence of these three vehicles [there].

If one is born in the Pure Land, regardless of whether one is an ordinary person or a sage, one is fixed toward nirvana, fixed in proceeding toward wholesome conduct, fixed in being born in good realms, fixed in practicing the six perfections, and fixed in attaining liberation; therefore, there is only the group of those with right determination (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), and no other two groups.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions" to "slandering the True Dharma," the commentary states:
This is the second [section], which cites the praises of all Buddhas to cause sentient beings to increase their resolve to depart [from saṃsāra].
Since all Buddhas have spoken of this together in praise, those who hear the name and desire to be born will certainly attain birth there. Some say:

This sutra excludes those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma because it refers to those in the group of the rightly determined (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*); however, because the *Contemplation Sutra* concerns those in the group of the wrongly determined (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), even those who have committed the five heinous crimes can be born there.
No. If it were as you say, then those born in that Pure Land from the lowest-of-the-low grade would not be of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma). Some say:
Even if one has committed the five heinous crimes, if they practice the sixteen contemplations, they will immediately attain rebirth; this is the intended meaning of that sutra.
If one is unable to practice the sixteen contemplations, then even if they perform other good deeds, they will certainly not attain rebirth; for this reason, this sutra excludes such cases.
This is also incorrect.
Since those born in the lowest grade of the lowest birth also cultivate the sixteen contemplations, it would necessarily contradict that sutra.
Furthermore, this very passage has already been explained previously, so there is no need for further interpretation.

Regarding the ten recollections mentioned previously and this present mention of "one recollection," these are cited alternately to represent both the minimum and the maximum; therefore, they do not contradict one another.
The Sūtra states, from "The Buddha told Ānanda" up to "there are three classes," which the commentary explains as follows:
This third section sets forth the causes for rebirth, enabling people to cultivate the aspiration for birth [in the Pure Land].
There are two [parts]:
this first one is the general heading. Some say:

In this context, since all three grades are born in the Land of Enjoyment for Others (*parabhogakṣetra*), they differ from the nine grades who are born in the Land of Transformation (*nirmāṇakṣetra*) as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The phrase "even if one cannot perform meritorious deeds" is a hypothetical concession; furthermore, the practice of ten recitations is also taught in the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā*.
No. That statement is made provisionally (*prajñapti*) in order to cause others to generate the bodhicitta by means of their remaining merits.
The word "provisionally" used in the sutra should be understood like other such expressions; it is also a definitive teaching (*bhūta-vāda*).

Furthermore, if these ten recitations constitute a state of mind that is not that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), why are they not mentioned for the upper and middle grades, but only for the lower grade?

Now, by combining those nine grades into these three grades, their meaning remains no different; thus, one should not raise the objection that in that sutra, those of the upper-middle and middle grades both become śramaṇas, see the true Buddha, yet do not resolve upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta), whereas those of the lower-middle and lower grades do not become śramaṇas in this life, do not see the Buddha at all, and do not resolve upon the Great Mind.

Regarding the claim that those of the middle grade do not become śramaṇas, yet see a transformation Buddha and resolve their minds on bodhi—these points must necessarily be contradictory—it is because there are many categories within the middle grade;
each of the two sūtras speaks from its own perspective, and thus there is no contradiction between them.

As for the statement that one "should generate the bodhicitta," it is intended to show that those born there must necessarily have generated the Great Mind (mahācitta), thereby distinguishing them from those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) who cannot be born there.
Other passages that appear contradictory are all of this same category.

Some say: there are further rebirths that do not belong to the three grades. This refers to the five types of people mentioned in the subsequent text who harbor doubts; while they cultivate various merits within a state of doubt and believe in both sin and merit, they practice the roots of goodness only slightly and vow to be born in that land. Because their faith is not settled, they do not belong to the first six grades, nor do they belong to the latter three; for this reason, they are not included within the nine grades.
This is also not the case.

Bo Qian states that those of the middle grade harbor doubts and do not believe; although they are born in that land, for five hundred years within that city they do not see the Buddha, hear the sutras, or behold the sages. Therefore, it is absolutely impossible to say that ordinary people with doubtful wisdom are not included among the nine grades.

Some say: "If one does not resolve the four doubts, although they may be born in that land, they will reside in a border region; this constitutes a distinct category not included within the nine grades. Therefore, one should not give rise to groundless doubts."
This is also not the case.

Since the precious cities where those of middle and lower capacities mentioned in the two sutras each number five hundred, they must be like this present sutra; for the precious palaces where ordinary people of doubtful wisdom reside must likewise be borderlands.

If it were not so, it would contradict the sūtra which states: "The dwelling places they inhabit are on the ground; they cannot cause them to be as high or large as they wish in the midst of space, and furthermore, they remain very far away from Amitābha Buddha."

Some say that those who harbor doubts regarding the Buddha’s wisdom are precisely the "middle class" mentioned in the *Contemplation Sūtra*. Thus, the *Sūtra* translated by Bo Qian regarding the middle class states: "Those who uphold the precepts, practice giving, provide food for śramaṇas, build monasteries, and erect stupas, yet later harbor doubts and do not believe—such persons, though their faith wavers between belief and disbelief, continue to cultivate the roots of goodness and fulfill their vows, thereby attaining rebirth [in the Pure Land]."

"Even though one is born in that land, one will not be able to proceed to the presence of Amitāyus Buddha; instead, on the way back, one will see a spontaneously arisen jewel city at the border of the Buddha-land, and for five hundred years, one will be unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma," and so forth.
It is not appropriate to protect the sutra through unrighteous means by harboring doubts regarding the Buddha’s wisdom for those of the lowest grade.
This is also incorrect.

Since those of the lower grade, such as Bo Qian, were also in the city on the road and did not see the Buddha during the five hundred years [of decline], why should one doubt that his wisdom applies only to those of the middle grade and not the lower?

If it is argued that those of the middle grade include those who harbor doubts regarding Buddha-wisdom because their cultivation of causes resembles [the true path], and thus, although they belong to the middle grade, they are not of the lower grade; then by the same logic, those of the lower grade who receive results resembling the middle grade should also be included among those who harbor doubts regarding Buddha-wisdom.
Although the fruits are similar, they do not include the wisdom of doubt; although the causes are likewise the same, how could there be room for the wisdom of doubt?
Furthermore, what that person said—that [the fruit] belongs to the middle or upper grades within the nine grades—is logically impossible.

In the *Amitābha Sūtra*, there are the middle-upper [faculties], whereas in this sūtra, there are those with doubtful wisdom; since the benefits obtained—such as the blossoming of the lotus, the seeing of the Buddha, and the hearing of the Dharma—are all different, [the two cannot be equated].

If you argue that there is no such fault because the middle-upper itself has many varieties and thus encompasses doubtful wisdom, then would it not also be the case that the middle-lower has many varieties and thus likewise encompasses doubtful wisdom?
Therefore, I now suspect that the Buddha’s five wisdoms are subsumed within the two births of the middle-lower and lower-upper grades.
For this reason, the latter two classes among Bo Qian’s followers all claim to be in the city; they have not been able to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or behold the sages for five hundred years.
Whether categorized as three grades or nine ranks, there is no distinction of breadth or narrowness, for they encompass all who attain rebirth.

Among them, the three grades are defined such that the accumulation of merit constitutes the superior grade, the cessation of evil constitutes the middling grade, and the commission of evil constitutes the inferior grade; the details therein should be reflected upon according to principle.
Within this, the distinctions between the three grades have three meanings:
first, the difference in body and mind.
Regarding the mind, they all simultaneously give rise to the bodhicitta and single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha; in these respects, they are largely the same.
First, regarding the distinction of status: to leave the household life is superior, while remaining in the secular world is middling or inferior.
Second, regarding the distinction of cultivating causes:
to fully cultivate all practices is superior; to cultivate merit to a limited extent is middling; and to recite the name of that Buddha ten times or even once is inferior.
Third, the differences in the conditions for rebirth:

namely, the highest is to be welcomed by the true bodies of Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara; the middling is to be welcomed by their transformation bodies; and the lowest is to see the Buddha’s body in a dream.
There are four distinct meanings regarding the three classes of *bōyán* (silk banners):
first, the distinction between body and mind.
That is, those who have left the household life and resolved upon bodhicitta are superior; those remaining in secular life with sincere hearts are middling or inferior.
Second, differences in practice:

practicing all various deeds is superior, as evidenced by dreaming of the sages; practicing good deeds in small measure without ceasing day or night is middling, as evidenced by dreaming of the sages; and merely severing attachment and anger while recollecting the Buddha for ten days and ten nights without interruption is inferior.
Third, the difference in seeing the Buddha;
this is identical to these same three types.
Fourth, the difference in receiving the fruit.

Upon being born in that land, those who dwell in aerial palaces (*vimāna*) high above and near the Buddha constitute the superior class; those whose dwellings are on the ground at the jeweled city and far from the Buddha constitute the middle and lower classes.

Although the translations by Zhi Qian are mostly consistent with others, there are differences: to desire rebirth in that land, one should suspend various silks and brocades to construct Buddhist temples and erect stupas, provide food for śramaṇas, sever attachment and anger, maintain the purity of the precepts, and single-mindedly recollect the Buddha for ten days without interruption; this is designated as the practice for those of the lowest grade.
When comparing those two sutras with the *Dharmarakṣa* edition, while the "upper grade" is the same, the "middle" and "lower" grades differ.
In those two versions, the two classes [of practitioners] harbor doubts in their hearts and do not give rise to the aspiration for the Way;
here, however, both classes of practitioners have given rise to the mind of the Way because of their resolute faith.

The reason for this discrepancy is that although the Sanskrit original was complete, Bo Qian translated only those passages concerning rebirth through both doubt and faith, whereas Dharmarakṣa translated only those concerning the cultivation of causes through pure faith; this was because he intended to demonstrate later that those who harbor doubts are people of wisdom who reveal their own transgressions.

Although these statements may appear as sharp as a spearhead and a shield, their underlying principle is necessarily not different.
