If one is born in the Pure Land, that is the birth of one who has attained Buddhahood, termed "one-life" (ekajāti).
Now, to distinguish this from the literal sense, it is also called "the position of the successor" (kṣetrajāta).
Some may harbor doubts, saying:

If the bodhisattvas in that land were all in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), they would not be able to travel about to transform others; therefore, having relinquished their original vows, none suffer untimely death.
The Sūtra says, "Ānanda, in that land... up to "...the great trichiliocosm. The commentary states:
This is the second [feature], the excellence of its radiance.
There are two [points]:
this first one indicates the irregularity of the light.
The *Yupian* states: "One *xun* is eight *chi*."
Furthermore, the statement that [the body] is seven feet tall seems incorrect, as it should be the same as the blade [of the sword].
The scripture says, "Ānanda addressed the Buddha," up to "will be born by transformation in that land"; the commentary states:
following this, he further elaborates in response to the objection.
Since it is stated that one cultivates the bodhisattva practices in this land, we know that King Araṇemin is in this region, and so too is Ratnasāgara.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Ānanda, whoever... up to "...the thirty-two marks," the commentary states:
This is the third [section], concerning the perfection of the physical marks.
Because the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are not fixed, they are not mentioned here.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "the perfection of wisdom" to "the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the commentary states:
This is the fourth [excellence], the supreme and wondrous quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
Some say: because one realizes and attains the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it is called "profoundly entering all dharmas";
because one exhaustively masters the subtle expositions, it is called "thoroughly elucidating the essential subtlety."
This is certainly not the case.
If sentient beings were born there and attained these two types of knowledge, there would be no ordinary persons or followers of the Lesser Vehicle.
As for "entering all phenomena" right now, it refers to awakening to that which is signified.
To clarify the essential subtlety: it is because they are proficient in the means of expression (*abhidhāna*).
Some say that the faculties (*indriya*) are precisely the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
No. Since faith and the other [faculties] are themselves dull faculties, they are now identical to the six faculties. Some say:

The two types of patience refer to the two patiences regarding the arising of phenomena (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*), as well as the first two of the five patiences; the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) refers to the fourth patience.
This [interpretation], however, is likely incorrect.

Because the patience toward the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is itself the patience toward the arising of dharmas, it transcends the patience of conformity (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*); thus, [the Buddha] suddenly speaks of non-arising without any other specific reason.
Now, those of middling and lower capacity attain only the two patiences of resonance and conformity.
Those of the superior grade attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding incalculable dharmas; hence it is said they are "incalculable.

Since there are both those of sharp and dull faculties, they must necessarily be at the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), and thus this does not refer to the sharpness or dullness of their spiritual capacity (*indriya*).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Furthermore, that bodhisattva" to "just like my own land," the commentary states:
This refers to the fourth repetition [of the ritual], during which four *cun* of earth were accumulated.
*Xi* (熙) means "joyful"; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "harmonious and cheerful," and according to the *Fangyan*, it means "cheerful and delighted.
Regarding the passage from "The Buddha told Ānanda" to "without transgression or loss," the commentary states:
This is the eighth [section], in which the virtues of practice are perfectly complete.
There are two parts:
first, individual praise;
second, a concluding summary.
Furthermore, there are seven initial points;
this first concerns the cultivation of practice free from faults.
It has three parts:
This first [section] concerns the transformation of conduct free from faults;
that is, it accords with the wisdom of Amitābha Buddha.
The Sūtra says, "In that land" up to "a mind free from attachment. The commentary states:
This second [point] concerns being without fault in one’s own practice.
It has two parts;
this first [sub-section] concerns cultivating one's own practice.
There are six [points];
this first one concerns the practice of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Because he is free from [false] views, he has no sense of "mine" (*amama*); because his mind is free from craving, he has no mind of attachment.
The Sūtra says, from "coming, going, advancing, and stopping" to "no contention and no litigation.
The Commentary states:
This is the second [section], the cultivation of the practice of precepts.
Because he is free from faults of the body.

"In going, coming, advancing, and halting, his mind has no attachments; he acts with ease according to his will. Because he is free from faults of the mind, "he has no preferences or aversions, and neither 'other' nor 'self' exists.
Master Wei states: "Shi" (適) means to go; "mo" (莫) means to stop.
If that were so, it would entail the same fault as [the views on] going and stopping being separate from the body.
Now, only the *Lunyu* states: "In the world, there is nothing to which one is partial (*shi*) or indifferent (*mo*).
Here, "partial" refers to the intimate, and "indifferent" refers to the distant.
Because one is free from verbal transgressions, there is no contention and no litigation.
Since both self and other have already ceased, there is no contention or litigation.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "toward all sentient beings" to "purified by being free from hindrances," the commentary states:
This is the third: the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
Because there is no malice, one is gentle; because there is no arrogance, one is disciplined.
Since malice does not arise, resentment ceases.
By this, one is also purified of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "being free from weariness and indolence" up to "the superior mind and profound mind," the commentary states:
"This is the fourth [stage], the cultivation of diligent practice."
Because one seeks the good without ceasing, there is no mind of indolence.
Because there is no practice that is not cultivated, it is called the "equal mind.
Because there is no lowering of the feet, it is called the "superior mind."
Because there is no shrinking back or despondency, it is called the "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*).
As for the "concentrated mind" mentioned in the Sūtra, the commentary states:
this is the fifth, the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it is free from all distractions, it is called "a concentrated mind.
Regarding the phrase "a mind that loves the Dharma, delights in the Dharma, and rejoices in the Dharma," the commentary states:
this is the sixth [stage], the practice of wisdom through cultivation.
Some say: craving is desire, pleasure is faith, and joy is greed. Others say:
That "love" (*preman*) pertains to the time of completion, "joy" (*sukha*) to the time of hearing [the Dharma], and "delight" (*prīti*) to the time of seeking—
both of these views are incorrect. This is because desire, faith, and so forth are themselves the constituent practices (*parivāra-caryā*) of giving, ethical discipline, and the rest.
Because there is no distinction between the end and the beginning, following their respective order:
here, because one delights in the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), it is called "loving the Dharma" (*dharmakāma*);
because one relishes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is called "rejoicing in the Dharma" (*dharmarata*).
Cultivating wisdom moistens the spirit; hence it is called the "joyful mind.
The Sūtra states, "Extinguishing all afflictions and departing from the mind of the evil realms," which the commentary explains as:
this is the second [stage], the departure from faults.
Some say: "Defilements are extinguished because their causes are exhausted, and the mind that leads to the evil destinies is abandoned because its fruits are exhausted.
This is not correct.

Because the fruit is not merely mind, it is now free from delusion; thus, one is free from afflictions (*kleśa*). Because karma is exhausted, one is free from the mind of the evil destinies (*apāya*).
As for the Sūtra’s statement, "Ultimate in all the practices of Bodhisattvas," the commentary says:
This is the third section, the summary.
As for the scripture stating, "Fully accomplishing immeasurable merit," the commentary says:
this is the second section, the perfection of accomplished virtues.
There are two [parts];
this is the first, a general praise.
The Sūtra says, from "attaining profound meditative concentration" to "fully awakening to the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*); the commentary states:
Following this, there is a separate eulogy in two parts;
this first part establishes one's own virtues.
Dhyāna, the supernormal powers (abhijñā), the clear knowledges (vidyā), wisdom (prajñā), and the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) are virtues already accomplished.

"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "samādhi" refers to the four formless attainments (ārūpya); "supernormal powers" refers to the six abhijñās; "clear knowledges" refers to the three vidyās; "wisdom" refers to the three types of prajñā; and the seven factors of enlightenment are also included because they belong to the stage of the path of vision (darśanamārga) and because one advances toward the pursuit of the Buddha's virtues.
Regarding the virtues sought through the Buddha-dharma of cultivating the mind, although these virtues are immeasurable, the five eyes are briefly enumerated here.
Both the flesh eye and the divine eye take pure matter (*rūpa*) as their essence.
The physical eyes of those in that land can see the forms of countless worlds with total penetration; therefore, they are said to be "clear and transparent.
What is seen is precise and real, and thus there is nothing not understood. Some say:
It is not that the fleshly eye sees forms within obstructions,
for that would contradict its nature of being transparent and clearly discerning.

That which now illuminates present forms and images is called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); the eye produced by reliance on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is able to see sentient beings dying here and being reborn there, is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
It is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because that which is seen is vast and manifold; it is also called "unlimited" (*ananta*) because it extends over a long duration.

The Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) takes wisdom as its essence; because it is able to perceive the faculties, desires, natures, and minds of sentient beings, as well as all Buddha-dharmas, it is named the Dharma-eye.
Because one universally knows the distinctions among the dharmas of the paths of the three vehicles, it is said that "one has reached the ultimate of all paths.
The wisdom-eye takes the knowledge of emptiness as its essence; because it illuminates the principle of true emptiness, it is said that "one sees the truth."
Having exhausted the source of ultimate truth, one is said to "cross to the other shore.
"Crossing" means to arrive.
The Buddha-eye inherently possesses two aspects, namely the general and the particular.
Specifically, it takes all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its essence; because there is no phenomenon that it does not illuminate, it is said to be "complete.
Furthermore, because it perceives the Buddha-nature, it is said to "awaken to the dharma-nature."
In total, these are the four aforementioned eyes; because the objects of observation attained by the Buddha are equally exhausted, it is said that they are "fully perfected.
As for the scripture stating, "He expounds the teaching for others with unimpeded wisdom," the commentary says:
this subsequently constitutes the virtue of transformative efficacy (*nirmāṇa-guṇa*).
This refers to preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings by means of the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
The Sūtra states, from "equally contemplating the three realms" up to "the affliction of the defilements"; the commentary explains:
this is the third [perfection], the fulfillment of the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā-sampad*).
There are two [parts];
this first is the practice of cultivation.
To contemplate that the three realms are empty and non-existent is precisely the practice of relinquishing birth and death.
Within the three realms, such as the desire realm, there is not a single realm that is not empty; therefore, it is called "equal contemplation.
One who aspires to seek the Buddha-dharma is one who joyfully practices for bodhi.
Possessing eloquence (*pratibhāna*) refers to the virtue of benefiting others, namely the four types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and so forth.
"Extinguishing the afflictions and sufferings" refers to the benefit of transforming others.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Born from the Tathāgata" up to "the two remainders are both exhausted," the commentary states:
Following this, there is the accomplishment through cultivation.
This consists of two parts;
first, accomplishment through one's own practice.
Furthermore, there are two [aspects]:
first, the simultaneous accomplishment of understanding and practice. Some say:
That which arises from the Tathāgata as the understanding of the suchness of all phenomena (dharmatā-tathatā) is "understanding through realization" (*prativedha-avabodha*).
Skillfully knowing the means for the cessation of the accumulations (*saṃskāra*) is "understanding through instruction" (*deśanā-avabodha*).

Since this understanding arises through the Tathāgata’s teaching and transformation, and because one understands that all phenomena are themselves suchness, it is said that "understanding of the suchness of all phenomena arises from the Tathāgata."
The teaching of practicing good is called "cultivating sound," and the teaching of extinguishing evil is called "extinguishing sound.
Because one understands these well and possesses skillful knowledge, it is said that one "skillfully knows the expedient means."
This still does not exhaust the meaning, for the teaching and understanding also arise from the Buddha’s transformation.
Some say: "Habituation" refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), while the intention also encompasses the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which implicitly includes the Path (*mārga*).
Because cause and effect interpenetrate, it is said that the teaching of the Four Noble Truths is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) expressed through sounds.
This, however, is not the case.
Although that which is accumulated is necessarily suffering, there is suffering that is not accumulated.
Since cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) differ from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), suffering and the path cannot be subsumed under accumulation and cessation respectively.
The phrase "now born from the Tathāgata" generally reveals the source from which the Bodhisattva attains liberation.
The phrase "understanding the suchness of phenomena" specifically articulates the wisdom that realizes the non-established reality.
"Those of good wisdom practice cessation" refers specifically to the understanding that realizes the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*).
"Practice cessation" employs the expression "exhausting" to refer to the causes of defilement and the fruits of purification.

The Truths of the Four Noble Realities are taught by transcending all phenomenal characteristics; they are merely provisional designations established for instruction. Therefore, it is said that "sounds are skillful means.
Because one is able to thoroughly understand the noble teachings, one does not delight in worldly discourse but finds joy in correct treatises.

Some say: "Because he has abandoned the four verbal transgressions, he does not delight in worldly speech; because he employs the four noble modes of expression, he takes pleasure in correct discourse.
This is incorrect.
Since the notion that "the words of the Sage must necessarily be orthodox treatises" is not itself a correct argument, it is understood that this [previous position] is indeed established as such.
Those who revere the Buddha-way seek the mind of bodhi;
those who know the quiescence of dharmas cultivate the practices of remedial counteraction.
Regarding the second point, "the remainder of both being exhausted," this refers to the practice that eliminates the obstacles and suffering. Some say:
the physical body is the remainder of karmic retribution, while afflictions are the remainder of the fragmented existence (*pariccheda*).
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the end, the two remaining types of *pariṇāma-vipariṇāma* (transformative and transformative-residual) are to be exhausted.
Some say: both the afflictions (*kleśa*) and their residual impressions (*vāsanā*)—the two types of remainders—are exhausted.
Neither of these two positions is correct.

Within the first seven stages (*bhūmi*), one still experiences the residual traces of afflictions regarding the fragmented body; these are termed "residual habits" (*vāsanā*) precisely because they are not [actual] afflictions.

Following this sequence, in the present life, one is already within the body that constitutes the cause of suffering from retributive afflictions; since both the causes and effects of these two types of residue have been exhausted, it is the actualization of practice (*caryā-saṃpanna*).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "hearing the profound Dharma" to "constantly being able to practice," the commentary states:
"After this, both understanding and practice are cultivated together. Some say:
Because one can understand the profound, one has no doubt; because one can enter the profound, one has no fear.
This is not so, for entering is itself a form of understanding.

Because one can now believe in the profound teaching, one has no doubt; because one can understand the profound meaning, one has no fear. To advance in the cultivation of understanding is precisely this.
"Constantly practicing" refers to advancing in the practice of cultivation.
Because one must practice what is heard without interruption, it is said that one "constantly cultivates.
The Sūtra says, from "That which is Great Compassion" up to "there is nothing it does not cover and sustain. The commentary states:
Following this, the transformational practice is perfected.
"Profound and subtle" praises the depth and gravity of the [Buddha’s] mind.
"Nothing that is not covered or supported" praises the universality and vastness of his salvation.
It is not merely a matter of providing compassionate shelter; he also enables beings to transcend death, which is why it is said that he "supports" them.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, “The ultimate One Vehicle reaches the other shore,” the commentary says:
This is the fourth [section], on the extraordinary excellence of the accomplishment of virtues.
It has two parts:
First, the perfection of one's own virtues;
second, the perfection of transformative virtues.
Within the first, there are again two parts:
This first [section] is the excellence of the accumulation of merit.
It consists of three pairs;
this first pair is the pair of wisdom and abandonment.
The One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is itself wisdom; although there are three vehicles, their ultimate reality is non-dual, and thus it is called the One Vehicle. Some say:
within this One Vehicle, one exhaustively reaches the name "ultimate" and arrives at the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that one reaches the other shore.
No. If one were to exhaustively reach the One Vehicle up to nirvana, one would no longer be a bodhisattva.
Since one now attains faith and understanding at this ultimate limit, it is called "ultimate."
The "other shore" (pāra) is cessation; having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through the knowledge of cessation, it is called "reaching the other shore.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "decisively severing the net of doubt" to "encompassing all without exception," the commentary states:
this refers to the correspondence between the sequence [of practice], the principle, and the teaching.
Revealing reality in order to eliminate delusion, it is said that "the net of doubt is severed.
Since true understanding arises from the center, wisdom emerges from the mind; because "mind" carries the meaning of the central reality, this refers to the wisdom that realizes the principle.
Because it penetrates [reality] without remainder, it encompasses all things without exception; this is precisely what is meant by "penetrating the understanding of the teaching. Some say:
the wisdom that realizes selflessness does not come from without; therefore, this wisdom arises from the mind.
Knowing that the teachings manifest from the mind, one concludes that they encompass all things without exception.
Yet, this is still not exhaustive.

The wisdom of non-self arises through transformation from the Buddha and manifests upon the mind; since the teaching is not itself of the nature of the mind, it cannot be said to appear from the mind.
To know that the mind is substantially real within, and that there is nothing external remaining, is precisely the teaching on wisdom (*jñāna*).
As the Sūtra says, from "wisdom is like the great ocean" up to "it is like the Snowy Mountains," the commentary states:
following this, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are presented in contrast.
Because his wisdom is as deep and vast as the ocean, and his concentration is as lofty and supreme as a mountain;
because the function of his wisdom is luminous and pure, surpassing the sun and moon, and his concentration can fulfill all virtues like the Snowy Mountains.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, “Because it illuminates all merits as equal and pure,” the commentary explains:
Following this, there is the excellence of removing hindrances,
which is twofold:
This is the first part, the general heading.

Master Weishi states: "The following twenty phrases all distinguish the capacity of wisdom. However, since wisdom is never separate from meditative concentration, it is said that those who possess both concentration and wisdom are superior in overcoming obstacles.
There is not a single virtue that is not free from defilement; therefore, it is said to be "equally and purely one.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Just like the great earth" to "because it is undefiled," the commentary states:
this follows [the previous section] as a separate explanation.
There are three pairs:
first, the pair of cause and arising.

That is to say, the "different mind" is the cause of the two hindrances, being the defilement of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*); it gives rise, respectively, to the wisdom-hindrance and the affliction-hindrance through such mental attention.
Next is the pair of the supported and the support;
that is, the afflictions and the hindrances, which are respectively the supported and the support for the two obstacles of delusion and knowledge.
Finally is the pair of non-attachment and non-defilement.
That which exists within the three realms of existence is also an obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it is defiled solely by afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for the passage in the Sūtra from "Just as in the Mahāyāna" to "because of great compassion and so forth," the commentary states:
Second, the accomplishment of the virtue of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).
There are thirteen phrases, which can be briefly condensed into six pairs.
First is the pair of "leaving the mundane and entering the sacred," which refers to the first three [phrases].
"Vehicle" (yāna) means a chariot.
"Multitudes of beings" refers to ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles.
They are transported beyond the two deaths of the ordinary and the small by hearing the provisional and the real, whereby the sprouts of their goodness are nourished.
Second, the "counteraction of the heterodox and the pursuit of the wholesome" corresponds to the following two phrases.
Third, the pair of "universally covering" and "rarely seen," which refers to the following two lines.
Fourth, the pair of "subduing the heterodox" and "returning to the orthodox," which refers to the following two lines.
"Having nothing stored up" is because it is the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
5. The pair of being unsurpassed and being unstained refers to the following two lines:
because no virtue can surpass it, as it subdues all defilements.
6. The pair of fearlessness and compassion refers to the final two lines.
There is no evil to be feared, because there is no joy to be found in it.
The Sūtra says, from "destroying the mind of envy" up to "practicing the six points of harmonious respect. The commentary states:
This is the fifth [section], the progressive cultivation of practice.
There are two:
first, the cultivation of the basic level;
second, the cultivation of superior progress.
The first [section] also has two parts:
first, the practice of skillful means.
Subduing and destroying the mind of envy is the skillful means for benefiting others, for if one possesses envy and jealousy, one cannot benefit sentient beings.
Seeking the Dharma without satiety is the skillful means for one's own benefit, for those who possess a sense of satiety will certainly not progress in their practice.
Next is the diligent cultivation of correct practice;
that is, constant correct practice and the constant desire to extensively expound it, which constitutes the practice for benefiting others.
Because one cultivates the mind without weariness, there is a desire to explain it extensively; this refers to the excellence of the mind being explained.
"Beating the Dharma drum" and so forth refer to the excellence of what is explained.
"Shining the sun of wisdom" and so forth refer to the excellence of the benefit conferred.
The sun of the three types of wisdom shines in order to eliminate ignorance.
To cultivate the six points of concordant respect (*ṣaḍ-ānuśaṃsa*) is the practice for one's own benefit.

Because their cultivation of the three karmas, as well as their views and precepts, are all identical, they become mutually affectionate and respectful, with no discord in their feelings; hence it is called the "six points of concordant respect."
Regarding the passage from "constantly practicing the gift of Dharma" to "wandering through the various supernormal powers," the commentary states:
Second, the cultivation of superior progress.
This has three stages:
First, the beginning of superior progress:
this is the beginning of constantly practicing the gift of Dharma for the benefit of others, and the beginning of self-benefit through a courageous resolve that is not weak.
Second, the middle of superior progress.
Regarding "acting as a lamp, a field of merit, and so forth," this refers to the category of benefiting others.
Because they can produce understanding in sentient beings, they are called "Lamps Illuminating the World.
Because they also engender goodness in people, they are called "Supreme Fields of Merit."
Because they enlighten and transform others through wisdom, they are called "Guiding Teachers.
Because their benefit and merit are impartial, they harbor no partial affection.
To delight in the Path without either elation or dejection constitutes the aspect of self-benefit.
Because one cultivates goodness, it is called "delighting in the Way"; because one eliminates transgressions, there is "nothing remaining.
Subsequently, through superior progress, cultivation is perfected.

This constitutes the accomplishment of altruistic practices, such as uprooting the thorns of desire; by transforming others to leave behind faults, one brings peace to all beings, and by guiding them to follow what is good, one’s virtue becomes supreme and worthy of veneration.

The elimination of the three stains and so forth constitutes the perfection of one's own practice; because greed, hatred, and the like are eliminated, the perfection of the abandonment-practice is achieved; and because one sports with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the perfection of the qualities of practice is achieved.
Some say that the three stains are precisely afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*).
No. This is because karma and suffering are not necessarily defiled.
As for the passage in the Sūtra from "the power of causes and the power of conditions" up to "the powers of the various supernormal knowledges and clarities," the commentary states:
This is the sixth [perfection], the full endowment with the powers (*bala*).
It has three [aspects]:
this is the first, the full endowment with one's own power (*svabala*).
There are seven pairs:
first, the pair of causes and conditions, namely the power of the cause and the power of the condition.
Roots of goodness from previous lives are called the power of the cause; drawing near to virtuous friends and hearing the Dharma is called the power of the condition.
2. The pair of intention and aspiration (*chanda-adhimokṣa*), namely the power of intention (*cetanā-bala*) and the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*). Some say:
the mind that seeks Buddhahood is called the power of intention, while the aspiration that initiates practice is called the power of aspiration.
Some say that generating the bodhicitta is called the power of intention (*cetanā-bala*), while aspiring for the fruit of Buddhahood is called the power of vow (*praṇidhāna-bala*).
Both of these views are incorrect.
Because the seeking, the aspiration, and the undertaking of practice have one identical meaning, the arousal of the bodhicitta is itself the longing for the fruit of Buddhahood.

Accordingly, in their respective order: that which is now called "proper mental attention" (yoniśo-manasikāra) is termed the power of the mind; the seeking of the bodhicitta is termed the power of the vow.
Third, the combination of the general and the specific: "the power of skillful means" is the general, while "the power of constancy" and "the power of goodness" are the specific.
It is the power of constancy because one practices without interruption; it is the power of goodness because evil dharmas do not intervene.
Because these two powers involve skillful application (*prayoga-kauśalya*), they are called the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*).

Fourth, because the practice of *śamatha* is perfected, it is called the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*); because the practice of *vipaśyanā* is perfected, it is called the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
Fifth, the pair of hearing and practice: that is, the power of extensive learning is the understanding of cultivation, because the six perfections such as giving are what is to be practiced.

Sixth, the pair of mindfulness and concentration: that is, the mindfulness that dispels signs is the power of right mindfulness, because the removal of distraction and the realization of truth is the power of right observation.
There is an alternative version that reads, "Because of right concentration, cessation, and contemplation. Master Wei explains that cessation is concentration and contemplation is wisdom.
It should likely read "right contemplation" (*samyak-darśana*).

Seventh, the "combined clarity of the dual powers": this refers to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) as the power of spiritual penetration (*ṛddhibala*), and the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*) as the power of clarity (*vidyābala*).

Question:
Between cultivating the causes for the Pure Land and Tuṣita Heaven, which is more difficult? Answer:
Some say that Tuṣita is a realm (*dhātu*) while the Pure Land is not bound [to the realms], and therefore it is easier to be born in the Pure Land than in Tuṣita.
This is incorrect.
For what is called a "realm" is a place of saṃsāric transmigration, whereas the Western Pure Land is a place of transcendence.
The karma of cyclic existence is difficult to cultivate, whereas the causes for renunciation are easy to practice; [to claim otherwise] would surely contradict correct reasoning.
Some say that the virtuous masters of old who performed the karma for Tuṣita all refrained from doing so because they considered rebirth in the Western [Pure Land] difficult to achieve.
Now, seven points of meaning are used to prove that rebirth in the Western Land is easily attained:
first, because one practices for only a short time.
This is as stated in the *Contemplation Sutra*: "Those of the three lower grades, at the moment of death, shall all attain rebirth through even a single thought-moment or ten thought-moments."
Second, because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
this refers to the *Praise Sūtra* (*Candrapradīpa-sūtra*), which says, "The Buddhas of the six directions protect and remember [them]," and so forth.
Third, because they are embraced by light.
This is precisely what the *Contemplation Sūtra* means when it says, "The Buddha embraces and does not abandon those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of him.
Fourth, because they rely on the Buddha’s original vow; this refers to what this very sūtra describes as "the forty-eight great vows of Amitābha Buddha."
Fifth, because those sages come to welcome him.
This refers to what was stated in the preceding passage: "I vow that when I am born in my land, if they do not come to welcome me, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment."
Sixth, because all provide assistance through recitation.
This means that at the time of death, fellow practitioners assist one another in providing recitations to escort the deceased.
Seventh, because the Sages have taught that rebirth [in the Pure Land] is easy.
This text states: "It is easy to go there, yet no one does; that land is not opposed [to them].
Now, although this interpretation is indeed marvelous and supernatural, it is logically impossible, for Maitreya would not fail to have made a vow.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "confused and tumultuous" to "diligently suffering in urgent affairs," the Commentary states: Following this, there are four types of creating evil and receiving retributive suffering: 1. The suffering of being born into a lowly family; 2. The suffering of being born with a deficient physical form; 3. The suffering of encountering a wicked teacher; 4. The suffering of performing evil deeds and receiving their retribution. The first, the suffering of being born into a lowly family, refers to being born into families such as those of outcasts, hunters, fishermen, or those who serve the royal court. The second, the suffering of being born with a deficient physical form, refers to being born blind, deaf, mute, or deformed. The third, the suffering of encountering a wicked teacher, refers to associating with those who hold false views and who do not believe in cause and effect. The fourth, the suffering of performing evil deeds and receiving their retribution, refers to engaging in various unwholesome actions and subsequently undergoing their painful consequences. These are called the four sufferings of the present life. Furthermore, there are four sufferings of the future life: the suffering of falling into the hells, the suffering of being born as a hungry ghost, the suffering of being born as an animal, and the suffering of being born as a human with the five obstacles. These are collectively termed the eight great sufferings. Because one has committed evil in the past, one undergoes these retributions in the present and future. Thus, it is said that after death, one will fall into the three miserable realms and experience immeasurable suffering. This concludes the section on the four sufferings of the present life. According to these two sūtras, all world-systems possess both thirty-six heavens and thirty-three heavens;
although they are fundamentally one and the same, the differences arise from the distinct translators.

According to the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, there are twenty-six heavens: namely, the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ten Brahmā heavens, five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the four heavens of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*).

That verse says: "Having transcended the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as the celestial palaces of the Non-conceptualizers and so forth, the Buddha dwells in reliance upon the Ghanavyūha.

According to the *Mūlaprakṛti-sūtra*, there are twenty-eight heavens: namely, six in the realm of desire; four in each of the dhyāna stages; and one for the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa). This account does not mention the Non-conceptualizers (*asaṃjñin*), but instead includes the Great Tranquility (*mahāśubhakṛtsna*) heaven and the four formless (*ārūpya*) heavens.

According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are thirty-two heavens: namely, the six heavens of the desire realm; five in the first dhyāna; four each in the three higher dhyānas; five in the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens; and the four formless realms, as the Heaven of Non-conception is not mentioned.

In short, Zhi Qian’s original version was essentially the same as the *Avataṃsaka*; therefore, although it does not mention "non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñā*) or "great tranquility" (*mahāśānti*), it contains thirty-two [marks].
As for Bo Yan’s statement that there are thirty-six [levels], this is likely a corruption.
This can be verified by comparing his original draft with Bo Yan’s own scripture; for Bo Yan’s scripture contains many corruptions.
Although the Formless Heavens exist, they abide in dependence upon the Desire and Form Realms, as there is no separate location for them.
Now, I shall inquire only regarding the adornments up to those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Although there are Śuddhāvāsa deities, those who are *śamathacarita* (of a tranquil nature) and *anāgāmins* (non-returners) will certainly not be born in those pure lands.

Regarding the statement, "In these various stages, one gradually eliminates desire; though dwelling there, it is not the ultimate, and one soon returns to be born in Ghanavyūha," this is not contradictory, for that land of Ghanavyūha is the place where Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are born.

One may wonder: although Amitābha possesses great vows, among the myriad classes of sentient beings, is he truly able to guide and lead the devas and humans of the ten directions to be born in that land?
Therefore, it is said that they do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom.
Since Amitābha has realized the one true Dharma-realm, there is no virtue that is not perfected and no affliction that remains;
his merit is inexhaustible throughout all time, and he welcomes beings in accordance with his original vows. Thus, all sentient beings who possess the necessary conditions are born in that land.
One must not harbor such doubts within one's heart.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is called the inconceivable wisdom. Upon hearing the sutra state that "those with heavy karma of good and evil, or heavy merit and demerit, are drawn forward first," one may then doubt that reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha will necessarily lead to rebirth in that land. One might argue: "I have constantly committed various evils, and my evil intentions are deep and grave; how could a mere succession of ten recitations—a subtle goodness—be able to extinguish all such sins, allowing me to be reborn there and enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) from which there is never again regression?"
Therefore, it is said that one does not fully comprehend inconceivable wisdom.
This inconceivable wisdom possesses great majestic power, for it is not an object of discursive thought.
Have you not heard that a single-sided mirror reflects every image? How then could one doubt that the power of a single wisdom can eliminate all karmic obstacles?

Furthermore, just as even ten thousand catties of fine hair can be consumed by a small fire, so too does a single recitation of the Buddha's name—ten such recitations—individually eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. What cause for wonder, then, is there in being reborn in the Pure Land?
The Wisdom of Equality is called the Incomparable Wisdom.
There are those who, having heard of the Buddha’s wisdom, feel it to be remote from the Dharma, and harbor doubts, saying: "Names must necessarily be relative.
To name 'awakening' in dependence upon 'non-awakening'—what remoteness is there? By merely thinking of this, one will obtain great merit."
Now, to resolve this doubt, it is revealed that the Buddha possesses an ineffable wisdom.

The Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) realizes the principle of the two-fold emptiness; in this state, object and wisdom are equal, transcending all conceptual description. Yet, by using names to dispel names, one expresses this profound intent; for those who awaken to this intent, words vanish.
Since the object cannot be described, one may say that wisdom is also indescribable; because it is indescribable, the merit of one who recollects it is great.
For this reason, one should not harbor doubts or conceptual entanglements in the mind.
The wisdom of wondrous observation is called the "vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

There are those who hear of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and all attain rebirth there, yet they give rise to doubts, saying: "Although the Buddhas of the past and present are immeasurable, they have not exhausted the beings to be saved."
If a single Buddha were able to deliver all sentient beings, there should be no further need for other Buddhas to manifest and teach.
How then is it that those who recite the name of Amitābha Buddha are all reborn in his land?
Therefore, it is said that such a person does not understand the vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

The wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna) constantly contains both wisdom and compassion for all sentient beings; there are none among those with whom it has a connection who are not transported into nirvāṇa.

However, because sentient beings each have their own particular affinities, even when those with whom [a Buddha] is connected have been exhausted, those with whom he is not yet connected still remain; therefore, other Buddhas continue to appear in the world to bring about transformation and benefit.
It is with this intent that it is said: "By means of this mindfulness of the Buddha, all shall be born in the Pure Land.
That which is called "Accomplishment of What is to be Done" (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna) is the peerless, incomparable, supreme, and most excellent wisdom.
Some, hearing that the Tathāgata did not answer regarding the fourteen undeclared points, may doubt whether the Buddha is unable to know all phenomena universally.
Since it lacks superior function, what merit could mindfulness possess?
Therefore, it is said that it does not realize the peerless wisdom (*asama-jñāna*).

The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) universally takes the six sense objects as its object; because it is unlike that of ordinary beings, it is called "peerless" (*asama*).

Although he perceives the myriad objects of experience, he remains constantly in wondrous samādhi; unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles, whose entry into and emergence from concentration differ, he is thus called "peerless.

With the two obstacles entirely exhausted, he manifests transformative activity through the three karmas and provides the four types of prophetic answers—tasks that no other bodhisattvas are capable of performing—and is therefore called "supremely victorious."

Some say: "The True Dharma (Saddharma) of Śākyamuni lasted five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma) a thousand years, and the Final Dharma (Śeṣadharmakāla) ten thousand years; since all these have now passed, it is said that [the Dharma] has been extinguished."
It is said that although the Dharma has already perished, the Buddha, out of compassion and pity for suffering sentient beings, uniquely left this sutra behind to save them for a hundred years.
This is likely not the case.
Not only does such a claim contradict the teachings of the various sages, but the matter itself is also incomplete.

Now, according to the *Dharmasthitigāthā*, it is said: "At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the unsurpassed Dharma to sixteen great arhats and their retinues, commanding them to protect and uphold it so that it would not perish or disappear."
Furthermore, he commanded that his own person serve as a true field of merit for all donors, enabling those who give to obtain great rewards.
These were the sixteen great Arhats, such as Piṇḍola-bharadvāja and others, who protect and uphold the True Dharma and bring benefit to sentient beings.

When the lifespan of the people here in Jambudvīpa reaches its extreme minimum of ten years, the kalpa of weapons will arise and they will slaughter one another; at that time, the Buddha-dharma shall temporarily perish.

After the kalpa of weapons, the human lifespan gradually increases until it reaches the stage of one hundred years; at that time, the people of this continent, weary of the suffering and harm caused by the previous kalpa of weapons, again delight in practicing virtue.

At that time, these sixteen great arhats, together with their retinues, returned once more to the human realm to proclaim and expound the unsurpassed True Dharma; they delivered immeasurable multitudes by causing them to leave the household life and performed deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings.

In this manner, it continues until the time when the human lifespan on this continent reaches sixty thousand years; at that time, the unsurpassed True Dharma will circulate in the world, flourishing and never ceasing.
Later, when the human lifespan reaches seventy thousand years, the unsurpassed True Dharma will finally perish forever.

At that time, these sixteen great arhats, together with their retinues, assembled here on this continent; by means of their supernormal powers, they constructed stūpas made of the seven precious jewels—magnificent, lofty, and vast—and collected all the remains of the body of Śākyamuni Tathāgata within them.

At that time, the sixteen great arhats, together with their retinues, circumambulated the stūpa, making offerings of incense and flowers, and paid homage and praise while circling it hundreds of thousands of times.
Having gazed upon and paid homage, they all ascended into the air and, facing the stūpa, spoke these words:
"We pay respectful homage to the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Having received these instructions, I have protected and upheld the True Dharma and brought benefit to devas and humans.
Now that the treasury of the Dharma has vanished and my karmic conditions have been fulfilled, I take my leave to enter parinirvāṇa.
Having spoken these words, they simultaneously entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Through the power of their prior vows and meditative concentration, a fire arose and consumed their bodies; like the extinguishing of a lamp’s flame, not even a trace of bone remained.
At that moment, the stūpa sank into the earth and came to rest only upon reaching the level of the golden wheel.
Thereupon, the unsurpassed True Dharma of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni was forever extinguished and no longer appeared within this trichiliocosm.

Immediately following this, seventy billion pratyekabuddhas appeared simultaneously within this buddha-field; when the lifespan of humans reached eighty thousand years, the assembly of pratyekabuddha sages all vanished, after which Maitreya Tathāgata appeared in the world.

Judging from this, it is only when the human lifespan reaches seventy thousand years that the unsurpassed True Dharma will finally and eternally perish; therefore, it is said that the Way of the Sūtras is extinguished.
When the sixteen Great Sages entered parinirvāṇa, their stūpas immediately sank into the earth.

The *Wuliangshou jing lianyi shuwen zan*, Scroll Lower, concludes. Alas! How few commentaries exist for this sutra, yet it remains as if the Buddha himself were adorned with exquisite ornaments.
Adorned with various rare and exquisite jewels, and decorated with intricate ornaments,
hundreds of thousands of them were scattered and displayed outside;
thus, the virtue of the Buddha becomes all the more worthy of veneration.
Furthermore, the faith of the multitude of living beings has its roots made even firmer.
This sutra is profound and subtle; it is difficult to fathom and understand.
Nevertheless, this commentary is provided to assist it.

Furthermore, among the great observers of the world,

The Great Master has reached the pinnacle of craftsmanship in this work;

I had previously worried that this scripture would not circulate far.
